items.title: Threat actors use agentic AI tooling to find and abuse exposed secrets
items.summary: In this article From exposed secrets to cloud compromise Follow-on actions Mitigating application credential abuse activity Defending against agentic AI attacks Microsoft detections Advanced hunting queries Microsoft Threat Intelligence has observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, including credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services. These threat actors can then use the secrets for further malicious activity against the compromised organization. Searching open code repositories for exposed credentials, secrets, keys, and other authentication material is a well-documented technique that has historically been limited by the time required for human operators to find code repositories, review the data in the repositories, and leverage authentication material for further action. However, agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain. In at least one case, Microsoft observed an AI agent advance from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. Microsoft has also investigated follow-on activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials. As early as October 28, 2026, Microsoft began observing successful service principal sign-ins from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84 involving multiple application IDs across some impacted customers, including cases where a multitenant application credential was compromised at the source (vendor-owned application) and used to access multiple downstream tenants. The threat actor used the compromised credentials for cloud resource discovery, and credential and data exfiltration, including from Azure Key Vaults and Storage Accounts, and abuse of Azure AI services consistent with the activity described above. Additionally, Microsoft observed malicious activity originating from two IP addresses potentially associated with this campaign. We identified malicious operations from 65.87.223[.]26, including indications of vulnerability exploitation by embedded shell commands in a user agent and attempts to obtain App Service authentication tokens. A similar campaign involving the same IPs addressed was also reported by Todyl . Separately, Microsoft observed reconnaissance operations from 157.22.126[.]128 targeting AI workloads deployed by victims on Azure AI services. Microsoft encourages organizations to scan their code in GitHub and determine where any secrets are present. In addition to removing the secrets from the code base, affected organizations should immediately rotate any exposed keys or credentials. GitHub monitors public repositories by automatically scanning for secrets. In addition to scanning their own repositories, organizations can enable public monitoring through GitHub to detect secrets leaked in secondary public repositories across GitHub. This extends secret scanning beyond the repositories an enterprise owns to follow potential secret exposure across the platform. GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps scans for credentials and other sensitive content in source code. Push protection can also block supported secrets before they’re pushed. Organizations need either GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps or, for organizations using the standalone experience, GitHub Secret Protection for Azure DevOps enabled. Secrets are exposed in public repositories when code containing the secret is committed to GitHub. Developers might store secrets in configuration files, scripts, or other code to quickly operationalize the OAuth application or avoid configuring more modern authentication flows. Organizations can reduce exposure by protecting workload identities and secrets, enforcing least privilege, safeguarding recovery resources, and enabling relevant Microsoft Defender for Cloud protections. Publicly exposed credentials remain usable until revoked or rotated; removing the original disclosure alone does not remediate the exposure. Microsoft recommends that developers migrate OAuth applications away from secret-based authentication . While storing long-lived application client secrets in code is a common practice, using managed identities for application authentication eliminates the possibility of secret exposure in code, manual processes associated with secret management, and barriers to securely scaling applications. This activity illustrates an ongoing trend of threat actors accelerating all stages of the attack chain with agentic AI penetration testing frameworks, including ARTEX. As these capabilities evolve, defenders must similarly use AI to investigate and respond across large environments. From exposed secrets to cloud compromise Starting in August 2026, Microsoft observed threat actors using an agentic AI offensive framework to submit large volumes of queries to GitHub for secrets. The queries submitted by the AI framework often included the name of a target organization, keywords for secrets, a keyword linked to cloud services, or a keyword linked to another AI service provider. Organizations that find their secrets exposed in public repositories must assume that the exposed secrets and associated applications are compromised. Follow-on actions Credential abuse via Entra ID In one follow-on attack that began as early as October 28, 2026, an agentic framework used valid leaked or stolen application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-ins primarily came from two IP addresses: 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. The latter IP address is a Tor exit node, which might be associated with unrelated malicious activity, including from unrelated sources. The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants.. Service principals are the identities that applications use to authenticate and give direct, programmatic access to whatever the application is authorized to reach. The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access. In some tenants, the threat actor sent Microsoft Graph API requests, which were mostly searches to find content of interest. The threat actor enumerated subscriptions, resource groups, permissions, AI model deployments, and service configurations in Azure to map the environment. Additionally, the threat actor attempted to validate stolen Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, as identified using Defender for Cloud’s AI threat protection. Observed activity suggests that the threat actor might have attempted to abuse some of these compromised AI resources to facilitate their broader attack activity. Figure 1. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) observed across the credential abuse attack chain Cloud API adjustments indicative of adaptive behavior Additionally in this attack the agent’s operations on a victim’s Azure Resource Manager (ARM) instance originating from 199.19.77[.]84 demonstrated sequences consistent with adaptive troubleshooting, where failed cloud API requests were followed by changes to HTTP methods or API versions and subsequent HTTP 200 responses: A batch of ARM requests attempting to enumerate secret metadata across multiple Azure Key Vault resources returned HTTP 400 (Bad Request). These requests specified a version associated with Key Vault’s data-plane APIs against ARM (control-plane) APIs. Approximately 28 seconds after the first failed response, a batch rerun began against the same vault resource paths using the ARM API version 2023-07-01 and returned HTTP 200. A GET request to enumerate an Azure SQL server’s firewall rules specified an outdated API version and returned HTTP 400. Approximately 60 seconds after that request, a matching GET began using a supported version and subsequently returned HTTP 200. The URL changed only in its api-version parameter. An ARM POST request to an Application Insights query endpoint returned HTTP 400 because an outdated API version was specified. Approximately 80 seconds after the failed request, another POST began against the same endpoint, specifying a supported API version, and subsequently returned HTTP 200. OAuth application abuse In multiple cases, Microsoft observed the same agentic AI tools subsequently obtain a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In some cases, the agents exfiltrated secrets from the organization’s Azure Key Vault. The agents once authenticated have also searched Azure DevOps for secrets. Until the secrets are revoked or rotated, they can allow a threat actor to maintain persistence in the organization, compromise additional identities, or hijack resources. In one observed case, an AI agent progressed from searching for the client secrets in GitHub to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes. The agents also used the compromised OAuth application to use the Run Command , which runs scripts in Azure VMs. With access to this functionality on a VM, a threat actor can access unsecured credentials and other stored data, compromise associated workload identities, or run code that provides persistence or lateral movement. During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services). Multiple public reports have documented threat actors using agentic AI tools to compromise credentials for AI services, sometimes to run the same agentic AI workflow. Mitigating application credential abuse activity Microsoft recommends the following mitigation steps to contain, detect, and investigate this threat. Containment Block 199.19.77[.]84/32 as a named location in a Conditional Access policy targeting workload identities, assigned directly to service principals, and in a user-scoped block policy to cover replayed sessions. Note that workload identity policies require Workload ID Premium licensing and cover only single-tenant apps registered in your tenant. Block the exact IP rather than the whole ASN. For affected users, revoke Entra sessions, Azure DevOps PATs and SSH keys. For any affected application, remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials, including those added by the threat actor and disable the service principal if needed. Tokens already issued remain valid until expiry. Rotate everything stored in any Key Vault the affected application could read, and any credentials found in accessed documents. MSPs: Review Partner Center access, GDAP relationships, and customer tenants, and notify affected customers per your agreements. Detection and hunting Review Entra service principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18 including failed attempts. Sign-in errors AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS7000222 (expired secret) indicate someone holds a credential for your app; a failure followed by a success is urgent. Review Azure Activity, Key Vault and Storage diagnostics, Entra audit, Azure DevOps audit and Microsoft 365 unified audit logs for the address, including secret reads, blob and file downloads, and changes to apps, permissions or pipelines. In Azure DevOps auditing, review PAT creation and first use, federated service connections, pipeline runs and edits, and unfamiliar user agents. Enable auditing if it is off. Look for behavior as well as the IP: one address authenticating to three or more service principals with mixed success, or one app requesting tokens across Azure Resource Manager, Key Vault, Storage and Graph in a short window. Search as far back as retention allows. Defending against agentic AI attacks Threat actors can and do change the source IP address, user agent strings, and other fingerprints left by the agentic AI penetration testing tools they use. This can make identifying and blocking malicious network traffic early difficult for defenders. Several behavioral signals can help organizations determine that they are being targeted by threat actors using agentic AI. Agentic AI frameworks scanning a target send a wide variety of requests in a brief time and retry variations on the same technique or move on to next-stage actions at machine speed. Agentic AI frameworks use existing penetration testing tools. For example, ARTEX by default uses Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients, Norma SDK WebFetch, and headless Chromium through Playwright, among others. These tools may send network traffic with distinctive characteristics, such as default user agent strings. While blocking network traffic with these characteristics will not stop an attack by an AI agent, which will quickly change them, identifying them can alert defenders to the activity. Defensive honeypots , decoys, tarpits, and fake wins can pull autonomous AI attacks away from legitimate targets. Honeypots and decoy surfaces such as Microsoft Sentinel Deception give the agent attractive but worthless targets to pursue. Tarpits consume the agent’s time and budget. Fake wins present convincing evidence that the agent’s objective is complete, which can cause it to stop on a false success. In Microsoft’s testing, these controls helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets and produced high-confidence, attribution-quality signal. Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat. Protect and continuously assess application credentials and secrets. Avoid storing service principal credentials, storage keys, connection strings, and other secrets in source code, configuration files, public repositories, issues, or other locations where they might be inadvertently exposed. To find credentials in source code, consider using tools like GitHub Advanced Security or other OWASP source code analysis tools . Rotate compromised or exposed credentials immediately and establish credential lifecycle practices. Treat credentials that have been publicly exposed as compromised, even if the original location has subsequently been edited or deleted. Removing the content does not invalidate the credential or eliminate copies retained in edit history, caches, archives, logs, or other systems. Immediately revoke or rotate the affected credentials and investigate their historical use. Where supported, organizations should favor mechanisms that reduce reliance on long-lived credentials. Learn more about protecting secrets with Defender for Cloud . Enable appropriate Microsoft Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads. Consider enabling workload protections relevant to the resources in your environment, including Defender for Resource Manager, Defender for Storage, Defender for Key Vault, Defender for App Service, and Defender for Databases. Learn more in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud overview . Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities. Review the Azure role-based access control (RBAC) permissions assigned to service principals and restrict their privileges to the resources and operations required by their applications. Learn more about best practices for Azure RBAC . Protect backup and recovery infrastructure as part of resilience. Restrict access to backup and recovery resources and closely monitor attempts to modify or remove their protection controls. Learn more about Azure Backup security best practices . Hardening OAuth applications against compromise involves managing the permissions of the applications in your organization and securing application secrets. To triage applications in your environment, enforce security policies with new applications as they are created, and address existing applications over time beginning with the most recent ones. Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The Cloud app catalog page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this. Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate. Use Conditional Access policies for workload identities . Consider augmenting identity signals with workload identity risk protection . Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the application developer role to privileged users. Review the list of least privileged roles by task to help scope role-based access control in your environment. Integrate enterprise applications with Microsoft Entra ID . Microsoft detections Microsoft Defender and Microsoft Sentinel customers can refer to the list of applicable detections below. Microsoft Defender coordinates detection, prevention, investigation, and response across endpoints, identities, email, and apps to provide integrated protection against attacks like the threat discussed in this blog. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender and Sentinel coverage Initial access Multiple identity-protection alerts identified authentication attempts from anonymized or high-risk infrastructure. This pattern can indicate attempted access through proxy, VPN, or previously reported malicious network sources. Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Anonymous IP address Initial access Attack-analysis detections identified OAuth application activity consistent with compromise. This type of detection is useful when evaluating whether an app identity, rather than only a user identity, may have been abused. Microsoft Defender XDR – Potentially compromised OAuth application identified through attack activity analysis Initial access, Discovery Unattributed network indicators related to ARTEX use are flagged by Microsoft Threat Intelligence research and surfaced across multiple alerts. Suspected ARTEX use can include activity beyond the GitHub repository scanning activity discussed in this blog. Microsoft Sentinel – Abnormal Deny Rate for Source IP – Abnormal Port to Protocol – Inbound Network Attack detected – Malformed user agent – Password spray attack against Azure AD application Microsoft Defender XDR – Account compromised following a password-spray attack – Anomalous OAuth device code authentication activity – Multiple Service Principal Sign-ins from Single IP – Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP address Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps – Activities from suspicious user agents – Multiple failed login attempts – Multiple failed user log on attempts to an app – OAuth application activity from an uncommonly visited ISP – Suspicious OAuth app registration Microsoft Defender for Cloud – Key vault unusual access denied – user/application accessing high volume of denied key vaults – Access from an unusual location to a sensitive blob container – Azure Resource Manager operation from suspicious IP address Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Atypical travelMalicious IP addressPassword Spray – Verified threat actor IP Credential access Identity-protection detections observed password spray behavior. This indicates repeated authentication attempts across accounts or tenants using a common source pattern. Microsoft Entra ID Protection – Password spray Microsoft Defender for Identity – Suspicious service principal sign-in following credential addition Credential access Azure Key Vault access Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Defender for Key Vault) – Unusual operation pattern in a key vault – High volume of operations in a key vault – Unusual application accessed a key vault – Suspicious secret listing and query in a key vault – Unusual access to the key vault from a suspicious IP (Non-Microsoft or External) Command and control Suspicious Microsoft Graph API usage was observed from campaign infrastructure. The activity involved Graph requests that can support discovery, collection, or follow-on cloud operations. Microsoft Defender for Identity – Suspicious Entra Graph API query observed Advanced hunting queries The following hunting queries are related to the October 28 Entra ID service principal sign-in activity. Find successful and failed application sign-ins from the suspicious IP addresses let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, Application, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalName, ServicePrincipalId, ResourceDisplayName, ResourceId, ResourceTenantId, IPAddress, ErrorCode, UserAgent, CorrelationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc Find Microsoft Graph API requests from the two IP addresses, including searches and response status let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); GraphAPIAuditEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IpAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, TenantId, ApplicationId, ServicePrincipalId, AccountObjectId, IpAddress, RequestMethod, RequestUri, ResponseStatusCode, ResponseSize, Scopes, EntityType, TargetWorkload, UniqueTokenIdentifier, ClientRequestId, OperationId, RequestId | order by Timestamp asc Find available Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Azure cloud activity details from the suspicious IP addresses let startTime = datetime(2026-10-28T00:00:00Z); let endTime = now(); CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp between (startTime .. endTime) | where IPAddress in ("199.19.77.84") | project Timestamp, Application, CloudAppId = ApplicationId, ActionType, ActivityType, AccountType, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, UserAgent, ObjectName, ObjectType, ObjectId, ActivityObjects, ReportId, RawEventData | order by Timestamp asc CloudAuditEvents table to identify suspicious controlplane operations CloudAuditEvents | where IPAddress has_any ('199.19.77.84','65.87.223.26') CloudStorageEvents table to identify possible exfiltration from Storage Accounts. CloudStorageAggregatedEvents | where IPAddress in ('199.19.77.84','65.87.223.26') | where SuccessfulOperationsCount > 0 Microsoft Security Copilot Microsoft Security Copilot is embedded in Microsoft Defender and provides security teams with AI-powered capabilities to summarize incidents, analyze files and scripts, summarize identities, use guided responses, and generate device summaries, hunting queries, and incident reports. Customers can also deploy AI agents , including the following Microsoft Security Copilot agents , to perform security tasks efficiently: Threat Intelligence Briefing agent Phishing Triage agent Threat Hunting agent Dynamic Threat Detection agent Security Copilot is also available as a standalone experience where customers can perform specific security-related tasks, such as incident investigation, user analysis, and vulnerability impact assessment. In addition, Security Copilot offers developer scenarios that allow customers to build, test, publish, and integrate AI agents and plugins to meet unique security needs. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft Defender XDR customers can use threat analytics reports in the Defender portal (requires license for at least one Defender XDR product) to get the most up-to-date information about the activity and techniques discussed in this blog. These reports provide intelligence, protection information, and recommended actions to prevent, mitigate, or respond to associated threats found in customer environments. Activity Profile: Stolen application credentials used to sign in as Entra ID workload identities and access Azure, Microsoft 365 resources Microsoft Security Copilot customers can also use the Microsoft Security Copilot integration in Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence, either in the Security Copilot standalone portal or in the embedded experience in the Microsoft Defender portal to get more information about this threat. Learn more For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog . To get notified about new publications and to join discussions on social media, follow us on LinkedIn , X (formerly Twitter) , and Bluesky . To hear stories and insights from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community about the ever-evolving threat landscape, listen to the Microsoft Threat Intelligence podcast .

  • Identify and catalog applications running in your cloud environment. The Cloud app catalog page in Defender for Cloud Apps is one service that can help accomplish this.
  • Use Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps Cloud Discovery tools to identify unmanaged apps, and prioritize the most frequently used apps to migrate and integrate.
  • Use Conditional Access policies for workload identities. Consider augmenting identity signals with workload identity risk protection.
  • Set permission restrictions to limit who can create an application in the tenant. This can be achieved by setting the ability for users to register apps to “No” and limiting the application developer role to privileged users. Review the list of least privileged roles by task to help scope role-based access control in your environment.
  • Integrate enterprise applications with Microsoft Entra ID.

State of the Broker: October 2026
items.summary: October was the first full month of the Agentic Identity Broker as an open-source project. The team spent the first half of it hardening what we had published on 15 September, and the second half adding the features that people asked for once they connected the broker to real third-party services. Along the way, three people landed their first commits, and we moved most of our spec-driven workflow onto GitHub. This is the first post of a monthly series. Each month, I want to write down what changed in the broker, how the project numbers moved, who wrote about it, what got in the way and what we look at next. If you are new to the broker, my retrospective on building it with coding agents explains what it does and why we built it. Hardening what we released # The first two weeks of October were mostly security fixes, some of them for findings from dependency and code scanners ( #192 , #272 ) as well as agentic security assessments using Claude Mythos 5.1 and OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue. I made the broker reject wildcard CORS origins ( #170 ), redact rejected PostgreSQL connection URLs from its logs ( #167 ) and limit where its admin API is reachable ( #155 ). I also restricted the TLS bypass for the key management service to explicit development setups ( #168 ) and closed a server-side request forgery (SSRF) bypass in the fetcher for Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) in production ( #169 ). The second theme was observability. I taught the broker to classify why it denies a grant authorization ( #197 ) and to record grant lifecycle changes in its audit log ( #201 ). My refactoring of the classification contract had a side effect: it dropped audit fields from the Open Policy Agent (OPA) integration, and we had to restore them a few days later ( #219 ). Connecting more third-party services # Most new features that arrived in October make it easier to connect the broker to OAuth 2.0 services that we don’t control. The team added discovery of OAuth 2.0 protected resources for third-party services ( #191 ), so an operator no longer has to list every protected resource by hand. We also made it possible to supply a trust anchor’s public keys inline or from a file ( #221 ) instead of fetching them from a JSON Web Key Set (JWKS) URL. I added filesystem credential sources ( #183 ), so client secrets for third-party services can come from mounted files. CIMD clients can now authenticate with private_key_jwt ( #237 ), which unblocks ChatGPT as a client ( #220 ). A token exchange can now expect a different audience in its client assertion ( #283 ). We also added public outbound CIMD clients ( #280 ) and allowlisted private-use redirect URIs for agents ( #273 ). For people running the broker in Kubernetes, the Helm chart can now deploy extra manifests ( #254 ) and schedule the job that sweeps expired sessions, and the broker reports session health metrics ( #247 ). Keeping users logged in to third-party services # The most visible problem in October was that users lost their third-party sessions too often. When a provider session ends, the user has to go back to the consent screen before the agent can use that service again. We attacked this from several sides. I reduced unnecessary session logouts ( #218 ) and fixed how the broker asks for consent again when a refresh fails ( #200 ). We specified proactive token refresh ( #196 ), and I added regression tests for it ( #217 ). At the end of the month, we made the broker stop refreshing a refresh token that the provider has already rejected with invalid_grant ( #271 ), and the session card in the UI now offers a new login only when the session can no longer be renewed ( #300 ). We internally observed a drastic decline of users reporting lost sessions after these fixes. Running Spec Kit on GitHub # We build the broker spec-first with Spec Kit , and until October that workflow ran in each maintainer’s local agent harness. In October, we moved it onto GitHub. Since #238 , GitHub Agentic Workflows run the Spec Kit phases (specify, plan, implement) with the Pi coding agent, and maintainers steer them with slash commands in pull requests ( #295 ). A maintainer now signs off on a decision with a single 👍 ( #315 ), and each pull request gets one status comment instead of a wall of them ( #317 ). On 30 October, we also added a grumpy reviewer, a workflow that answers questions about the repository, and an architecture review agent that only a maintainer can start ( #326 , #327 , #328 ). Getting there took quite some iterations. In October, the workflows filed 9 issues about their own failed or incomplete runs, and we merged 8 fixes for phase handoffs, feature selection and the sandbox of the implement phase. We also changed our constitution twice: version 4.1.0 keeps each feature within its scope and defers unrelated findings ( #228 ), and version 4.2.0 requires concrete examples in every feature spec ( #229 ). Thank you, new contributors # Three people landed their first commits in October. Santhosh K ( @x418 ) made the Helm chart deploy extra manifests ( #254 ), scheduled the session sweep from the chart with session health metrics ( #247 ) and fixed several session and token endpoint issues, such as refreshing tokens that a provider had already rejected ( #271 ). João Santos ( @jmcs ) added private_key_jwt authentication for CIMD clients ( #237 ). XY ( @XY-code1 ) picked up a good first issue and added the client assertion audience for token exchange ( #283 ). Thank you! The month in numbers # Measure October 2026 Commits on main 93 , of which 12 from Dependabot Pull requests opened / merged 139 / 95 Issues opened / closed 33 / 15 Releases 60 , from v0.1.69 to v0.1.128 People with commits 7 , of them 3 for the first time Stars 34 on 30 October, from 27 on 1 October Forks 5 on 30 October The broker publishes a release for almost every merge to main , so the release count says more about our merge rate than about features. The two of us who maintain the broker still wrote most of the commits: 67 of 93, 35 of them mine. Who wrote about the broker # Alejandro Saucedo published the second part of his series on agent security and identity on 4 October. He runs the broker on a local Kubernetes cluster with his Kubernetes Agent Orchestration System (KAOS) and walks through allowed and denied requests for two users and two agents. HackerNoon republished part 1 on 21 October and part 2 on 23 October. The KAOS documentation also lists the broker as one of three agent identity issuers. On 9 October, Mike Moore from Solo.io, the company that created agentgateway, published a guide to token exchange in agentgateway with a case study on the broker. He points out that our gateway guide used the broker’s own external processing sidecar instead of agentgateway’s native oauthTokenExchange policy. That was true at the time, and we documented the native policy at the start of November ( #275 ). What we look at next # Our biggest topic right now is moving beyond on-behalf-of cases. Today, the broker assumes that a person delegates to an agent, and we also want to support headless agents that a machine invokes without a human in the loop. Along with that, we want the broker to take part in more authorization decisions. One issue proposes an AuthZEN Access Evaluation endpoint , so that policy engines can ask the broker about delegations in a standard format, and I opened an issue for a pluggable interface to an external decision model that could help with removing UX friction from tool approvals. For the people who delegate, we plan an activity and audit ledger. It will power the activity UI that I proposed as well as other auditing interfaces. In the same area, we are revisiting the granularity of the consent screen and want incremental authorization with per-service virtual scopes for MCP step-up, which would also fix an existing re-authentication loop with optional services. We are also working on the repository itself. Now that Spec Kit runs on GitHub, we continue making the repository easier for agents to work in and add more agentic support for maintaining it. If you run the broker and something gets in your way, please open an issue . In October, people outside the maintainers asked for client_secret_basic on the token endpoint ( #314 ) and for Google scope hierarchies in token exchange ( #313 ), and I’d like to cover more of these requests in next month’s post.

items.title: “I Don’t Need a SIEM, I Have Ollama!” (Yes, You Do!)
items.summary: Warning : this blog is an experiment. The idea for a blog came from a real conversation I had with somebody. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Opus 5.5 performed a peer review, and tore some parts to shreds. Then rewrote them. And then I very lightly edited it, and tuned a few jokes. I replaced a food fight joke with a pillow fight joke, specifically. Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise! — A security peer recently shared a proposal they had just heard in the wild: instead of paying for a SIEM, why not load several days of raw log data into a locally run open-weights model, ask it “what looks risky?”, and review whatever the model highlights? No SIEM ingest tax! No cloud token bills! No SIEM license fees! No writing correlation rules! No tuning anomaly detection! Just a gaming GPU under a desk and pure, artisanal AI-native vibes. Ahhh, magic! Gemini illustration Wait. Really? My first instinct, forged by 24 years of staring at logs since I first met a SIM in January 2002, was to laugh, pour a drink, and move on. Surely everyone knows this is a terrible idea, right? Right?! Wrong. If an engineer, an IT director, or a cost-cutting CFO pitches “local LLM as a poor man’s SIEM” in your organization, you cannot just roll your eyes and mutter “hallucinations.” People keep inventing this idea for real reasons. SIEM ingest pricing still hurts: some vendor cost explainer works out 5 TB per day at $2 to $4 per GB as $3.6 to $7.3 million a year on ingestion alone. Detection engineering is still hard work. And yes the AI hype machine has spent two years promising executives that models can “reason over any unstructured data.” So let’s dissect why dumping a week of raw logs into a local model breaks four basic laws of “operational physics”, and then carve out the narrow 10% where a local model does help with logs. The short version fits on a sticker: the LLM writes the parser, it never runs as the parser. And the twist is that the problem here is “raw,” not “local.” Token Arithmetic and Naive Chunking (Or: How Big Do You Think 7 Days of Logs Is?!) Let’s start with grade-school arithmetic, because clearly nobody pitching this architecture has ever opened a calculator… Forget the enterprise. Take a tiny environment, a single server rack generating a measly 1 GB of raw text logs per day. Seven days of logs is 7 GB of text, or roughly 1.75 billion tokens at 4 characters per token. That is generous, since IP addresses, GUIDs and hex strings tokenize worse than English (Wow, really? Yes, really — at least Claude thinks so! He would know, right?) Now look at that “free” 8B or 70B parameter model on your GPU workstation. Its usable context window, before the KV cache devours your VRAM and the fans sound like a Boeing 747 on takeoff, is maybe 32K to 128K tokens. You are shoving 1.75 billion tokens through a 128K keyhole, which is about 13,700 full context windows. Painful enough yet? Well, it gets worse. Assume your box reads a generous 2,000 tokens per second (benchmark your own, I’ll wait). Reading those 1.75 billion tokens takes about 10 days. You need 10 days to read 7 days of logs, so you never catch up! Scale that to the 5 TB per day example above and it is about 20 years of GPU time for each day of logs. Hilarity ensues! Replacing a deterministic stream processor with a token-by-token text predictor is like replacing your municipal water pipes with a guy carrying a silver espresso spoon from a well 10 miles away. “Fine, Anton,” the DIY enthusiast says, “we’ll chunk the logs into 2,000-line batches and loop the local model over them all weekend!” Or we will get a bigger boat… eh… server rack to run the model. Chunking naively, by just loading the data in batches, fails hilariously. Here is how: Attack chains get cut. The phish on Tuesday lands in one batch, the lateral movement on Thursday lands thousands of batches later, and no prompt ever sees both. Each batch gets judged alone. Merging the summaries does not bring the signal back. By the time you summarize the summaries, the one quiet line was already dropped in round one. So “naive+” fails as well. Position inside the batch matters. Liu et al.’s “Lost in the Middle” found that models do best when the relevant information sits at the start or end of a long context and degrade sharply in the middle. They tested question answering and key-value retrieval, not logs, but picture a quiet privilege escalation on line 1,482 of your batch. Worst seat in the house. Researchers keep running into this. Cai, Ryan and Karie note that iterative approach is limited by context capacity and that map-reduce style summarization is computationally heavy (and requires some luck). Even so, that is a proof of concept on up to 20,000 rows per dataset, and they say enterprise volumes remain to be validated. So smarter chunking exists (reminder: it is not magic, in this area nothing truly is): parse, cluster, then retrieve by entity and time. At that point you are building the first half of a SIEM. Congratulations! As I wrote in The Ancient Art of SIEM , cost pain is eternal and only the currency changes. In 2003 you ran out of hardware, in 2015 you ran out of cloud budget, and in 2026 you run out of tokens and VRAM. The Input-Centric Time Machine: Back to 2002 Batch Review Notice the most revealing phrase in this idea: “load 1 to 7 days of log data… and then review what the model highlights.” That is not real-time detection. That is batch-mode log archeology! When intruders can go from initial access to data theft in hours (soon: minutes for some incidents), reviewing a week of logs in a batch means you are running a weekly book club about how you got breached last Wednesday. But hey … is your SIEM faster? Well, it should be! Worse, asking an LLM to “highlight what looks risky” violates the most important lesson of two decades of detection engineering. In Output-driven SIEM, 13 years later , I revisited my favorite 2011 mental model: think about what you want to see at the output before you collect, and AI does not change this. Asking a model to “find risk” in raw logs with zero detection engineering is the ultimate input-centric anti-pattern . It failed with ML in mid-2010s, and LLM is not different (in this regard). Now, about determinism. The lazy objection is “the answers change on every run,” and a sharp engineer will reply “so pin the seed.” Fair enough! Run-to-run randomness is an engineering problem: Thinking Machines got 80 unique completions out of 1,000 at temperature 0, then 1,000 identical ones after fixing their kernels. But is it actually bad? Maybe if you run 5 times, you will find 2x more “fun” things. But hey … also probably at least 5x more noise. The harder test is stability. Take the same 48 hours of domain controller logs, shuffle the order or change one irrelevant line, and run it again. Given what we learned, I would bet real money the verdict moves. Well-crafted SIEM rule does not care what order the lines arrive in. Zero Local Context Equals Hallucinated Risk Why can’t a local model tell an active nation-state intrusion from Tuesday’s messy IT administration? Because raw logs do not contain your organizational reality! Shocking, eh? A raw syslog or CloudTrail line says that svc_deploy_04 logged into prod-db-02 at 3:14 AM from an internal jump host and ran an encoded PowerShell script. Is that a five-alarm breach or the legacy billing batch job that Bob in accounting wrote in 2017 and nobody dares to touch? This is a dated example, on purpose. Insert your own fun example involving a shadow AI agent! In Part 3 of the Stop Building a 2003 SOC series , I argued that the #1 reason AI fails in the SOC is the absence of Context as Code : machine-readable, owned, and expiring knowledge of your assets, business processes, and weird administrative exceptions. In Part 2 , we warned about automation bias: humans reviewing plausible, well-written machine verdicts approve them. Also, the test from Can AI Let You Jump SOC Maturity Levels? applies here: does this exist because someone had to spend time, or because someone had to learn something about us? Writing a parser is a time cost. Knowing about Bob’s job is a learning cost, and no model downloaded from the internet has paid it. Feed raw logs into a naked local LLM with no CMDB enrichment, no threat intel, no identity graph, and no 90-day baseline, and its only source of “context” is its pre-trained weights. So it flags every scary-looking word (ERROR, DENIED, admin, root, failed) and writes you a convincing fictional thriller about your own network. The Confused Deputy Trap: When the Attacker Prompts Your “SIEM” via User-Agent Now put on an attacker hat for 30 seconds. What is a log file? A log file is untrusted, attacker-influenced input . Every public-facing web server, SSH daemon, API gateway, and email relay faithfully records whatever string an outsider sends in an HTTP User-Agent, a failed username field, or a JSON payload. Log processors have been attacked through logged strings before (hi, Log4Shell !), but that was a bug you could patch. It also — theoretically — eliminates an endless stream of unpredictable token costs flowing to a frontier model provider. Small models are not the villain. In the same paper, a structured design called Aida (separate agents for investigating, challenging and judging, working through a SIEM) used open-weight Qwen3.5 9B and it was workable for the task they had. “What about an agent querying a log store?” Now we are talking! What is missing from this proposal is the SIEM… The Raw-Logs-to-Local-LLM Delusion Matrix For explaining this to an enthusiastic colleague (or a budget-slashing executive) without starting a pillow fight: Wait, Is a Local LLM Good for Anything in Log Land? (The 10% Where It Shines!) I am a constructive cynic, not a Luddite (At least Gemini 4 Argon thinks so!). As I noted in the SOC maturity post , AI can jump the artifacts, and parsers are on that list (with caveats for tricky log sources). So point your local model at logs as an engineering sidecar , not an ingestion engine: Writing the parser, not being the parser. Instead of feeding 50 million lines from a weird legacy mainframe into an LLM, feed 20 sample lines and ask for a regex, OCSF mapping, or pipeline rule. The LLM writes the code once, and deterministic CPU code parses the 50 million lines at wire speed. This mostly works, I swear. Post-trigger micro-slice investigation. Once a rule or EDR alert fires on a specific host and 15-minute window, pull 200 pre-filtered, enriched log lines and ask the model for a timeline. When an engineer or cost-conscious VP suggests “let’s dump our noisy firewall logs into a local Ollama box,” they aren’t trying to sabotage your SOC. They have a log source that is too expensive to send to the SIEM, and they want a free way to “keep an eye on it.” Here is how to solve that without a science project: Don’t use a GPU box as a poor man’s data lake. Before the demo starts, ask: “How many GB per day is the raw source, how fast does the model read, and what deterministic step selects the tiny slice that reaches a context window?” If the answer is “we’ll just load it in batches,” kill the project on the spot. It’s this “just” word. Fix ingest pain with tiering (30-day play). If this idea surfaced because a log source is too expensive for your SIEM, solve that: drop repetitive keepalive chatter, route compliance-only logs to cheap storage, and keep output-driven security data in your detection tier. Make “the LLM writes the parser, never runs as the parser” a standard (architecture play) — that is, if you write parsers at all. Call it a SIEM or call it a pile of parsers, a query engine, detections and retention. You need those things, and a GPU under a desk does not replace them. By all means run a model next to them, I promise it will be fun! The part that worries me most is how this fails. A detection rule that misses can be tested, tuned, and re-run. A model that misses hands you a nice summary, and nobody knows what was not in it. As I said in September, skipped maturity used to fail loudly, and now it fails quietly. items.summary_html:
Warning: this blog is an experiment. The idea for a blog came from a real conversation I had with somebody. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Opus 5.5 performed a peer review, and tore some parts to shreds. Then rewrote them. And then I very lightly edited it, and tuned a few jokes. I replaced a food fight joke with a pillow fight joke, specifically. Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise!

—

A security peer recently shared a proposal they had just heard in the wild: instead of paying for a SIEM, why not load several days of raw log data into a locally run open-weights model, ask it “what looks risky?”, and review whatever the model highlights?

No SIEM ingest tax! No cloud token bills! No SIEM license fees! No writing correlation rules! No tuning anomaly detection! Just a gaming GPU under a desk and pure, artisanal AI-native vibes. Ahhh, magic!

Gemini illustration

Wait. Really?

My first instinct, forged by 24 years of staring at logs since I first met a SIM in January 2002, was to laugh, pour a drink, and move on. Surely everyone knows this is a terrible idea, right? Right?!

Wrong.

If an engineer, an IT director, or a cost-cutting CFO pitches “local LLM as a poor man’s SIEM” in your organization, you cannot just roll your eyes and mutter “hallucinations.” People keep inventing this idea for real reasons. SIEM ingest pricing still hurts: some vendor cost explainer works out 5 TB per day at $2 to $4 per GB as $3.6 to $7.3 million a year on ingestion alone. Detection engineering is still hard work. And yes the AI hype machine has spent two years promising executives that models can “reason over any unstructured data.”

So let’s dissect why dumping a week of raw logs into a local model breaks four basic laws of “operational physics”, and then carve out the narrow 10% where a local model does help with logs. The short version fits on a sticker: the LLM writes the parser, it never runs as the parser. And the twist is that the problem here is “raw,” not “local.”

Token Arithmetic and Naive Chunking (Or: How Big Do You Think 7 Days of Logs Is?!)

Let’s start with grade-school arithmetic, because clearly nobody pitching this architecture has ever opened a calculator…

Forget the enterprise. Take a tiny environment, a single server rack generating a measly 1 GB of raw text logs per day. Seven days of logs is 7 GB of text, or roughly 1.75 billion tokens at 4 characters per token. That is generous, since IP addresses, GUIDs and hex strings tokenize worse than English (Wow, really? Yes, really — at least Claude thinks so! He would know, right?)

Now look at that “free” 8B or 70B parameter model on your GPU workstation. Its usable context window, before the KV cache devours your VRAM and the fans sound like a Boeing 747 on takeoff, is maybe 32K to 128K tokens. You are shoving 1.75 billion tokens through a 128K keyhole, which is about 13,700 full context windows. Painful enough yet?

Well, it gets worse. Assume your box reads a generous 2,000 tokens per second (benchmark your own, I’ll wait). Reading those 1.75 billion tokens takes about 10 days. You need 10 days to read 7 days of logs, so you never catch up! Scale that to the 5 TB per day example above and it is about 20 years of GPU time for each day of logs. Hilarity ensues! Replacing a deterministic stream processor with a token-by-token text predictor is like replacing your municipal water pipes with a guy carrying a silver espresso spoon from a well 10 miles away.

“Fine, Anton,” the DIY enthusiast says, “we’ll chunk the logs into 2,000-line batches and loop the local model over them all weekend!” Or we will get a bigger boat… eh… server rack to run the model.

Chunking naively, by just loading the data in batches, fails hilariously. Here is how:

  • Attack chains get cut. The phish on Tuesday lands in one batch, the lateral movement on Thursday lands thousands of batches later, and no prompt ever sees both. Each batch gets judged alone.
  • Merging the summaries does not bring the signal back. By the time you summarize the summaries, the one quiet line was already dropped in round one. So “naive+” fails as well.
  • Position inside the batch matters. Liu et al.’s “Lost in the Middle” found that models do best when the relevant information sits at the start or end of a long context and degrade sharply in the middle. They tested question answering and key-value retrieval, not logs, but picture a quiet privilege escalation on line 1,482 of your batch. Worst seat in the house.

Researchers keep running into this. Cai, Ryan and Karie note that iterative approach is limited by context capacity and that map-reduce style summarization is computationally heavy (and requires some luck). Even so, that is a proof of concept on up to 20,000 rows per dataset, and they say enterprise volumes remain to be validated.

So smarter chunking exists (reminder: it is not magic, in this area nothing truly is): parse, cluster, then retrieve by entity and time. At that point you are building the first half of a SIEM. Congratulations!

As I wrote in The Ancient Art of SIEM, cost pain is eternal and only the currency changes. In 2003 you ran out of hardware, in 2015 you ran out of cloud budget, and in 2026 you run out of tokens and VRAM.

The Input-Centric Time Machine: Back to 2002 Batch Review

Notice the most revealing phrase in this idea: “load 1 to 7 days of log data… and then review what the model highlights.”

That is not real-time detection. That is batch-mode log archeology! When intruders can go from initial access to data theft in hours (soon: minutes for some incidents), reviewing a week of logs in a batch means you are running a weekly book club about how you got breached last Wednesday. But hey … is your SIEM faster? Well, it should be!

Worse, asking an LLM to “highlight what looks risky” violates the most important lesson of two decades of detection engineering. In Output-driven SIEM, 13 years later, I revisited my favorite 2011 mental model: think about what you want to see at the output before you collect, and AI does not change this. Asking a model to “find risk” in raw logs with zero detection engineering is the ultimate input-centric anti-pattern. It failed with ML in mid-2010s, and LLM is not different (in this regard).

Now, about determinism. The lazy objection is “the answers change on every run,” and a sharp engineer will reply “so pin the seed.” Fair enough! Run-to-run randomness is an engineering problem: Thinking Machines got 80 unique completions out of 1,000 at temperature 0, then 1,000 identical ones after fixing their kernels. But is it actually bad? Maybe if you run 5 times, you will find 2x more “fun” things. But hey … also probably at least 5x more noise.

The harder test is stability. Take the same 48 hours of domain controller logs, shuffle the order or change one irrelevant line, and run it again. Given what we learned, I would bet real money the verdict moves. Well-crafted SIEM rule does not care what order the lines arrive in.

Zero Local Context Equals Hallucinated Risk

Why can’t a local model tell an active nation-state intrusion from Tuesday’s messy IT administration? Because raw logs do not contain your organizational reality! Shocking, eh?

A raw syslog or CloudTrail line says that svc_deploy_04 logged into prod-db-02 at 3:14 AM from an internal jump host and ran an encoded PowerShell script. Is that a five-alarm breach or the legacy billing batch job that Bob in accounting wrote in 2017 and nobody dares to touch? This is a dated example, on purpose. Insert your own fun example involving a shadow AI agent!

In Part 3 of the Stop Building a 2003 SOC series, I argued that the #1 reason AI fails in the SOC is the absence of Context as Code: machine-readable, owned, and expiring knowledge of your assets, business processes, and weird administrative exceptions. In Part 2, we warned about automation bias: humans reviewing plausible, well-written machine verdicts approve them.

Also, the test from Can AI Let You Jump SOC Maturity Levels? applies here: does this exist because someone had to spend time, or because someone had to learn something about us? Writing a parser is a time cost. Knowing about Bob’s job is a learning cost, and no model downloaded from the internet has paid it.

Feed raw logs into a naked local LLM with no CMDB enrichment, no threat intel, no identity graph, and no 90-day baseline, and its only source of “context” is its pre-trained weights. So it flags every scary-looking word (ERROR, DENIED, admin, root, failed) and writes you a convincing fictional thriller about your own network.

The Confused Deputy Trap: When the Attacker Prompts Your “SIEM” via User-Agent

Now put on an attacker hat for 30 seconds. What is a log file?

A log file is untrusted, attacker-influenced input. Every public-facing web server, SSH daemon, API gateway, and email relay faithfully records whatever string an outsider sends in an HTTP User-Agent, a failed username field, or a JSON payload.

Log processors have been attacked through logged strings before (hi, Log4Shell!), but that was a bug you could patch. In a raw-log-to-LLM setup there is no parser boundary to patch, because instructions and data share one channel. You just handed the attacker write access to your detection engine’s prompt!

Summaries are also scary, BTW. Pandey and Bhujang found that the classic “ignore all instructions” override failed completely against the one model they tested, but context manipulation reached 96% success on summarization with no defenses and 38% even with constrained output.

In How to Solve the Mystery of AI Defense in Depth (and my October 2026 collaboration with Usman Chaudhary, The Model Has Preferences, but the Harness Got Controls), I emphasized that a model’s statistical preferences are never a security boundary, and only a deterministic harness is. Feed unparsed logs straight into a local LLM with no harness, and any kid with curl can blind your review or flood your team with fabricated critical alerts…

The Problem Is “Raw,” Not “Local”

Let’s be fair to the local crowd, because they have a point.

  • Local solves a real problem. Logs are full of secrets, PII and internal hostnames. Not shipping them to a third-party API is a legitimate reason to want a model on your own hardware. It also — theoretically — eliminates an endless stream of unpredictable token costs flowing to a frontier model provider.
  • Small models are not the villain. In the same paper, a structured design called Aida (separate agents for investigating, challenging and judging, working through a SIEM) used open-weight Qwen3.5 9B and it was workable for the task they had.
  • “What about an agent querying a log store?” Now we are talking! The model forms a question, a database searches 7 days of logs deterministically, and the model reads a small result. That is a very different architecture, and it needs parsed data, a query engine, detections to start from, retention and access control. Sound familiar?

So keep your local model if you want it. What is missing from this proposal is the SIEM…

The Raw-Logs-to-Local-LLM Delusion Matrix

For explaining this to an enthusiastic colleague (or a budget-slashing executive) without starting a pillow fight:

Wait, Is a Local LLM Good for Anything in Log Land? (The 10% Where It Shines!)

I am a constructive cynic, not a Luddite (At least Gemini 4 Argon thinks so!). As I noted in the SOC maturity post, AI can jump the artifacts, and parsers are on that list (with caveats for tricky log sources). So point your local model at logs as an engineering sidecar, not an ingestion engine:

  • Writing the parser, not being the parser. Instead of feeding 50 million lines from a weird legacy mainframe into an LLM, feed 20 sample lines and ask for a regex, OCSF mapping, or pipeline rule. The LLM writes the code once, and deterministic CPU code parses the 50 million lines at wire speed. This mostly works, I swear.
  • Post-trigger micro-slice investigation. Once a rule or EDR alert fires on a specific host and 15-minute window, pull 200 pre-filtered, enriched log lines and ask the model for a timeline. Those lines still contain attacker strings, so treat the summary as untrusted and let the model request actions only from a closed list.
  • Ad-hoc query translation. Translate an analyst’s question into KQL, SPL, or SQL, so the database searches 7 days of logs deterministically. This also mostly works, but some YMMV.
The Lean Team Reality

What if you are the CISO of a regional insurer or hospital with a small security team, a hybrid stack, strict state regulators, and an MDR provider? When an engineer or cost-conscious VP suggests “let’s dump our noisy firewall logs into a local Ollama box,” they aren’t trying to sabotage your SOC. They have a log source that is too expensive to send to the SIEM, and they want a free way to “keep an eye on it.” Here is how to solve that without a science project:

  • Don’t use a GPU box as a poor man’s data lake. Route a noisy source to cheap, searchable object storage, or strip verbose fields in a pipeline before ingest. This is my old two-tier answer (a SIEM plus a broad, cheap log store), and it has aged well.
  • Hold your MDR to the same standard. When they brag at the next QBR about “AI-powered log analysis,” ask whether deterministic detections run first or whether it is an LLM wrapper over unparsed telemetry. This point alone is worth the price of reading this blog (A.C. — this is me, not AI)
  • Channel the DIY energy. Give your smart engineer 50 anonymized lines from your gnarliest legacy application and ask for three high-signal filter rules you can deploy in your real pipeline.
Action Items for Security Leaders

Is there anything you need to actually do?

  • Run a napkin token audit on any AI log proposal (Monday morning). Before the demo starts, ask: “How many GB per day is the raw source, how fast does the model read, and what deterministic step selects the tiny slice that reaches a context window?” If the answer is “we’ll just load it in batches,” kill the project on the spot. It’s this “just” word.
  • Fix ingest pain with tiering (30-day play). If this idea surfaced because a log source is too expensive for your SIEM, solve that: drop repetitive keepalive chatter, route compliance-only logs to cheap storage, and keep output-driven security data in your detection tier.
  • Make “the LLM writes the parser, never runs as the parser” a standard (architecture play) — that is, if you write parsers at all. Allow LLMs at design time (parsers, mappings, queries from small samples) and at post-alert time (small, bounded, enriched slices), but not as the runtime ingestion or anomaly engine over raw logs. Put it in your MDR requirements too… otherwise they will keep whining that it takes 7 weeks to integrate a log source forever.
  • Test your existing AI log workflows for prompt injection (60-day play). If your SOC or MDR summarizes anything containing attacker-controlled strings, test it in your next purple-team exercise. Do not stop at a naive “ignore instructions” canary, because passing that proves little. Try persona and context-rewriting payloads, plus payloads split across lines.
So, Do You Need a SIEM?

Call it a SIEM or call it a pile of parsers, a query engine, detections and retention. You need those things, and a GPU under a desk does not replace them. By all means run a model next to them, I promise it will be fun!

The part that worries me most is how this fails. A detection rule that misses can be tested, tuned, and re-run. A model that misses hands you a nice summary, and nobody knows what was not in it. As I said in September, skipped maturity used to fail loudly, and now it fails quietly.

We had 23 years of progress, and the best practice is still “have a plan and don’t ingest garbage.” That goes for your context window too.

[A.C. — note to self: this is v6 skill]

“I Don’t Need a SIEM, I Have Ollama!” (Yes, You Do!) was originally published in Anton on Security on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Phone return scams: where a real delivery and a fake return end up in a bill for you
items.summary: A caller offers you a free phone upgrade or an exclusive deal from your mobile provider. A new phone arrives at your home. So far, everything seems to check out. Then comes another call: There’s been a shipping mistake. You received the wrong phone, and the company needs you to send it back. You send it back, but the phone never reaches your provider, leaving you with a large charge or long-term contract to pay. Now police are warning about this scheme after residents lost devices and were left facing the associated payments. How phone return scams works The scam usually starts with a call from a spoofed number. In the US we’re seeing several examples in anonymized Malwarebytes Scam Guard records of the impersonated company being Canadian mobile provider Rogers. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre warns: “After collecting personal information required for credit checks, they’ll order a new phone in your name.” Next, a genuine device arrives through a legitimate delivery service. That delivery makes the next part of the story easier to believe. The caller gets back in touch and claims something went wrong. Perhaps the company sent the wrong device, or an extra phone arrived by mistake. To put things right, you need to send it back using the label or shipping QR code they provide. The shipping label is the real trick. Rather than directing the package to the provider’s returns facility, it sends the device to an address chosen by the criminals. The result: You no longer have the phone, but your provider has not received it back. Victims can be left facing a contract, financing agreement, or monthly payments for the missing device. How to stay safe The most important protection against most types of scams is having someone you can trust and deliberate whether something is a scam. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can be that partner if you’re on your own. You don’t need to decide on the spot about whether a caller sounds convincing. Break the conversation and verify the offer separately. Pause and check if you encounter any of the following: An unexpected call offering a free phone, loyalty reward, or unusually attractive upgrade. A caller asking for personal, financial, or account information to arrange the offer. A follow-up call claiming the wrong device was shipped or that another delivery mistake needs correcting. Instructions to use a return label or QR code supplied by that caller. A return destination that you have not confirmed directly with your provider. If you’ve already sent a phone, contact your mobile provider immediately using verified contact details. Explain that you believe you were targeted by a phone return scam, identify the affected orders, and ask for a fraud investigation. If you shared your account password or PIN, change it through the provider’s official channels. Rogers advises customers who disclosed their credentials to reset them and contact customer service to check for unauthorized transactions. Keep the evidence: messages, emails, the shipping label, tracking details, order confirmations, bills, and a timeline of the calls. These records can help explain what happened to support a billing complaint and fraud report. Something feel off? Check it before you click. items.title: NIKKE PC launcher compromise put players’ passwords and personal files at risk
items.summary: Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account. The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted. Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen. Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know. SEE PLANS Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN). Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23. According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to: Run programs and system commands. Browse folders and download files. Take screenshots. Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials. Collect browser passwords and cookies. Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets. Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data. The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear. How to stay safe Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite , so they do not need to take any additional security measures. Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked. If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps. Close the launcher and check your PC . MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack. Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully. Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised. If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase. Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information. Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you. From reporting threats to removing them. Players of Goddess of Victory: NIKKE are being urged to check their PCs after attackers tampered with files used by the game’s Windows launcher. Opening the launcher could allow malicious software to run, potentially exposing much more than a player’s game account.

The incident occurred as part of a supply-chain attack, where services or software used by the company in question is compromised. In practice, this meant that instead of persuading players to download a fake game or install a suspicious add-on, the attackers compromised resources used by the legitimate launcher. Players could therefore encounter the threat simply by opening software they already trusted.

Game publisher Level Infinite has released fixes and added a malware-checking feature to the official PC client. However, fixing the delivery mechanism does not undo an infection, nor does it recover passwords and other information that may have been stolen.

Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know.

SEE PLANS

Independent researcher MotherSphere identified malicious code in four JavaScript files hosted on Level Infinite’s official content delivery network (CDN).

Players should be aware of a discrepancy in the published timelines. Level Infinite says malicious-program distribution began on October 30. while MotherSphere reports evidence of the remote-control agent running as early as October 23.

According to the researcher’s analysis, the distributed remote-control agent supported commands to:

  • Run programs and system commands.
  • Browse folders and download files.
  • Take screenshots.
  • Retrieve saved NIKKE login credentials.
  • Collect browser passwords and cookies.
  • Search for developer credentials, API tokens, and other secrets.
  • Collect cryptocurrency wallet-extension data.

The number of compromised PCs and the full extent of any data theft remain unclear.

How to stay safe

Mobile-only players are not affected, according to Level Infinite, so they do not need to take any additional security measures.

Level Infinite says it replaced three abnormal script files early on November 4, then refreshed the CDN’s cache for the remaining file later that day. MotherSphere subsequently reported that all four files were clean on the four CDN servers checked.

If you opened the Windows launcher during the period identified above, take the following steps.

  • Close the launcher and check your PC. MotherSphere’s report includes user-reported Malwarebytes detections for traces associated with the attack.
  • Follow the removal instructions published by NIKKE carefully.
  • Secure your accounts from a clean device. Do not change passwords on a computer that may still be compromised.
  • If a cryptocurrency wallet or its recovery phrase may have been exposed, use a clean device to move funds to a newly created wallet with a new recovery phrase.
  • Level Infinite asks players who believe they were affected, including those experiencing problems with external accounts or financial losses, to contact its customer support team, so keep relevant records without handing over personal information.

Please note that the NIKKE wiki’s unofficial cleanup guidance recommends scanning with Malwarebytes. Although the guide describes this as a one-time free option, Malwarebytes Free lets you continue running manual scans and removing detected malware after the Premium trial ends. The trial provides additional features, including real-time protection, so decide what is best for you.

From reporting threats to removing them.
