items.title: Frida 17.26.0 Released
items.summary: Stalker no longer writes below the target’s stack pointer, and lends transforms a register of its own. The emulated realm on Android’s native bridge got a thorough going-over after @leonitousconforti ’s reports, and our Windows mapper now works on every Windows from Vista to 11, with XP thrown in, thanks to a report by @liufeias . Add Linux hardening from @washedbeast , a round of Idun fixes by @mrmacete , and QNX fixes, and it adds up to a minor bump. Stalker Stalker has always spilled its scratch registers to the target’s stack, below the stack pointer and past the red zone. That was a shortcut I took when designing it, and one I have been meaning to fix for a long time, as it breaks an invariant Stalker is otherwise careful to uphold: it must have the same side effects on the target’s stack as the original code would have had. A CALL is rewritten into a push of the return address that the original would have pushed, which is what lets a thread unfollow deep in a call chain without repairing the stack. Romain Thomas published a post on detecting Stalker through those spills, which was the nudge I needed. Stalker now keeps them in its own per-context stack on x86, x86_64, ARM and ARM64, and the ARM and Thumb writers emit far branches through the literal pool rather than pushing a scratch register. This also made the arm64 emulation of instructions that misaligned the stack pointer before a branch, there only to avoid the crash our spills caused, unnecessary, so it is gone. Thanks, Romain! Once spills moved off the stack, Stalker needed scratch registers of its own, and now controls them on every backend. That made a long-standing wish cheap: getUserDataReg() on the transform iterator returns a register that has been loaded with the data value given to Stalker.follow() , picked so that it doesn’t clash with the instruction being transformed. CModule transforms get it too, as an architecture-neutral GumCpuReg . Tools like frida-itrace used to track which registers were free at each instruction themselves. That logic now lives in Stalker, which makes such tools simpler. The typings in @types/frida-gum 19.13.0 cover it. Two smaller Stalker changes. The pointer to the execution context that we keep in thread-local storage is now masked with a random per-process cookie, so walking the TLS slots no longer finds it. Romain documented that technique being used in the wild back in 2022, in his analysis of the SingPass app’s RASP. And Linux arm64 never detected pointer authentication, so return addresses on the chained-return path kept their PAC bits; we now query HWCAP_PACA from the auxiliary vector. A word on how we approach RASP, since these two changes are a good illustration. Frida will never mitigate a specific RASP product, as that only leads to a never-ending escalation, cat-and-mouse style. What we will do is keep improving our stealth, as above, where the fix is a better Stalker regardless of who is looking. For everything else, we make sure you have the APIs to change Frida’s behavior and bypass whatever you are dealing with yourself. That is why Interceptor lets you pick the scratch register it clobbers to reach its trampoline, through the scratchRegister option, and even lets you write the redirect yourself, through writeRedirect() . Fragmentation is the goal: when every user can make Frida look and behave differently, there is no single Frida for a RASP vendor to fingerprint, and each bypass is one of many. And with our Barebone agents running in kernel mode, Frida’s user-mode threads, memory ranges and the rest are hidden from inside the process, so a RASP looking from there finds nothing to see. Android Leo kept digging into the emulated realm on x86_64 Android with a native bridge, and found that Process.enumerateThreads() aborted the target. Under a native bridge, the guest Bionic’s pthread functions are trampolines into the host’s, so the guest has no thread list of its own, and our detection of the pthread internals failed. We now walk the host Bionic’s thread list, and for threads inside a guest call, take the CPU context from the guest state that Berberis publishes through a TLS slot. He also found that findExportByName() returned null for the app’s own libraries, while enumerateExports() listed them. The emulated agent’s dlopen() runs in a namespace that can’t see the app’s classloader namespace, so the module ended up without a handle. Exports are now resolved through the export table whenever there is no handle, which also covers the linker, so its special case is gone. Thanks for the reports! Thread observers didn’t work in the emulated realm either, as threads are created and torn down by the host’s Bionic, which the emulated agent’s Interceptor can’t hook. The native agent now feeds its thread registry to the emulated one, as a snapshot followed by added, removed and renamed events, and shares its cloak the same way, so the emulated agent doesn’t see the native agent’s threads when it walks the host’s list. Both go through new Gum interfaces, ThreadProvider and CloakObserver , for embedders in the same situation. Along the way, Frida’s own threads are now hidden from observers from the start, rather than announced and then cloaked. @tubibibo found that Houdini v3 rejects the deprecated NativeBridgeLoadLibrary() entrypoint, which surfaced as “Process is not using emulation”. We now retry through the extended entrypoint. Thanks! Windows liufeias reported that spawning on Windows 10 failed with “Unable to locate the ntdll loader TLS routines”. The mapper’s heuristics for finding LdrpHandleTlsData() and LdrpReleaseTlsEntry() only matched recent Windows 11 builds, so mapping any image with static TLS aborted elsewhere. They are now recognized by what they do: the former queries the TLS directory of the entry’s base, and the latter looks up the entry’s TLS record, unlinks it, and frees its index. The matcher follows branches, since some builds split the bodies into chunks, and tracks arguments passed on the stack, as 32-bit Vista and 7 use stdcall for these. This was validated against ntdll from XP, Vista, 7, 8.1, and 76 Windows 10 and 11 builds, both x86 and x64, and by running the mapper tests on Vista through Thanks for the report! XP’s loader can’t set up static TLS for modules loaded at runtime, so the mapper does it by hand there, registering the module in ntdll’s TLS list and growing the TLS arrays of existing threads under the loader lock. And GetThreadId() , which XP lacks, is now resolved dynamically, as importing it kept anything linking Gum from loading. Going back in time turned up more. On Vista, 7, 8.1 and Windows 10 up to 1909, RtlVirtualUnwind() is the implementation itself rather than a thunk, so the unwind broker crashed as soon as it got activated. The PE module parser now skips chained function entries and ARM function fragments, which are not function starts, and parses every field as little-endian, so PE images load correctly on big-endian hosts. And the x86 writer didn’t set REX.R for r8 through r15 in RIP-relative and absolute moves, nor emit the SIB byte for r12 . Linux washedbeast sent three fixes from the Android trenches. Mapping names in /proc/ /maps aren’t always valid UTF-8, and on kernels before 5.17 an anonymous mapping’s name is read from a user pointer every time, so a name whose string got unmapped shows up as garbage, which is what happens to apps that inherit a mapping from Zygote under Zygisk. Our regex refused the line, the iterator yielded no mappings at all, and attach failed. The maps are now parsed as raw bytes. Next, the code swap fallback used when libc can’t be found in the target never recognized memfd mappings, as the path reads /memfd:… , so it picked ART’s read-only JIT zygote cache and the first write failed. And strings from syscall tracing could hold any byte, which crashed frida-server when they went into a GVariant. Thanks! @adilalperenciftci fixed a crash reported by @merrygreek when an ELF module has no accessible backing file. The live mapping then stands in, but the section header offsets are not covered by any loadable segment, so they often land in an unmapped gap. Those ranges are now probed first, and the module loads without section details instead. Thanks! Idun Francesco went through Idun with a USB device in hand. Transfers now fail once the device is closed, rather than crashing when the NCM driver flushes after the fact. Devices are keyed by ID so that reconnecting doesn’t leave a stale transport behind, a device leaving while settling, as during boot, no longer does either, and the UDID is still known by the time detachment is reported. The daemon closes relays when either side closes, as keeping the device side open blocked single-client services. And two lwIP fixes: received data is acknowledged immediately, as delayed ACKs held back by Nagle on the device side cost 250 ms per round trip on each tunnel layer, and a close racing with connect no longer leaves a stream claiming to be readable and writable while all I/O would block. Two frida-core fixes came out of the same session. Channel streams nobody else owns, such as one relayed by idund , were gone before being linked, as the registry only holds a weak reference. And kill() didn’t fall back to the process control service for non-debuggable apps, as LLDB errors have been Efni.Error since the move to Idun. Thanks! QNX Following a blocked thread from script deadlocked on QNX. Modifying a thread ran its callback inside a vfork() child, which runs on the calling thread but in a different process, so a lock the parent already holds can’t be re-acquired there, and a JS transform takes GumJS’s mutex. Only the register transfer runs in the child now. And on QNX 6.5SP1 the program path lacked its leading slash when launched through an absolute path, so we resolved it against the current directory. Reported by @KazWolfe , thanks! Enjoy! Changelog stalker: Keep register spills off the target’s stack on x86, x86_64, ARM and ARM64. stalker: Add getUserDataReg() to the transform iterator and CModule callouts. stalker: Mask the execution context pointer stored in TLS. stalker: Detect PAC support on Linux arm64. stalker: Set V8’s stack limit while callbacks run on the Stalker stack. arm-writer: Avoid the stack for far branches. thumb-writer: Avoid the stack for far branches. x86-relocator: Allow saving the scratch register to a slot. x86-writer: Encode extended registers in near pointer moves. linux: Use the host’s thread list under a native bridge. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! elf: Fall back to the export table when a module has no handle. Thanks @leonitousconforti ! thread-registry: Add the ThreadProvider interface, and hide GLib threads from the start. cloak: Add the CloakObserver interface. agent: Feed the emulated thread registry and cloak from the native agent. agent: Retry an emulated load through LoadLibraryExt() . Thanks @tubibibo ! pe-mapper: Find the loader TLS routines by behavior, fixing static TLS on Windows older than recent 11 builds. Thanks @liufeias ! pe-mapper: Support static TLS on Windows XP. thread-registry: Resolve GetThreadId() dynamically, so Gum loads on XP. unwind-broker: Handle an unthunked RtlVirtualUnwind() . pe-module: Skip chained function entries and ARM function fragments. pe-module: Parse PE fields as little-endian. windows: Add missing includes, fixing the MinGW build. linux: Parse /proc/ /maps as raw bytes. Thanks @washedbeast ! linux: Fix the memfd check in the code swap fallback. Thanks @washedbeast ! linux: Make syscall-trace strings valid UTF-8. Thanks @washedbeast ! elf-module: Skip unreadable section data in online modules. Thanks @adilalperenciftci and @merrygreek ! idun: Fail USB transfers once the device is closed. Thanks @mrmacete ! idun: Key usbmux transports by device ID, handle USB removal while settling, and store the device’s UDID. Thanks @mrmacete ! idun: Close relays when either side closes. Thanks @mrmacete ! idun: ACK received data immediately, and fix close racing with connect. Thanks @mrmacete ! idun: Rename the QML module from Quickshell, add its Qt Multimedia dependencies to the packaging, and only use gioopenssl with a static GLib. channel: Keep streams alive until linked. Thanks @mrmacete ! fruity: Fix the kill() fallback for non-debuggable apps. Thanks @mrmacete ! qnx: Run thread callbacks in the parent, fixing a deadlock when following a blocked thread. qnx: Use _cmdname() to query the program path. Thanks @KazWolfe ! cmodule: Fix the bundled Capstone header on 32-bit ARM. compiler: Bump @types/frida-gum to 19.13.0.

items.title: Scammers use AI-generated images of missing pets to extort owners
items.summary: When your pet goes missing, it can be totally heartbreaking. So hearing that they’ve been found is no doubt very welcome news. Even better to see a photo of them looking safe and well. But while the photo may look exactly like your pet, that doesn’t mean the person who sent it has your pet or even ever saw it. The BBC reports how criminals are sending owners AI-generated images of their missing pets, demanding money for their return, and sometimes threatening to harm the animals when owners refuse to pay. The BBC interviewed two targets of this scam who were both contacted after posting a missing pet message on social media. The scammers sent them pictures of their beloved pets and demanded a ransom for their safe return. Messages like these exploit two powerful emotions in quick succession: relief that a beloved pet has been found, followed by fear that something terrible will happen unless the owner acts immediately. The scam typically follows this pattern: A scammer finds a missing pet appeal, which is typically posted to social media or local sites with an accompanying photo and contact details. The scammer contacts the owner and claims to have found the animal. An image fabricated with the help of AI makes the claim appear more convincing. They ask for money which may be described as a reward or as payment for emergency treatment . They add pressure. They might refuse to meet until payment arrives, or threaten to sell or harm the pet. Our data backs this report up. Over the last month, people anonymously submitted three distinctive types of pet related scam attempts to Malwarebytes Scam Guard : “We found your missing cat” message, with photos: Someone claimed to have found a user’s missing cat and had images of it. Found pet callback lure: A voicemail claimed to have found a lost cat and supplied a callback number. Humane Society impersonation and payment demand: A caller claimed a missing cat needed emergency surgery, and demanded successive Zelle payments. How to stay safe Sadly, while it can be very useful to use social media to retrieve lost pets, it also attracts scammers and other abuse. You don’t have to stop asking for help online, but you can put some safeguards between an unexpected message and any payment. Keep some identifying details private. Leave a distinctive feature out of the public description so you can ask a supposed finder about it later. Do not pay in advance to secure a reunion. Be particularly wary of someone who insists that you send money before they will let you see the animal. Arrange any legitimate handover in a safe, public location, and verify that it is your pet before paying a reward. Verify veterinary claims independently. If someone says your pet is at an animal hospital, find the hospital’s contact details yourself and call it directly. Do not rely on the number or payment link in the message. A second pair of eyes can help you assess a demand without the same emotional pressure. Malwarebytes Scam Guard can help you identify whether a message might be a scam and how to proceed. If someone is threatening your pet, remember that when they make threats to your pet, it is very likely they don’t have a clue where it is either, so don’t let them extort you. Something feel off? Check it before you click. Malwarebytes Scam Guard helps you analyze suspicious links, texts, and screenshots instantly. Available with Malwarebytes Premium Security for all your devices, and in the Malwarebytes app for iOS and Android . Try it free →

items.title: Core Skills in the Age of AI
items.summary: One of the biggest questions I get whenever I’m teaching anything focused on core skills—whether it’s network security, SOC analysis, or ecurity essentials—is whether any of these classes are even necessary anymore because of AI. The assumption seems to be that AI is going to eliminate the need for foundational knowledge. People believe that AI will simply handle the technical details for us, allowing security professionals to skip over the basics and move directly to the advanced work. Unfortunately, that assumption creates a sense of hopelessness. Junior analysts who are trying to enter the field start wondering whether it’s worth studying at all. Companies looking to hire are hesitant because they’re not sure what the workforce will look like in a few years. Everyone is waiting to see where things land. Context Is Everything When it comes to core information security skills, I believe we need to recognize something important: The fundamentals matter more today than they ever have. The reason is context. The more context and understanding you have about a technical problem, the more effective AI becomes. Artificial intelligence is not a replacement for expertise. It amplifies expertise. If you put AI in the hands of someone who doesn’t understand networking, operating systems, or security fundamentals, the impact is often limited. They may get answers faster, but they have no way to evaluate whether those answers are correct. Put the same tools in the hands of someone who understands TCP/IP, operating systems, network architecture, authentication, and how systems actually work, and AI becomes an incredible force multiplier. As we move into the future, it will become even more important for security professionals to understand the basics. Those foundational skills provide the context necessary to ask better questions, recognize bad answers, and effectively leverage increasingly powerful AI tools. What Chess Can Teach Us I also think we can look at chess as a preview of where our industry is heading. Chess is more popular today than it has ever been. There are more strong chess players than at any other point in history. At the same time, AI engines can defeat even the world’s best players without breaking a sweat. So why hasn’t AI killed chess? Because the chess community embraced it. Players use AI engines like Stockfish to analyze games, identify mistakes, study openings, improve endgame strategy, and accelerate learning. Tournament organizers use AI to help detect cheating. Coaches use AI to provide insights that would have been impossible to deliver at scale just a few decades ago. The result isn’t fewer chess players. In fact, it is the opposite. The other result is better chess players. Where Cybersecurity Is Heading I believe cybersecurity is heading down a very similar path. AI will help us learn faster. It will help us identify patterns more quickly. It will help us automate repetitive work and explore technical problems at a scale that wasn’t previously possible. But none of that eliminates the need for foundational knowledge. In fact, it increases its importance. The people who understand the fundamentals will be the ones who get the most value from AI. They’ll be able to guide it, challenge it, verify it, and use it to solve increasingly complex problems. The future of cybersecurity isn’t humans versus AI. It’s humans with strong fundamentals using AI to become dramatically more effective than ever before. Check out John’s Antisyphon courses (including Pay-What-You-Can options!) here: antisyphontraining.com/instructor/john-strand/

items.title: Magnet Witness 2.0: Expanded enhancement, large-case performance, and improved reporting
items.summary: Key takeaways Witness 2.0 adds Sharpen, De-Interlace, Line Doubling, and Frame Rate filters, reducing the need to move evidence between applications for routine enhancements. Improved case loading, clip-list responsiveness, large-report generation, and job monitoring, to help examiners work more efficiently with high-volume video evidence. Examiners can acquire, review, enhance, export, and report within a more connected workflow, with applied enhancements automatically documented to help maintain a clear record of the work performed. Forensic video examiner’s work rarely ends once the media has been acquired. You still need to review, prepare, enhance, document, and export video evidence, often while working through large clip collections and managing long-running processes. Adjusting video evidence is often a necessary step before investigative or legal review to clarify details or restore video to reflect more accurately what was recorded. And, when your case contains a high volume of clips, slow case loading, large reports, and lengthy processing can make that work even harder. Witness 2.0: Enhanced Investigations at Scale release addresses both challenges by expanding the enhancement filters you can apply within Witness and improving how you manage large cases, reports, and long-running jobs. Previously, a routine enhancement could mean performing multiple exports and ingestions using different applications to get the job done. After exporting video from Witness, another application was needed to apply simple adjustments such as brightness and contrast. To complete the task, you would need to export it again, and separately document what changed. Now, Witness helps you avoid those extra steps by keeping common enhancement tasks and reporting within the same workflow. Earlier this year we introduced Enhancement Filters in Magnet Witness , bringing commonly used capabilities—including Brightness & Contrast, Levels, Aspect Ratio, Resize, Crop, Rotate, Mirror, and Overlay—directly into your workflow. These filters let you perform routine adjustments without moving evidence between applications, streamlining the end-to-end forensic video evidence workflow: Acquire → Preview → Enhance → Export → Share You can check out these capabilities in action here , these capabilities help you complete many routine enhancement tasks directly within Witness while maintaining a forensically sound workflow. Expanded video enhancement capabilities in Witness When video evidence requires routine adjustments before investigative or legal review, Witness lets you keep the work within one application. These four new filters further streamline your workflow: Sharpen: When details in a video appear soft or difficult to distinguish, sharpening helps bring greater clarity without requiring you to move the video into another application. De-Interlace: Many surveillance and legacy video systems still produce interlaced footage, which can introduce visible scan-line artifacts or combine multiple camera channels, making analysis more difficult. The De-Interlace filter converts interlaced video into a smoother progressive format or assists in isolating the channel of value. Line Doubling: Line Doubling resizes video content by doubling horizontal or vertical lines, improving visibility, and supporting more accurate visual examinations. Frame Rate: When playback speed needs to be adjusted, frame rate allows you to do so without adding or removing frames. High-performance efficient workflows with large investigations As video data sets grow, examiners need tools that stay responsive. Large clip collections can slow case loading and navigation, while large reports can leave you waiting without enough visibility or control. Witness 2.0 helps you keep your work moving with improved large-case and report handling, report-job monitoring and cancellation, clearer processing and export guidance, and improved file and folder naming. Navigate larger cases more efficiently: Open and work with high-volume clip collections with improved case loading and clip-list performance. Generate and manage large reports: Create PDF reports for large evidence collections with improved generation, access and review. Stay in control of long-running jobs: Monitor and cancel report-generation jobs directly within Witness. One workflow from acquisition to evidence handoff The value of Witness 2.0 extends beyond individual filter or performance improvements. It helps you manage disconnected steps, reduces workflow friction, and gives you a transparent record of the work being done. With the latest performance, reporting and enhancement updates in Magnet Witness, you can: Acquire, preview, enhance, export and convert, supported video within one application. Work large cases more efficiently with improved clip list responsiveness and report performance. Reduce time spent exporting and ingesting videos between different tools for routine video enhancements. Automatically document applied enhancements in reporting, creating a transparent record of the word performed Monitor progress of long-running report and export jobs with clearer progress and messaging. For organizations, this means a more streamlined workflow for routine video enhancement tasks while still maintaining the forensic rigor expected in digital investigations. Witness 2.0 gives examiners a faster, more connected workflow for handling video evidence. With fewer tool changes, optimized performance in large cases, clearer job visibility, and automatically documented enhancements, teams can complete routine work more efficiently and confidently while maintaining forensic rigor. items.title: Introducing AWS account access manager: IAM role flexibility with centralized workforce access
items.summary: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager , a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center , with user-level visibility built-in. Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points. Why use account access manager? Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets. Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims , for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization. Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions. Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows. Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used. How it works Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation . Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives. Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement . The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login . You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) ( aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation , and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi , so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access , separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events. How to enable account access manager Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment. Prerequisites An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled. Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either: Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM. Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory . IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first. Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post). Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account. For CLI access : Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer. Step 1: Enable account access manager Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization: aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager: Console: Sign in to your organization’s management account. In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access , choose account access manager . The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance. If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager. Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console AWS CLI: Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run: aws account-access create-application \ --region \ --identity-source '{ "identityCenter": { "instanceArn": " " } }' As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated. After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability. Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console. Account access manager ARN : the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance. Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN. Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack. Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/* Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it. Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace , (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and (from the Settings page of the console). Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details IAM role trust policy: { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com" }, "Action": [ "sts:AssumeRole", "sts:SetContext", "sts:TagSession" ], "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "aws:SourceAccount": " ", "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access: : :application/ " } } } ] } Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides. Best practice: Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/ and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise. Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference. Step 4: Assign access to users and groups Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts , Users , or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI. Assign from the console: Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name. Select the user, then choose Assign new access . Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access . Assign a user using AWS CLI: aws account-access create-entitlement \ --region \ --application-arn " " \ --entitlement '{ "principalRole": { "principal": { "identityCenter": { "userId": " " } }, "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam:: :role/ " } }' To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": " " . To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID. Note: The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand. Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment. IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours. Step 5: How workforce users can sign in Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways: Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws , or a vanity URL) and sign in. Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed. Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day. Access through a web browser Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser. Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials. On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to. Expand the account to see the roles you can assume. Select a role (for example, Developer ). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role. Access through the AWS CLI Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started: Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer). Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles. On the AWS CLI, run: aws login Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2). Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated. Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session. The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser. Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure , don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login , refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager. Create shortcut links to specific console destinations The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them. Customer managed key considerations If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center. Best practices summary Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin. Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention. Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege. Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access. Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account. Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions. Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers. Leading identity providers Okta , PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono , BeyondTrust , Britive , Sonrai Security , C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on. Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale. Conclusion Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login . It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions). To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video , which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment. To learn more and get started, visit the AWS Identity and Access Management User Guide . We encourage you to enable account access manager in a test organization, assign your first entitlement, and explore how centralized, user-attributed access can simplify your AWS environment. With over 14 years of security expertise, she has delivered high-impact security innovations for Fortune 500 enterprises and Global Systems Integrator partners. With 15 years of security experience spanning multiple industries, his goal is to help customers understand and improve their security and compliance posture in a scalable way. items.summary_html:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is introducing account access manager, a flexible new way to manage workforce access to your Amazon Web Services (AWS) accounts. This combines the IAM role flexibility your teams already rely on, delivered through the centralized federation of AWS IAM Identity Center, with user-level visibility built-in.

Account access manager streamlines the assignment of your existing IAM roles from individual AWS accounts to your workforce users and groups in an organization instance of IAM Identity Center, giving you a clear path to centralized access management at scale. You can adopt account access manager on its own or alongside IAM Identity Center permission sets; both draw on the same users and groups you already synchronize from your corporate identity provider. That means you assign your existing IAM roles to those users and groups directly, without duplicating identities or managing per-account federation points.

Why use account access manager?

Enterprises scaling on AWS have long faced a difficult choice in workforce access: the flexibility of IAM roles or the central control of IAM Identity Center. Until now, granting workforce access to AWS accounts generally meant choosing one of two approaches, each with trade-offs to consider. Federating into each account separately with IAM roles gives you the full flexibility of IAM roles—custom trust policies, tags, and paths—but requires you to configure an identity provider and manage role assignments independently in each account, making it harder to assign a group across multiple accounts or maintain a unified view of who has access where. Federating once through IAM Identity Center with permission sets gives you a single federation point with centrally provisioned, uniform access, but permission sets can feel restrictive for teams whose roles vary from account to account, or that have difficulty generalizing their existing roles into uniform sets.

Account access manager removes the trade-offs. It’s built for customers who want the single federation point and identity-propagation benefits of IAM Identity Center together with the flexibility of IAM roles. Because it uses the IAM roles you already own, you keep the tailoring capabilities you rely on today:

  • Attribute-based access control (ABAC) – Use IAM role tags, or session tags populated from your identity provider as SAML claims, for fine-grained, attribute-driven authorization.
  • Precise trust policies – Restrict role assumption with network conditions or identity provider (IdP)-asserted claims, such as group membership, department, or cost center, as trust-policy conditions.
  • Role paths for organization at scale – Use IAM role paths to group roles and simplify administration as your environment grows.

Because roles are managed in the account you provision access to, account access manager scales with your account usage rather than relying on Identity Center specific quotas. Assignments are made to users and groups, reducing administrative overhead, and providing accountability and auditability to the specific user and role being used.

How it works

Access flows through IAM Identity Center and carries the user’s identity through trusted identity propagation. Even when multiple users assume a shared IAM role, each role session contains user context that attributes every action to the individual user. Access is granted and audited against the actual user, so you can see who assumed which role in which account. The result is user-level visibility across your organization, not just at the point of sign-in. You also maintain access to the full set of IAM role capabilities, such as role paths, tagging, naming conventions, and other IAM primitives.

Figure 1: Account access manager connects IAM Identity Center federated workforce users and groups to AWS accounts specific IAM roles

To grant a user access to a specific role in an account using account access manager, an administrator creates an entitlement. The user can then access that account from the new account access manager application portal or from their IAM Identity Center access portal, or retrieve credentials from the command line with aws login.

You can manage account access manager through the AWS Management Console for IAM and programmatically through the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) (aws login and the account-access API namespace), AWS SDKs, AWS CloudFormation, and HashiCorp Terraform and Pulumi, so you can enable it and manage role assignments the same way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. It exposes its own API namespace, account-access, separate from the IAM API, with its own permissions and AWS CloudTrail events.

How to enable account access manager

Here’s how to enable account access manager in your own environment, from prerequisites through your first role assignment.

Prerequisites
  1. An organization instance of IAM Identity Center enabled.
  2. Users or groups in IAM Identity Center that you want to entitle with IAM roles from individual AWS accounts. If users or groups don’t exist already then either:
    • Connect Identity Center to your external identity provider to automatically provision your corporate identities into Identity Center using SCIM.
    • Create users and groups in the Identity Center directory.
  3. IAM roles in the individual AWS accounts that you want to assign to users and groups of IAM Identity Center. If the role you need doesn’t exist, create a role using custom trust policies first.
  4. Appropriate permissions to enable account access manager and manage assignments (see the IAM policy examples later in this post).
  5. Both the organization instance of IAM Identity Center and account access manager must be enabled in your organization’s management account.
  6. For CLI access: Install or update to the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2.36.0 or newer.
Step 1: Enable account access manager

Before enabling account access manager, run the following command from the AWS organization management account to grant account access manager access to your organization:

aws organizations enable-aws-service-access --service-principal account-access.amazonaws.com

Next, use one of the following methods to enable account access manager:

Console:

  1. Sign in to your organization’s management account.
  2. In the AWS Management Console for IAM navigation pane, under Multi-account access, choose account access manager.
  3. The console Region should be set to the primary Region of your IAM Identity Center instance.
  4. If there is no organization instance of IAM Identity Center, you’ll be prompted to enable one before continuing. Otherwise, choose Enable account access manager.

Figure 2: Account access manager enablement from the IAM console

AWS CLI:

Fetch the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of your IAM Identity Center organization instance, confirm the Region code matches its primary Region, and run:

aws account-access create-application \
 	--region  \
  	--identity-source '{
    		"identityCenter": {
      			"instanceArn": ""
    		}
 	}'

As an output, the account access manager application ARN will be generated.

After you enable account access manager (through the console or AWS CLI), you will get the account access URL and the account access manager ARN along with other details on the capability.

  • Account access portal URL is the single sign-on entry point for your workforce. This is where your users will go to access AWS accounts. Its format is - https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws , found on the Settings tab of the account access manager console.
  • Account access manager ARN: the identifier for the application instance created when you enable account access manager. Note this ARN to use in your IAM role’s trust policies so that only your specific account access manager application can assume those roles, providing confused-deputy protection (see Step 3 for details) and pass it as --application-arn when creating entitlements using the AWS CLI so each assignment is tied to the correct application instance.

Figure 3: Account access manager settings after enablement

In the AWS CLI, run the command aws account-access list-applications to get the application ARN and tenant-ID of the enabled account access manager instance ARN.

Step 2: Update firewalls and gateways

If you filter access to specific AWS domains or URL endpoints with a next-generation firewall (NGFW) or Secure Web Gateway (SWG), allowlist the account access portal domains and endpoints in the following list. Account access manager has no IPv4-only endpoints; endpoints are dual-stack.

  • Account access portal URL – https://[Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws
  • Portal APIs – [Tenant-ID].account-access.[Region].app.aws/api/* and /auth/*
  • Control plane – account-access.[Region].api.aws
  • Runtime – account-access-runtime.[Region].api.aws
  • Console – console.aws.amazon.com/account-access
Step 3: Prepare your IAM roles

Before assigning IAM roles to users and groups, update the role’s trust policy to allow account access manager service to assume it.

Add the following statement to the role’s trust policy (or paste the entire policy that follows if you’re creating a new role). Replace , (your IAM Identity Center primary Region), and (from the Settings page of the console).

Figure 4: Account access manager ARN details

IAM role trust policy:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "AccountAccessManagerIAMRoleTrustPolicyStatement",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Service": "account-access.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": [
        "sts:AssumeRole",
        "sts:SetContext",
        "sts:TagSession"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:SourceAccount": "",
          "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:account-access:::application/"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Define the Condition block to enforce confused-deputy protection. It helps ensure that the role can be assumed only by the specific account access manager application instance (defined using the application ARN) created when you enabled the service, and only when the request originates from your AWS account where that instance resides.

Best practice:

  • Propagate identity attributes with ABAC – The sts:TagSession action listed in the preceding IAM role trust policy allows upstream attributes from your identity provider (group memberships, department, cost center) to flow through as principal tags on the session. Without it, role assumption still succeeds; only session-tag propagation is suppressed. Add it when downstream IAM policies use aws:PrincipalTag/ and the tag is populated from your IdP SAML claims; leave it out otherwise.
  • Automate the trust-policy update – We recommend updating your IAM role-creation workflows to add this trust-policy statement automatically wherever it’s needed, so new roles are assignable from day one. You can use this sample-aam-migration tool as a reference.
Step 4: Assign access to users and groups

Like IAM Identity Center role entitlements, an entitlement in account access manager requires three components: a user or group ID, an account ID, and an IAM role ARN (instead of a permission set ARN). You can create assignments from the Accounts, Users, or Groups tabs in the console, or using the API or AWS CLI. For assignments where the same role needs to be assigned to multiple users, you must create each assignment individually. You can automate it using the account access API, the AWS SDK, or AWS CLI.

Assign from the console:

  1. Choose the Users tab and search by username or display name.
  2. Select the user, then choose Assign new access.

    Figure 5: Assign new access in account access manager

  3. On the Assign account access page, enter the workforce user or group, account ID, and IAM role name, then choose Assign access.

Assign a user using AWS CLI:

aws account-access create-entitlement \
  --region  \
  --application-arn "" \
  --entitlement '{
    "principalRole": {
      "principal": {
        "identityCenter": {
          "userId": ""
        }
      },
      "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam:::role/"
    }
  }'

To assign a group, replace the userId block with "groupId": "". To remove access, use aws account-access delete-entitlement with the entitlement ID.

Note:

  • The console can search users, groups, and accounts, but it can’t detect IAM roles because they can come from different AWS accounts in your organization; you must know the role name beforehand.
  • Only IAM roles whose trust policy grants account access manager as an allowed service principal are eligible for assignment.
  • IAM role sessions assigned by account access manager use the maximum session duration configured on the underlying IAM role in each AWS account, up to 12 hours.
Step 5: How workforce users can sign in

Workforce users can federate to AWS accounts using IAM roles assigned through account access manager in any of the following ways:

  1. Directly through the account access portal URL – Navigate to the portal URL (for example, https://aa-xxxxxxxxx.account-access.us-east-2.app.aws, or a vanity URL) and sign in.
  2. Through the AWS access portal – Go to the Applications tab, select the Account Access application, and you’ll be redirected to the account access portal, where your assigned accounts and their respective roles are listed.

Tip: We recommend that users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal for faster navigation. In addition, if you use a supported IdP, such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity, you can add the account access portal as a bookmark app in the IdP’s dashboard, giving users authenticated, single-click access to the portal directly from the tools they already sign in to each day.

Access through a web browser

Use the following steps to use account access manager through a web browser.

  1. Navigate to the account access portal URL and sign in with your credentials.
  2. On the portal, find the AWS account you need. Search by account name or ID to filter the list of accounts you’re assigned to.
  3. Expand the account to see the roles you can assume.
  4. Select a role (for example, Developer). A new tab opens, signed into that account with the selected role.
Access through the AWS CLI

Account access manager works with the aws login command. To get started:

  1. Install the latest AWS CLI (v2.36.0 or newer).
  2. Sign in through your default browser – Sign in to your account access portal and into the target AWS account using one of your assigned roles.
  3. On the AWS CLI, run: 
    aws login
  4. Set a default Region if prompted – If you haven’t set one, the AWS CLI will prompt you for a Region (for example, us-east-2).
  5. Select your session – The AWS CLI opens a browser page; select the tile for the session you initiated.
  6. Confirm and return to the CLI – The page confirms that your credentials were shared successfully. Close the tab and keep working in the AWS CLI for the duration of your session.

The temporary credentials are automatically rotated by the AWS CLI, AWS Tools for PowerShell, and AWS SDKs, and remain valid for the default session duration of an IAM role. After the session expires, you’re prompted to sign in again on the browser.

Note: IAM Identity Center–specific commands, such as aws sso configure, don’t work with account access manager assignments; use aws login instead. If you want to continue to use aws sso login, refer to AWS CLI Integration for IAM Account access manager.

Create shortcut links to specific console destinations

The portal also lets you create a shortcut link that opens a specific console destination for a given account and role. Shortcut links work only with accounts and roles already assigned to the user—they can’t grant new access—and URL parameters must be URL-encoded. Because shortcut links are Regional and expose the account ID and role name in plain text, review your organization’s sharing policies before experimenting with them.

Customer managed key considerations

If your IAM Identity Center instance is encrypted with an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, which is required when you replicate IAM Identity Center to additional Regions, check the key policy before you enable account access manager. We recommend implementing the current baseline KMS key policy to ensure account access manager can read user, group, and instance data from IAM Identity Center.

Best practices summary
  • Enable in the right place – Enable account access manager in your organization’s management account and in the same Region as your IAM Identity Center instance and confirm your organization instance is in place before you begin.
  • Automate trust-policy updates – Build the account access manager trust-policy statement into your role-creation pipelines so every new role is assignable from day one, with no manual intervention.
  • Add sts:TagSession only when you need it – Include it only where downstream policies consume principal tags; otherwise leave it off to keep sessions lean and least-privilege.
  • Assign roles to groups, not individual users – Granting access at the group level reduces administrative overhead and strengthens the auditability of user-level access.
  • Scope administrator permissions tightly – Separate managing the feature from managing assignments, and enable delegating administration to keep day-to-day operations out of the management account.
  • Allowlist the portal domains before rollout – Add the account access portal domains and endpoints to your next-generation firewall or Secure Web Gateway ahead of launch to avoid access disruptions.
  • Prepare your workforce users – Have users bookmark both the account access portal and the AWS access portal and communicate the aws login flow clearly to your developers.
Account access manager launch partners

Account access manager launches with a broad ecosystem of AWS identity and access-governance partners who have integrated the service into their existing solutions, making it available to our joint customers from day one. Leading identity providers Okta, PingIdentity and Cisco Duo extend account access manager so customers can manage human workforce access to AWS accounts directly from the identity platforms they already use. Alongside them, access-governance and privileged-access partners Apono, BeyondTrust, Britive, Sonrai Security, C1.ai and Lumos added capabilities to govern, provision, and audit that access through the tooling our customers already rely on.

Account access manager also integrates with leading infrastructure-as-code (IaC) partners, so teams can define and manage access assignments declaratively alongside the rest of their AWS infrastructure. Pulumi enables customers to codify account access manager role assignments as part of their existing provisioning workflows, bringing repeatable, version-controlled automation to workforce access at scale.

Conclusion

Account access manager combines the flexibility of the IAM roles your teams already own with the single, centralized federation point of IAM Identity Center, adding user-level visibility into what users or roles have done across your organization. You assign existing IAM roles to users and groups centrally, scale with your account usage rather than a fixed quota, and give developers a fast, secure command-line experience with aws login. It’s available at no additional cost, enabled by default in Commercial Regions (excluding opt-in Commercial Regions, GovCloud (US), China, and other non-commercial Regions).

To see account access manager in action, watch the enablement video, which walks through enabling the service, preparing your IAM roles, and assigning access to your workforce end to end. You can also extend account access manager through our launch partners; leading identity, access-governance, and IaC providers who have integrated the service into their platforms, so you can govern, provision, and automate workforce access to AWS using the tooling you already rely on. Review the preceding partner integrations to find the ones that fit your environment.

items.title: New investments to reduce on-premises security risk
items.summary: On-premises servers can be essential to business operations, but they are increasingly attractive targets to attackers. AI can help less-skilled actors analyze software, develop malicious tools, and repeat attack workflows at greater speed and scale, shortening the window between exposure and exploitation. Organizations need to strengthen security faster without disrupting the critical workloads they rely on. Today, we’re announcing a new on-premises security initiative, initially focused on server workloads. The initiative brings together guidance, migration , and product investments to help customers understand and prioritize risk, reduce their on-premises footprint wherever possible, and strengthen critical workloads that need to remain. Guidance for the initiative will soon be available through Secure Now , which also includes our AI readiness checklist in Microsoft Security Exposure Management and guidance for strengthening foundational security. Understand Identify the most important on-premises risks and prioritize actions customers can take now. Reduce Move workloads to Microsoft 365 where possible to take advantage of cloud-based security, resilience, and continuous innovation. Secure Strengthen critical workloads that need to remain on-premises and reduce the manual work required to keep them secure. This approach starts with understanding where to focus—and extends to making supported on-premises products more secure by default. Modernize where you can, and strengthen the security of what must remain. Making supported on-premises workloads more secure by default Within the Secure pillar of the on-premises security initiative, we’re also hardening the products themselves through On-Premises Baseline Security Mode, starting with supported Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server workloads. On-Premises Baseline Security Mode On-Premises Baseline Security Mode is designed to make the default security posture stronger—reducing the number of recommended security settings administrators must configure and maintain manually. For supported on-premises server workloads, it starts with a validated and tested secure-by-default configuration from initial deployment, while preserving administrator control. Building on protections available today, it progressively establishes and maintains more of the recommended security posture through the products themselves, adapting the baseline as threats and Microsoft security guidance evolve. The result is less manual effort and a stronger security posture maintained increasingly through the products themselves. We’re advancing this work across three areas: Patch, Configure, and Protect. Figure 1: On-Premises Baseline Security Mode builds on capabilities available today across Patch, Configure, and Protect, with greater automation and stronger defaults coming over time. Patch: close known vulnerabilities faster The need is clear in our deployment data: many Exchange Server deployments are not running the current security update, including a substantial share on unsupported versions. Closing this protection gap requires both releasing fixes faster and helping customers apply them sooner. Today. Since September 2026, Microsoft has released not only Critical but also Important security updates outside the traditional Patch Tuesday schedule when faster action is needed, helping customers address known vulnerabilities sooner. Next. In Q1 calendar year 2027, we’re targeting automatic application of security updates after a fixed period following release in connected SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server environments. Release fixes faster, then help those fixes reach servers faster. Configure: make the safer posture easier to maintain Security requires more than current software. Configuration and permissions can drift over time, creating gaps between the intended security posture and the environment administrators are operating. Customers need a clearer way to identify those gaps, establish recommended settings, and maintain them as environments evolve. Today. Tenant Configuration Management can help customers assess supported SharePoint, Exchange, and Skype for Business Server environments and identify where permissions are broader than intended. Next. In Q1 2027, we plan to introduce hardened default configurations for SharePoint Server, Exchange Server, and Skype for Business Server, moving from identifying configuration risk toward establishing Microsoft-recommended security settings by default. We also plan to identify configuration drift so administrators can see when environments move away from that baseline. Make the safer configuration easier to establish and harder to unintentionally lose. Protect: reduce exposure when threats can’t wait for a patch Some threats emerge before a permanent security update is available and fully deployed. During that window, customers need mitigations that can reduce exposure quickly without replacing the underlying security update. Today. Emergency Mitigation Service can automatically apply interim mitigations for certain emerging vulnerabilities, helping reduce exposure while a permanent security update is prepared and deployed. Mitigation addresses the immediate risk; the security update addresses the underlying vulnerability. Next. In December 2026, we plan to introduce Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 for Exchange Server and Skype for Business Server, enabling it by default and expanding the security mitigations it can apply. In January 2027, we are planning to extend Emergency Mitigation Service 2.0 to cover SharePoint Server. When threats move faster, protection needs to move faster too. Act today, prepare for what comes next Taken together, these investments represent an important shift: from providing customers with security guidance and tools toward building the recommended security posture into the products themselves. Microsoft continues to recommend moving workloads to Microsoft 365 wherever possible. Start by identifying which workloads can move and which must remain on-premises. For those that remain, move to supported releases, assess exposure, apply current security updates, and enable available protections. The Exchange Server, SharePoint Server, and Skype for Business Server teams will publish additional guidance on available protections, upcoming capabilities, and actions customers can take now. We also plan to bring practitioner-focused on-premises guidance to Secure Now to help organizations assess their environment, identify critical actions, and prioritize the steps they can take. Join us at Microsoft Ignite for Secure your on-prem estate (BRK215) to explore the initiative, upcoming investments, and steps you can take now. Modernize where you can. Strengthen the security of what must remain.
