items.title: Detecting and Controlling Hidden DNS Tunnel Attacks
items.summary: DNS turns domain names into IP addresses, and many network services depend on it. Attackers know that. They abuse DNS tunneling to build covert channels for data exfiltration and command-and-control (C2), hiding malicious traffic inside what looks like ordinary DNS queries. Many firewalls let DNS through with little inspection, which is part of why the technique works. This guide covers common DNS tunneling detection methods, how to read a DNS tunneling PCAP, and how to prevent, block, and mitigate tunnels. What is a DNS Tunneling Attack? In a DNS tunneling attack, the attacker packs data into DNS queries and responses so a compromised machine can talk to a server the attacker controls. Because DNS traffic often passes through firewalls uninspected, the channel stays hidden from most security controls. Tunnels run both ways. Outbound queries can carry stolen data, and the responses can bring commands, payloads, or extra tools back in, so watch inbound DNS responses too, not just outbound queries. MITRE ATT&CK tracks this behavior as T1071.004 (Application Layer Protocol: DNS) [1] . Its procedure examples include OilRig’s BONDUPDATER malware, which uses TXT records in a DNS tunneling protocol, Cobalt Group, which has used DNS tunneling for C2, and Ember Bear, which has used tools such as dnscat2 and Iodine. Open-source tools such as iodine and dnscat2 are common examples, and MITRE’s DNS tunneling detection analytics reference both. How DNS Tunneling Works DNS Tunneling Detection Techniques What Are the Common Methods to Detect DNS Tunneling? Teams usually combine several methods, since no single indicator confirms tunneling on its own: Payload analysis: query length, entropy, encoding, and record types Traffic analysis: query volume, unique subdomains, NXDOMAIN rates, and response sizes Behavioral and anomaly detection against DNS baselines Threat intelligence and domain reputation matching PCAP review to confirm and investigate suspected tunnels Critical Incident Response: Key Steps for the First 72 Hours What data has been potentially exposed? Incursion detection and Persistence detection How should I respond? Read the Guide Detection matters because tunneled traffic often passes through controls that never inspect DNS. Greg Farnham’s Detecting DNS Tunneling (GIAC GCIA Gold Certification paper, 2013) describes two main approaches: payload analysis, which looks at individual DNS requests, and traffic analysis, which looks at communication patterns over time. The paper is more than a decade old, but later surveys still use the same split, and the sections below add current guidance. Both approaches work better alongside behavioral analytics , threat intelligence, and endpoint context. Combinations matter more than any single signal. Many long, high-entropy, unique subdomains under one domain, sustained over time, make a stronger pattern than any one anomaly. Signals such as TTL, record type, NXDOMAIN rate, and destination geography are useful context, but they also appear in legitimate traffic. 1. Payload Analysis: Examining DNS Query Structures Payload analysis means inspecting individual DNS requests for anything that looks off. Key Indicators: Query Length: Tunneling often produces unusually long domain names and subdomain labels. DNS caps labels at 63 characters and full names at 253 in text form (RFC 1035 [2] ), but attackers get around that by spreading encoded data across several labels. Character Composition & Entropy: Tunneling queries tend to look random. They show high entropy, with no recognizable words and nothing a person would type. Uncommon Record Types: Attackers may abuse TXT, NULL, and CNAME records. TXT records can carry encoded text, and CNAME records can form part of a tunnel through encoded names and responses. Tunnels also work over ordinary A and AAAA records, and legitimate software uses TXT and CNAME records too, so no record type is a tunneling signal on its own. Detection Method: Flag and investigate DNS queries above a length threshold, such as 52 characters, and tune it to your environment. Watch for unusual volumes of TXT, NULL, or CNAME responses, and treat them as a reason to look closer, not a verdict. Apply entropy-based detection to find encoded payloads in subdomains. Use regular expressions to catch Base32, Base64, or hex-encoded patterns inside domain names. These thresholds are starting points. CDNs, cloud services, and security tools also produce long, random-looking names, so tune them to your environment. 2. Traffic Analysis: Identifying Suspicious DNS Query Patterns Traffic analysis looks at DNS activity as a whole, because tunneling leaves patterns that no single query shows. Key Indicators: High Query Volume: Tunnels move data in lots of small queries, so a sudden jump in DNS volume can point to one. Low-and-slow tunnels may not spike at all, and MITRE notes that DNS beacons can be hard to detect because they communicate infrequently. Frequent Queries to a Single Domain: Attackers register and control the domains they tunnel through. Heavy request rates to one domain deserve a look. A newly registered domain adds context, but domain age alone isn’t a strong signal. NXDOMAIN Response Volume: Tunneling tools often trigger failed lookups by querying subdomains that don’t exist. A lot of NXDOMAIN responses can be a supporting signal, though typos and misconfigurations cause failed lookups too. Unusual Geographic Destinations: Queries to name servers in regions where you have no business presence can add weight to other signals, but not on their own. DNS and CDN infrastructure is often spread around the world. Large or Asymmetric Responses: Large responses, or a high ratio of response bytes to query bytes, can mean data is coming in, particularly alongside other indicators. Detection Method: Watch query frequency per source IP. Sudden spikes are worth a look. Count the unique subdomains under each domain. Tunnels tend to generate a new subdomain for nearly every request. Track NXDOMAIN responses and flag hosts with lots of failed lookups. Treat unusually short TTL (Time to Live) values as supporting context only. Attacker infrastructure uses short TTLs, and so do legitimate DNS services, so weigh them alongside domain age, reputation, and query behavior. Compare response size to query size per domain. 3. Encrypted DNS Considerations (DoH, DoT, and DoQ) Watching port 53 won’t show you tunnels that run over encrypted DNS, and each protocol behaves differently. The ports below are defaults, and clients and servers can agree to use others, so port-based controls alone aren’t airtight. DoH [3] usually runs over HTTPS on TCP port 443 and can also use HTTP/3 over QUIC. That lets it blend in with ordinary web traffic, so port-based monitoring alone can’t tell them apart. You can look at known DoH resolver destinations, connection metadata , traffic patterns, and endpoint or browser telemetry. Wherever you can, enforce approved enterprise resolvers and compare network activity with resolver logs. MITRE’s T1071.004 page lists BRICKSTORM as having used DoH to resolve C2 infrastructure and obscure DNS traffic from inspection, and Brute Ratel C4 as able to use DoH for C2. DoT [4] usually uses TCP port 853, which makes unapproved connections easy to spot and restrict. DoQ [5] runs over QUIC, typically on UDP port 853. RFC 9250 also allows another port by agreement, including 443. Treat it the way you treat DoT. Without decryption or resolver logs, network monitoring sees only connection metadata, such as destinations, timing, volume, and TLS handshake details. It can’t see query names or record types inside the encrypted session. When visibility is limited, resolver logs from resolvers you control, endpoint telemetry , and policies that control which resolvers endpoints can use help fill the gap. 4. Behavioral and Anomaly Detection Fixed thresholds are easy for attackers to tune around, so behavioral detection adds the context thresholds lack. MITRE ATT&CK’s DNS tunneling detection strategy (DET0400 [6] ), updated in May 2026, covers high-frequency queries from unusual processes, long or frequent subdomains, encoded query patterns, and lookups tied to known malicious infrastructure. It spans Windows, Linux, macOS, network devices, and ESXi hosts. That analysis depends on what you can see. With visible DNS, models can work from query names, timing, volume, and destinations. With encrypted DNS and no resolver logs, they have only connection metadata, such as flow size, timing, and direction, and can’t inspect the queries themselves. Machine learning is an active research area for both cases, including DoH tunnel detection from flow features, but accuracy depends on training data, features, and baselines. It works best next to rule-based and threat intelligence detection. Detection Method: Baseline normal DNS per host, segment, or asset role, and alert on deviations. Combine entropy, query volume, timing, and the ratio of unique subdomains to total queries instead of leaning on one signal. If you have endpoint telemetry, check which process made the queries. Fidelis NDR takes this approach through Network Behavior Analysis , which learns baselines for long subdomain names and unique subdomain counts per domain. 5. DNS Tunneling PCAP Analysis A DNS tunneling PCAP is often the quickest way to confirm a suspicion. None of the filters below is a detection rule. Each one narrows a capture so you can review it, so correlate what you find. Detection Method: Find long query names with dns.qry.name.len > 52 && dns.flags.response == 0. The second condition limits results to queries, since responses repeat the query name. Review TXT (dns.qry.type 16) and NULL (dns.qry.type 10) traffic, but don’t rely on record type alone. Tunnels also use A, AAAA, and CNAME records, and TXT has legitimate uses. Review failed lookups with dns.flags.rcode == 3 (NXDOMAIN). This applies to responses, so match each one back to the client’s query. Pull fields out at scale with tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns.qry.name.len > 52 && dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name. Use ipv6.src for IPv6 traffic. Count unique subdomains per parent domain, sort by source IP, and look for evenly spaced queries. Check domain age and reputation, and rule out CDNs, cloud load balancers, update services, and security appliances, which legitimately generate long names. Record confirmed domains, resolvers, and hosts as indicators for blocklists and threat intelligence. One caveat: a PCAP of encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, or DoQ) won’t show query names unless you can decrypt the traffic or get matching resolver logs. Field names can also differ slightly between Wireshark versions, so test the filters on yours. How to Mitigate DNS Tunneling Attacks? Detection matters, but DNS tunneling prevention and mitigation take more than detection. These are the strategies that work best, including ways to block DNS tunneling at the resolver and at network egress: 1. Implement DNS Filtering & Threat Intelligence DNS filtering blocks malicious requests before they reach their destination, and pairing it with live threat intelligence lets you block known bad domains early. It’s a good first layer, but it can’t catch infrastructure nobody has listed yet. Actionable Steps: Deploy real-time threat intelligence feeds to track suspicious domains. Block or risk-score newly registered domains (NRDs). Use them as one signal alongside reputation and query behavior, not a standalone indicator, since new domains aren’t always malicious. Block domains categorized as DNS tunneling or known malicious at the resolver using protective DNS. Restrict DNS queries to external resolvers to prevent bypassing security policies. 2. Monitor & Analyze DNS Traffic Patterns Tunneling depends on high query volumes and odd request patterns, so continuous monitoring will show deviations from normal behavior. This is how you catch the tunnels blocklists miss, though it only works if you log enough DNS and have a baseline to compare against. Actionable Steps: Establish baselines for normal DNS traffic to detect anomalies . Monitor query volume per domain. High volumes to a single domain may indicate tunneling. Apply behavioral analytics and machine learning to spot unusual DNS query sequences, subdomain patterns, and traffic characteristics. For encrypted DNS, that means connection metadata unless you have resolver logs. 3. Implement DNSSEC Validation DNSSEC helps authenticate DNS responses and protects against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning. It does not prevent or detect DNS tunneling, and it does not encrypt DNS traffic. RFC 4033 [7] describes it as providing origin authentication and integrity protection, not confidentiality. Treat DNSSEC validation as one part of your DNS security strategy, next to traffic monitoring, resolver restrictions, and behavioral detection. Actionable Steps: Implement DNSSEC validation on recursive resolvers to catch forged or tampered responses. Sign your own zones so other resolvers can validate your records. Regularly audit DNS configurations to detect unauthorized changes. 4. Apply Query Rate Limiting & Anomaly Detection Attackers need lots of queries to move data through a tunnel, so rate limiting can slow them down. It works best where baselines are stable, like servers that should barely touch DNS. It slows a tunnel but won’t detect or stop one by itself. Actionable Steps: Set query-frequency thresholds from your baselines. Test them first and consider alerting before you enforce, because aggressive limits can break legitimate applications and DNS-dependent services. Limit allowed record types, such as NULL, where there’s no business need. Record type alone isn’t a reliable control, so pair it with behavioral detection. Review unusually short TTL values alongside domain age and reputation, since legitimate services use them too. 5. Restrict Direct External DNS Resolutions Many tunneling tools skip internal security by sending queries straight to external resolvers. Blocking that forces everything through resolvers you monitor, and it removes the easiest bypass these tools have. Actionable Steps: Configure firewall rules to block direct outbound DNS queries to public resolvers. Require all DNS queries to pass through internal resolvers for logging and monitoring. Implement split-horizon DNS to separate internal and external query handling. Allow outbound DNS only from approved resolvers and block direct port 53 traffic from other hosts. Control encrypted DNS: restrict DoT (TCP 853) and DoQ (UDP 853) to approved resolvers, keeping in mind that these are default ports, set browser and OS policies to use the enterprise resolver, and block or alert on known public DoH endpoints. That only covers resolvers you know about, so enforce approved resolvers at the endpoint as well. Investigate hosts that keep trying to reach unapproved resolvers, including the process behind the attempts. 6. Educate Employees & Conduct Regular Security Audits Many successful DNS tunneling attacks start with phishing or a compromised endpoint, so awareness and audits cut risk at the entry point. They cover how tunneling malware gets in and whether DNS settings have drifted, but they don’t replace technical controls. Actionable Steps: Conduct regular security training on identifying DNS-related threats. Perform routine DNS audits to detect unauthorized changes or misconfigurations. 7. Validate DNS Tunneling Defenses Through Penetration Testing Controls only count if they work. Authorized penetration testing with advanced tunneling and data exfiltration techniques shows whether your detection and blocking hold up before a real attacker tests them for you. Run it only against systems you own or have written permission to test. What to Validate: Whether tunneling attempts trigger alerts, and how fast. Whether low-and-slow tunneling, with a low query rate and shorter labels, gets past your detection. Whether test hosts can reach unauthorized resolvers or encrypted DNS endpoints. Whether your incident response process finds the source endpoint and contains it. Use test domains and resolvers you control, and send synthetic data, never real customer or employee data. Decide in advance whether the SOC knows about the test, and record what each control caught or missed. Get written approval first, save a PCAP of each test for tuning, and retest after fixes. Stopping DNS tunneling takes more than one control. Combine real-time threat intelligence , continuous DNS monitoring, resolver and egress controls, and behavioral detection so you can detect, block, and prevent covert tunneling. DNSSEC belongs in the baseline, but it is not a tunneling control. How Fidelis Network Detection and Response (NDR) Enhances DNS Security Fidelis Network ® is a network detection and response (NDR) solution built to catch advanced threats, DNS tunneling included. It offers deep network visibility and automated threat detection, plus response capabilities. Payload and traffic inspection are complemented by Network Behavior Analysis, which learns what normal DNS looks like and flags deviations. 1. Deep DNS Traffic Inspection Deep Session Inspection ® (DSI) reassembles full sessions and records rich metadata, which helps security teams investigate anomalous DNS queries and responses. Detects high-entropy DNS payloads, unusually long subdomains, and suspicious DNS request patterns linked to tunneling. Provides real-time analytics to flag unauthorized data exfiltration attempts. For encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, and DoQ), visibility without decryption comes from session metadata, not from the contents of the queries. 2. Integrated Threat Intelligence Fidelis Network ® uses real-time threat intelligence feeds to correlate DNS queries with known malicious indicators. It also integrates with STIX/TAXII feeds, Suricata rules, and proprietary Fidelis Insight ® intelligence. Helps surface emerging DNS-based attack techniques earlier. 3. Detecting Lateral Movement & Data Exfiltration Monitors east-west traffic within internal networks to detect attackers leveraging DNS tunnels for covert data transfers. Flags repetitive DNS requests to untrusted domains, an indicator of potential C2 communication or staged data exfiltration. Uses behavioral analytics to identify deviations from normal DNS usage patterns. Fidelis Network ® Behavior Analysis compares DNS behavior against established baselines and flags unusually long subdomain names, a high number of unique subdomains for a domain, rare domain usage, and DNS activity that’s abnormal for an asset. Any of these can mean DNS is being used as a covert channel for command-and-control or data movement. Fidelis Network ® goes beyond traditional detection by automating threat analysis, correlating alerts, and supporting rapid incident response . Teams using it get: Comprehensive network visibility: analysis of network activity across ports and protocols, including useful metadata from encrypted connections. Automated threat correlation: fewer false positives and faster decision-making. Proactive threat hunting : a way for security teams to detect threats before they cause harm. Unlock Powerful Network Security with Fidelis NDR See how Fidelis NDR boosts security with: Comprehensive Threat Detection & Analysis Data Loss Prevention (DLP) & Email Security Deep Session Inspection & TLS Profiling Download the Datasheet Conclusion DNS tunneling is still an effective way for attackers to steal data and keep a covert line open. But payload analysis, traffic analysis, behavioral detection, PCAP review, and NDR such as Fidelis Network ® give you a real chance to detect, block, and mitigate it. Frequently Asked Questions Does using encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, or DoQ) prevent DNS tunneling? No. Encrypted DNS protocols such as DoH, DoT, and DoQ protect privacy, but they don’t stop tunneling, and attackers can use those same channels. Without decryption or resolver logs, network monitoring sees only connection metadata, so behavioral analysis of that metadata and control over which resolvers endpoints can use matter more. What industries are most targeted by DNS tunneling? Finance, healthcare, and government are frequently targeted because they hold sensitive data and face persistent threats. Can DNS tunneling be used for legitimate purposes? Yes. Some organizations use DNS tunneling for secure remote access or to get around network restrictions. Because attackers abuse it too, unrestricted DNS traffic is a real security risk. What are the common methods to detect DNS tunneling? The main ones are payload analysis, traffic analysis, behavioral detection, and threat intelligence matching. Most teams use several, since no single indicator confirms tunneling. The detection techniques section above goes into each one. How do you block DNS tunneling? Route all DNS through approved, monitored resolvers, block direct outbound DNS and unapproved encrypted DNS, and filter known malicious domains with protective DNS. Behavioral detection covers what blocklists miss. How do you analyze a DNS tunneling PCAP? Filter for long query names, uncommon record types, and NXDOMAIN responses. Then confirm with unique subdomain counts, timing, and domain reputation. No single filter proves tunneling, and encrypted DNS won’t show query names unless you decrypt it.   • Apply entropy-based detection to find encoded payloads in subdomains.
  • Use regular expressions to catch Base32, Base64, or hex-encoded patterns inside domain names.
  • These thresholds are starting points. CDNs, cloud services, and security tools also produce long, random-looking names, so tune them to your environment.
2. Traffic Analysis: Identifying Suspicious DNS Query Patterns

Traffic analysis looks at DNS activity as a whole, because tunneling leaves patterns that no single query shows.

Key Indicators: 
  • High Query Volume: Tunnels move data in lots of small queries, so a sudden jump in DNS volume can point to one. Low-and-slow tunnels may not spike at all, and MITRE notes that DNS beacons can be hard to detect because they communicate infrequently.
  • Frequent Queries to a Single Domain: Attackers register and control the domains they tunnel through. Heavy request rates to one domain deserve a look. A newly registered domain adds context, but domain age alone isn’t a strong signal.
  • NXDOMAIN Response Volume: Tunneling tools often trigger failed lookups by querying subdomains that don’t exist. A lot of NXDOMAIN responses can be a supporting signal, though typos and misconfigurations cause failed lookups too.
  • Unusual Geographic Destinations: Queries to name servers in regions where you have no business presence can add weight to other signals, but not on their own. DNS and CDN infrastructure is often spread around the world.
  • Large or Asymmetric Responses: Large responses, or a high ratio of response bytes to query bytes, can mean data is coming in, particularly alongside other indicators.
Detection Method:
  • Watch query frequency per source IP. Sudden spikes are worth a look.
  • Count the unique subdomains under each domain. Tunnels tend to generate a new subdomain for nearly every request.
  • Track NXDOMAIN responses and flag hosts with lots of failed lookups.
  • Treat unusually short TTL (Time to Live) values as supporting context only. Attacker infrastructure uses short TTLs, and so do legitimate DNS services, so weigh them alongside domain age, reputation, and query behavior.
  • Compare response size to query size per domain.
3. Encrypted DNS Considerations (DoH, DoT, and DoQ)

Watching port 53 won’t show you tunnels that run over encrypted DNS, and each protocol behaves differently. The ports below are defaults, and clients and servers can agree to use others, so port-based controls alone aren’t airtight.

  • DoH[3] usually runs over HTTPS on TCP port 443 and can also use HTTP/3 over QUIC. That lets it blend in with ordinary web traffic, so port-based monitoring alone can’t tell them apart. You can look at known DoH resolver destinations, connection metadata, traffic patterns, and endpoint or browser telemetry. Wherever you can, enforce approved enterprise resolvers and compare network activity with resolver logs. MITRE’s T1071.004 page lists BRICKSTORM as having used DoH to resolve C2 infrastructure and obscure DNS traffic from inspection, and Brute Ratel C4 as able to use DoH for C2.
  • DoT[4] usually uses TCP port 853, which makes unapproved connections easy to spot and restrict.
  • DoQ[5] runs over QUIC, typically on UDP port 853. RFC 9250 also allows another port by agreement, including 443. Treat it the way you treat DoT.

Without decryption or resolver logs, network monitoring sees only connection metadata, such as destinations, timing, volume, and TLS handshake details. It can’t see query names or record types inside the encrypted session. When visibility is limited, resolver logs from resolvers you control, endpoint telemetry, and policies that control which resolvers endpoints can use help fill the gap.

4. Behavioral and Anomaly Detection

Fixed thresholds are easy for attackers to tune around, so behavioral detection adds the context thresholds lack. MITRE ATT&CK’s DNS tunneling detection strategy (DET0400[6]), updated in May 2026, covers high-frequency queries from unusual processes, long or frequent subdomains, encoded query patterns, and lookups tied to known malicious infrastructure. It spans Windows, Linux, macOS, network devices, and ESXi hosts.

That analysis depends on what you can see. With visible DNS, models can work from query names, timing, volume, and destinations. With encrypted DNS and no resolver logs, they have only connection metadata, such as flow size, timing, and direction, and can’t inspect the queries themselves. Machine learning is an active research area for both cases, including DoH tunnel detection from flow features, but accuracy depends on training data, features, and baselines. It works best next to rule-based and threat intelligence detection.

Detection Method:
  • Baseline normal DNS per host, segment, or asset role, and alert on deviations.
  • Combine entropy, query volume, timing, and the ratio of unique subdomains to total queries instead of leaning on one signal.
  • If you have endpoint telemetry, check which process made the queries.

Fidelis NDR takes this approach through Network Behavior Analysis, which learns baselines for long subdomain names and unique subdomain counts per domain.

5. DNS Tunneling PCAP Analysis

A DNS tunneling PCAP is often the quickest way to confirm a suspicion. None of the filters below is a detection rule. Each one narrows a capture so you can review it, so correlate what you find.

Detection Method:
  • Find long query names with dns.qry.name.len > 52 && dns.flags.response == 0. The second condition limits results to queries, since responses repeat the query name.
  • Review TXT (dns.qry.type 16) and NULL (dns.qry.type 10) traffic, but don’t rely on record type alone. Tunnels also use A, AAAA, and CNAME records, and TXT has legitimate uses.
  • Review failed lookups with dns.flags.rcode == 3 (NXDOMAIN). This applies to responses, so match each one back to the client’s query.
  • Pull fields out at scale with tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "dns.qry.name.len > 52 && dns.flags.response == 0" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e dns.qry.name. Use ipv6.src for IPv6 traffic.
  • Count unique subdomains per parent domain, sort by source IP, and look for evenly spaced queries.
  • Check domain age and reputation, and rule out CDNs, cloud load balancers, update services, and security appliances, which legitimately generate long names.
  • Record confirmed domains, resolvers, and hosts as indicators for blocklists and threat intelligence.

One caveat: a PCAP of encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, or DoQ) won’t show query names unless you can decrypt the traffic or get matching resolver logs. Field names can also differ slightly between Wireshark versions, so test the filters on yours.

How to Mitigate DNS Tunneling Attacks?

Detection matters, but DNS tunneling prevention and mitigation take more than detection. These are the strategies that work best, including ways to block DNS tunneling at the resolver and at network egress:

1. Implement DNS Filtering & Threat Intelligence

DNS filtering blocks malicious requests before they reach their destination, and pairing it with live threat intelligence lets you block known bad domains early. It’s a good first layer, but it can’t catch infrastructure nobody has listed yet.

Actionable Steps: 
  • Deploy real-time threat intelligence feeds to track suspicious domains.
  • Block or risk-score newly registered domains (NRDs). Use them as one signal alongside reputation and query behavior, not a standalone indicator, since new domains aren’t always malicious.
  • Block domains categorized as DNS tunneling or known malicious at the resolver using protective DNS.
  • Restrict DNS queries to external resolvers to prevent bypassing security policies.
2. Monitor & Analyze DNS Traffic Patterns

Tunneling depends on high query volumes and odd request patterns, so continuous monitoring will show deviations from normal behavior. This is how you catch the tunnels blocklists miss, though it only works if you log enough DNS and have a baseline to compare against.

Actionable Steps:
  • Establish baselines for normal DNS traffic to detect anomalies.
  • Monitor query volume per domain. High volumes to a single domain may indicate tunneling.
  • Apply behavioral analytics and machine learning to spot unusual DNS query sequences, subdomain patterns, and traffic characteristics. For encrypted DNS, that means connection metadata unless you have resolver logs.
3. Implement DNSSEC Validation

DNSSEC helps authenticate DNS responses and protects against DNS spoofing and cache poisoning. It does not prevent or detect DNS tunneling, and it does not encrypt DNS traffic. RFC 4033[7] describes it as providing origin authentication and integrity protection, not confidentiality. Treat DNSSEC validation as one part of your DNS security strategy, next to traffic monitoring, resolver restrictions, and behavioral detection.

Actionable Steps: 
  • Implement DNSSEC validation on recursive resolvers to catch forged or tampered responses.
  • Sign your own zones so other resolvers can validate your records.
  • Regularly audit DNS configurations to detect unauthorized changes.
4. Apply Query Rate Limiting & Anomaly Detection

Attackers need lots of queries to move data through a tunnel, so rate limiting can slow them down. It works best where baselines are stable, like servers that should barely touch DNS. It slows a tunnel but won’t detect or stop one by itself.

Actionable Steps: 
  • Set query-frequency thresholds from your baselines. Test them first and consider alerting before you enforce, because aggressive limits can break legitimate applications and DNS-dependent services.
  • Limit allowed record types, such as NULL, where there’s no business need. Record type alone isn’t a reliable control, so pair it with behavioral detection.
  • Review unusually short TTL values alongside domain age and reputation, since legitimate services use them too.
5. Restrict Direct External DNS Resolutions

Many tunneling tools skip internal security by sending queries straight to external resolvers. Blocking that forces everything through resolvers you monitor, and it removes the easiest bypass these tools have.

Actionable Steps: 
  • Configure firewall rules to block direct outbound DNS queries to public resolvers.
  • Require all DNS queries to pass through internal resolvers for logging and monitoring.
  • Implement split-horizon DNS to separate internal and external query handling.
  • Allow outbound DNS only from approved resolvers and block direct port 53 traffic from other hosts.
  • Control encrypted DNS: restrict DoT (TCP 853) and DoQ (UDP 853) to approved resolvers, keeping in mind that these are default ports, set browser and OS policies to use the enterprise resolver, and block or alert on known public DoH endpoints. That only covers resolvers you know about, so enforce approved resolvers at the endpoint as well.
  • Investigate hosts that keep trying to reach unapproved resolvers, including the process behind the attempts.
6. Educate Employees & Conduct Regular Security Audits

Many successful DNS tunneling attacks start with phishing or a compromised endpoint, so awareness and audits cut risk at the entry point. They cover how tunneling malware gets in and whether DNS settings have drifted, but they don’t replace technical controls.

Actionable Steps: 
  • Conduct regular security training on identifying DNS-related threats.
  • Perform routine DNS audits to detect unauthorized changes or misconfigurations.
7. Validate DNS Tunneling Defenses Through Penetration Testing

Controls only count if they work. Authorized penetration testing with advanced tunneling and data exfiltration techniques shows whether your detection and blocking hold up before a real attacker tests them for you. Run it only against systems you own or have written permission to test.

What to Validate:
  • Whether tunneling attempts trigger alerts, and how fast.
  • Whether low-and-slow tunneling, with a low query rate and shorter labels, gets past your detection.
  • Whether test hosts can reach unauthorized resolvers or encrypted DNS endpoints.
  • Whether your incident response process finds the source endpoint and contains it.
  • Use test domains and resolvers you control, and send synthetic data, never real customer or employee data.
  • Decide in advance whether the SOC knows about the test, and record what each control caught or missed.
  • Get written approval first, save a PCAP of each test for tuning, and retest after fixes.

Stopping DNS tunneling takes more than one control. Combine real-time threat intelligence, continuous DNS monitoring, resolver and egress controls, and behavioral detection so you can detect, block, and prevent covert tunneling. DNSSEC belongs in the baseline, but it is not a tunneling control.

How Fidelis Network Detection and Response (NDR) Enhances DNS Security

Fidelis Network® is a network detection and response (NDR) solution built to catch advanced threats, DNS tunneling included. It offers deep network visibility and automated threat detection, plus response capabilities. Payload and traffic inspection are complemented by Network Behavior Analysis, which learns what normal DNS looks like and flags deviations.

1. Deep DNS Traffic Inspection
  • Deep Session Inspection® (DSI) reassembles full sessions and records rich metadata, which helps security teams investigate anomalous DNS queries and responses.
  • Detects high-entropy DNS payloads, unusually long subdomains, and suspicious DNS request patterns linked to tunneling.
  • Provides real-time analytics to flag unauthorized data exfiltration attempts.
  • For encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, and DoQ), visibility without decryption comes from session metadata, not from the contents of the queries.
2. Integrated Threat Intelligence
  • Fidelis Network® uses real-time threat intelligence feeds to correlate DNS queries with known malicious indicators.
  • It also integrates with STIX/TAXII feeds, Suricata rules, and proprietary Fidelis Insight® intelligence.
  • Helps surface emerging DNS-based attack techniques earlier.
3. Detecting Lateral Movement & Data Exfiltration
  • Monitors east-west traffic within internal networks to detect attackers leveraging DNS tunnels for covert data transfers.
  • Flags repetitive DNS requests to untrusted domains, an indicator of potential C2 communication or staged data exfiltration.
  • Uses behavioral analytics to identify deviations from normal DNS usage patterns. Fidelis Network® Behavior Analysis compares DNS behavior against established baselines and flags unusually long subdomain names, a high number of unique subdomains for a domain, rare domain usage, and DNS activity that’s abnormal for an asset. Any of these can mean DNS is being used as a covert channel for command-and-control or data movement.

Fidelis Network® goes beyond traditional detection by automating threat analysis, correlating alerts, and supporting rapid incident response. Teams using it get:

  1. Comprehensive network visibility: analysis of network activity across ports and protocols, including useful metadata from encrypted connections.
  2. Automated threat correlation: fewer false positives and faster decision-making.
  3. Proactive threat hunting: a way for security teams to detect threats before they cause harm.

Conclusion

DNS tunneling is still an effective way for attackers to steal data and keep a covert line open. But payload analysis, traffic analysis, behavioral detection, PCAP review, and NDR such as Fidelis Network® give you a real chance to detect, block, and mitigate it.

Frequently Asked Questions
Does using encrypted DNS (DoH, DoT, or DoQ) prevent DNS tunneling?

No. Encrypted DNS protocols such as DoH, DoT, and DoQ protect privacy, but they don’t stop tunneling, and attackers can use those same channels. Without decryption or resolver logs, network monitoring sees only connection metadata, so behavioral analysis of that metadata and control over which resolvers endpoints can use matter more.

What industries are most targeted by DNS tunneling?

Finance, healthcare, and government are frequently targeted because they hold sensitive data and face persistent threats.

Can DNS tunneling be used for legitimate purposes?

Yes. Some organizations use DNS tunneling for secure remote access or to get around network restrictions. Because attackers abuse it too, unrestricted DNS traffic is a real security risk.

What are the common methods to detect DNS tunneling?

The main ones are payload analysis, traffic analysis, behavioral detection, and threat intelligence matching. Most teams use several, since no single indicator confirms tunneling. The detection techniques section above goes into each one.

How do you block DNS tunneling?

Route all DNS through approved, monitored resolvers, block direct outbound DNS and unapproved encrypted DNS, and filter known malicious domains with protective DNS. Behavioral detection covers what blocklists miss.

How do you analyze a DNS tunneling PCAP?

Filter for long query names, uncommon record types, and NXDOMAIN responses. Then confirm with unique subdomain counts, timing, and domain reputation. No single filter proves tunneling, and encrypted DNS won’t show query names unless you decrypt it.

items.title: HYFLOCK Ransomware Encrypts Only First 4KB of Larger Files, Leaves Parts of Victims’ Files Accessible
items.summary: HYFLOCK ransomware has an encryption weakness that leaves parts of larger files readable, giving affected organizations a limited chance to recover data without paying attackers. In the October 17 build, the malware encrypted only the first 4,096 bytes of larger files examined during testing, leaving content beyond that section accessible. The finding does not mean victims can unlock everything. Researchers recovered selected contents from encrypted Microsoft Office files, but did not restore complete documents or produce a general decryptor. An earlier October build presented a different danger: a processing defect could permanently discard file data, potentially preventing full recovery even with the correct key. Check Point Exposure Management researchers identified the updated HYFLOCK builds through threat hunting, tracing four generations from April through October 2026. Their published investigation into HYFLOCK separates observed behavior from operator claims, revealing stronger deployment features alongside uneven file processing. HYFLOCK Ransomware The October 17 sample produced 17 validated encrypted files. Fourteen larger files recorded an encrypted prefix of 4,096 bytes, while three smaller files were encrypted across their complete original lengths. Configuration settings indicated full encryption, but those settings did not match the larger files’ actual condition. Partial encryption also appears in other ransomware families. For example, Gunra’s configurable partial encryption lets attackers select how much content to encrypt. HYFLOCK’s finding, however, is specific to the tested build and collected files; it should not be treated as universal behavior across the family. Examining the untouched content, researchers recovered 73 internal components from seven encrypted Office files, including worksheet and shared-string data. Changes in HYFLOCK’s ransomware execution (Source – Check Point) Those components passed cyclic redundancy checks, supporting their integrity. The result demonstrates partial recovery, not decryption: the encrypted prefixes remained unavailable without matching key material or an exact trusted copy. The malware uses 16-byte symmetric keys, AES counter-mode processing, and RSA protection for recovery material. Each validated October 17 output retained its original-length body and added a 556-byte trailer containing encryption metadata and a wrapped key. Researchers recovered neither a plaintext encryption key nor an RSA private key. Recovery risks extend beyond inaccessible prefixes. The earlier October build could omit data during processing, echoing the broader problem illustrated by VECT’s damaging recovery flaws , where implementation errors undermine restoration. HYFLOCK can also continue encrypting when key wrapping or backup storage fails, creating another potential barrier to recovery. Updated Rust Encryptor Expands Deployment and Recovery Risks HYFLOCK appeared in underground promotion in March 2026 as a Ransomware-as-a-Service offering. By October 13, its leak site carried eight victim claims across manufacturing, business services, government, retail, and telecommunications. These remain unverified attacker claims; the investigation did not establish the victims’ initial compromise routes. The April sample already contained a Windows ransomware core written in Rust. July added a separate loader carrying the payload, configuration, and key material. An earlier October version used a Go carrier, while the October 17 build returned to a standalone Rust executable that copied itself into an update-like directory. During controlled testing, the newer build registered a scheduled task, processed network-share resources, and attempted to disrupt recovery. It generated 500 successful ransomware-extension renames, although only 17 collected files were independently validated as encrypted. Those counts describe different observations and should not be treated as interchangeable measures of damage. Recovery interference is also documented in Gentlemen ransomware’s backup disruption , but HYFLOCK’s results require qualification. Its recovery-sabotage commands had varied outcomes, and complete deletion of recovery objects was not proven. Likewise, administrative-share activity did not establish compromise of another computer. Successful domain-wide propagation was not observed, and Group Policy spreading was disabled in the recovered configuration. Advertised vulnerable-driver attacks and reliable execution after remote desktop sessions ended also remained unverified. Defenders should preserve affected files and execution evidence, then review scheduled tasks, share access, segmentation, and recovery protections before attempting restoration. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Source-confirmed artifact Investigative relevance Staging path ProgramData\EdgeUpdate_ \eu.exe October background-execution copy Configuration eu.cfg Staged execution settings Key-backup file system_config.dat Protected recovery-material storage File extension .locked_ October 17 rename pattern Trailer marker HFLKEY01 Validated encrypted-file structure Share artifact .hyflock_claim Share-coordination handling Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

An earlier October build presented a different danger: a processing defect could permanently discard file data, potentially preventing full recovery even with the correct key.

Check Point Exposure Management researchers identified the updated HYFLOCK builds through threat hunting, tracing four generations from April through October 2026.

Their published investigation into HYFLOCK separates observed behavior from operator claims, revealing stronger deployment features alongside uneven file processing.

HYFLOCK Ransomware

The October 17 sample produced 17 validated encrypted files. Fourteen larger files recorded an encrypted prefix of 4,096 bytes, while three smaller files were encrypted across their complete original lengths.

Configuration settings indicated full encryption, but those settings did not match the larger files’ actual condition. Partial encryption also appears in other ransomware families.

For example, Gunra’s configurable partial encryption lets attackers select how much content to encrypt. HYFLOCK’s finding, however, is specific to the tested build and collected files; it should not be treated as universal behavior across the family.

Examining the untouched content, researchers recovered 73 internal components from seven encrypted Office files, including worksheet and shared-string data.

Changes in HYFLOCK’s ransomware execution (Source – Check Point)

Those components passed cyclic redundancy checks, supporting their integrity. The result demonstrates partial recovery, not decryption: the encrypted prefixes remained unavailable without matching key material or an exact trusted copy.

The malware uses 16-byte symmetric keys, AES counter-mode processing, and RSA protection for recovery material.

Each validated October 17 output retained its original-length body and added a 556-byte trailer containing encryption metadata and a wrapped key. Researchers recovered neither a plaintext encryption key nor an RSA private key.

Recovery risks extend beyond inaccessible prefixes. The earlier October build could omit data during processing, echoing the broader problem illustrated by VECT’s damaging recovery flaws, where implementation errors undermine restoration.

HYFLOCK can also continue encrypting when key wrapping or backup storage fails, creating another potential barrier to recovery.

Updated Rust Encryptor Expands Deployment and Recovery Risks

HYFLOCK appeared in underground promotion in March 2026 as a Ransomware-as-a-Service offering. By October 13, its leak site carried eight victim claims across manufacturing, business services, government, retail, and telecommunications.

These remain unverified attacker claims; the investigation did not establish the victims’ initial compromise routes. The April sample already contained a Windows ransomware core written in Rust.

July added a separate loader carrying the payload, configuration, and key material. An earlier October version used a Go carrier, while the October 17 build returned to a standalone Rust executable that copied itself into an update-like directory.

During controlled testing, the newer build registered a scheduled task, processed network-share resources, and attempted to disrupt recovery.

It generated 500 successful ransomware-extension renames, although only 17 collected files were independently validated as encrypted. Those counts describe different observations and should not be treated as interchangeable measures of damage.

Recovery interference is also documented in Gentlemen ransomware’s backup disruption, but HYFLOCK’s results require qualification.

Its recovery-sabotage commands had varied outcomes, and complete deletion of recovery objects was not proven. Likewise, administrative-share activity did not establish compromise of another computer.

Successful domain-wide propagation was not observed, and Group Policy spreading was disabled in the recovered configuration. Advertised vulnerable-driver attacks and reliable execution after remote desktop sessions ended also remained unverified.

items.summary: 🔎 𝗞𝗤𝗟 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗲𝗸 | 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝘀𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗽𝘁𝘀 After a few weeks away, happy to be back in the hunting field, full of energy! 🔎🔥 When we talk about compromised identities in Microsoft Entra ID, we usually think about stolen passwords, compromised sessions, MFA bypass techniques, or suspicious user sign-ins. But what happens when the attacker doesn’t need a user account at all? A recent investigation published by Todyl 🔗 describes a campaign where attackers are using stolen application credentials, specifically client secrets, to authenticate against Microsoft Entra ID as legitimate applications. Depending on the permissions assigned to the compromised application, an attacker could potentially access Microsoft Graph, Azure resources, Key Vault, SharePoint, or other services. And in some environments, these applications could have permissions that were granted years ago and haven’t been reviewed since. Looking for invalid and expired client secrets As usual, I will not work or mention IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) as the IPs mentioned in the article because they can be easily rotated to new ones so a query would end obsolete. Focus on IOA (Indicators of Attack), one of the hunting opportunities mentioned in the investigation is looking at authentication failures involving application secrets. There are two Entra ID error codes worth checking: AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret. AADSTS7000222: Expired client secret. Of course, these errors are not automatically suspicious. Applications with outdated configurations, forgotten secret rotations, or deployment mistakes can generate exactly the same errors. Assessing the Risk: Here is the key, more insights, will help to know the risk score for every results with the mentioned Entra ID Error codes. The source IP, the application involved, the frequency of the failures, and whether there are successful authentications from the same IP or involving the same application. Hunting with KQL in Microsoft Defender XDR For this hunt, I’m using two tables: EntraIdSignInEvents — Entra ID sign-in events. EntraIdSpnSignInEvents — Service principal sign-in events. The idea is simple: search both tables for the two error codes over the last seven days, combine the results, and identify which table each event came from. let UserSignIns = EntraIdSignInEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ErrorCode in (7000215, 7000222) | project Timestamp, SourceTable = "UserSignIns", Application, IPAddress, Country, ErrorCode; let SpnSignIns = EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ErrorCode in (7000215, 7000222) | project Timestamp, SourceTable = "ServicePrincipalSignIns", Application, IPAddress, Country, ErrorCode; union UserSignIns, SpnSignIns | extend ErrorDescription = case(ErrorCode == 7000215, "Invalid client secret", ErrorCode == 7000222, "Expired client secret", "Other") This is a starting point, not a detection that should immediately generate an incident for every result. I would first review the applications involved, identify unusual source IP addresses, and check whether those same applications or IPs have successful sign-ins around the same period. If something looks interesting, the next step would be reviewing the application’s permissions and the resources accessed after authentication. One detail worth remembering: Service Principals Something I wanted to highlight with this query is the importance of including service principals in our identity hunting activities. We spend a lot of time developing detections for regular Entra ID users but if your organization uses service principals, they are also part of your identity environment. I’m not suggesting that every detection developed for users should also run against service principals. Their authentication behavior is different, and some detection techniques simply don’t apply. However, when developing a new identity-related detection, it’s worth asking whether service principal activity should also be included. Anyway, an interesting investigation and a good excuse to review how we’re monitoring application authentication in our environments. Original research: Todyl — Stolen App Credentials, Real Access: An Actor Is Signing Into Entra ID and Azure DevOps as Your Workloads 🔎 𝗞𝗤𝗟 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗲𝗸 | 𝗛𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗦𝘂𝘀𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁… was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

A recent investigation published by Todyl 🔗 describes a campaign where attackers are using stolen application credentials, specifically client secrets, to authenticate against Microsoft Entra ID as legitimate applications.

Depending on the permissions assigned to the compromised application, an attacker could potentially access Microsoft Graph, Azure resources, Key Vault, SharePoint, or other services. And in some environments, these applications could have permissions that were granted years ago and haven’t been reviewed since.

Looking for invalid and expired client secrets

As usual, I will not work or mention IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) as the IPs mentioned in the article because they can be easily rotated to new ones so a query would end obsolete. Focus on IOA (Indicators of Attack), one of the hunting opportunities mentioned in the investigation is looking at authentication failures involving application secrets. There are two Entra ID error codes worth checking:

  • AADSTS7000215: Invalid client secret.
  • AADSTS7000222: Expired client secret.

Of course, these errors are not automatically suspicious. Applications with outdated configurations, forgotten secret rotations, or deployment mistakes can generate exactly the same errors.

Assessing the Risk: Here is the key, more insights, will help to know the risk score for every results with the mentioned Entra ID Error codes. The source IP, the application involved, the frequency of the failures, and whether there are successful authentications from the same IP or involving the same application.
Hunting with KQL in Microsoft Defender XDR

For this hunt, I’m using two tables:

  • EntraIdSignInEvents — Entra ID sign-in events.
  • EntraIdSpnSignInEvents — Service principal sign-in events.

The idea is simple: search both tables for the two error codes over the last seven days, combine the results, and identify which table each event came from.

let UserSignIns = EntraIdSignInEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ErrorCode in (7000215, 7000222) | project Timestamp, SourceTable = "UserSignIns", Application, IPAddress, Country, ErrorCode;
let SpnSignIns = EntraIdSpnSignInEvents | where Timestamp > ago(7d) | where ErrorCode in (7000215, 7000222) | project Timestamp, SourceTable = "ServicePrincipalSignIns", Application, IPAddress, Country, ErrorCode;
union UserSignIns, SpnSignIns
| extend ErrorDescription = case(ErrorCode == 7000215, "Invalid client secret", ErrorCode == 7000222, "Expired client secret", "Other")

This is a starting point, not a detection that should immediately generate an incident for every result. I would first review the applications involved, identify unusual source IP addresses, and check whether those same applications or IPs have successful sign-ins around the same period.

If something looks interesting, the next step would be reviewing the application’s permissions and the resources accessed after authentication.

One detail worth remembering: Service Principals

Something I wanted to highlight with this query is the importance of including service principals in our identity hunting activities. We spend a lot of time developing detections for regular Entra ID users but if your organization uses service principals, they are also part of your identity environment.

I’m not suggesting that every detection developed for users should also run against service principals. Their authentication behavior is different, and some detection techniques simply don’t apply. However, when developing a new identity-related detection, it’s worth asking whether service principal activity should also be included.

Anyway, an interesting investigation and a good excuse to review how we’re monitoring application authentication in our environments.

Original research: Todyl — Stolen App Credentials, Real Access: An Actor Is Signing Into Entra ID and Azure DevOps as Your Workloads

items.title: How to Export Rapid7 InsightIDR Logs
items.summary: Use the Log Search API. Send a LEQL query for a log and a time window to https:// .rest.logs.insight.rapid7.com/query/logs/ with your API key in the X-Api-Key header. The API returns events in pages and gives you a link to the next one. Log Search in the UI can export results too. InsightIDR collects endpoint, network and cloud logs for Rapid7 customers, and its Log Search is where investigations usually start. Prime Core has 23,965 detection rules for InsightIDR, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get logs out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start An API key. Create one in the Insight Platform settings (an organization key or a user key) with access to InsightIDR. Your region. The host depends on where your data lives: us, us2, us3, eu, ca, au, ap. Log keys. Each log has a key, and queries run against one or more of them. List them with the API, as shown below. Retention. How far back Log Search goes depends on your subscription. Export with the Log Search API REGION=us BASE="https://$REGION.rest.logs.insight.rapid7.com" FROM=$(date -d '2026-10-19T00:00:00Z' +%s000) TO=$(date -d '2026-10-20T00:00:00Z' +%s000) Q=$(printf '%s' 'where(hostname=web-03)' | jq -sRr @uri) # list logs and their keys curl -sS -H "X-Api-Key: $R7_KEY" "$BASE/management/logs" | jq -r '.logs[] | "\(.id) \(.name)"' # query one log, following the pages URL="$BASE/query/logs/ ?query=$Q&from=$FROM&to=$TO&per_page=500" while [ -n "$URL" ]; do RESP=$(curl -sS -H "X-Api-Key: $R7_KEY" "$URL") echo "$RESP" | jq -c '.events[]?' URL=$(echo "$RESP" | jq -r '.links[]? | select(.rel == "Next") | .href' | head -1) done > r7_web03_1019.jsonl Long-running queries may first answer with a link to poll instead of results. Each event’s message field holds the log entry. Extract it with jq -r ‘.message’ when the source was text. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Look it over before you continue. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 or 403 Wrong key, or the key lacks InsightIDR access Check the key’s product access Connection errors Wrong region in the hostname Use your data region Query syntax error LEQL not URL-encoded Encode it, as with @uri above Only the first page Next link not followed Loop until there’s no Next link Nothing older than a certain date Subscription retention Check your plan’s retention FAQ Can I query several logs at once? Yes. The API also accepts queries across multiple log keys or a log set. What about investigations and alerts? Those have their own APIs. For LogTotal, export the log events behind them.

items.title: Researchers Discover White House Network IP Available for Rent Through 28 Proxy Services
items.summary: Researchers at Layer3 Intel found that 28 residential proxy services rent addresses on the White House network. Anyone with a few dollars could send web traffic through them. The activity ran from October 5 to November 3, 2026. The team spotted the activity while browsing its new Residential Proxy Observatory, a tool that shows proxy and hidden internet activity around the world. The traffic came from AS2650, a network block registered to the Executive Office of the President. In 30 days, the team’s tools exited through this network 236 times. The exits came from 6 addresses on 26 of the 30 days. Layer3 requested rotating global access through proxy services, which then revealed the White House addresses on their own. Additionally, Spur and Synthient, two other firms that specialize in proxy detection, also identify these addresses as proxy exits. This makes it unlikely that the identification of these addresses is merely a one-time error. Residential proxy activity (Source: Layer3Intel) White House Network IP for Rent A residential proxy sends web traffic through a real home or office connection, so the traffic looks like it comes from an ordinary user. Many device owners never agree to this. Hidden software in an app or a cheap device can sell bandwidth without the owner’s knowledge. Because the addresses look normal, simple blocklists often fail to catch them. About half of the activity fell between 5 p.m. and midnight Eastern time, and almost none happened in the early morning. Layer3 Intel says this looks like one person on the network in the evening, not a public guest Wi-Fi setup. The most likely cause is a personal device carrying a proxy software kit. The data shows only the exits. It does not show which device or person is behind them. The risk is that a weak proxy kit can give outsiders a path inside a network. Synthient’s earlier research on the Kimwolf botnet shows how this happens. Kimwolf reached more than 2 million devices, mostly Android boxes with an open debug service, by moving through residential proxy networks. In that case, attackers reached devices on private home networks that should have been out of reach. This is not a new pattern. Cyber Security News has already covered how Kimwolf infected 2 million devices and turned them into proxy nodes . It also reported that Google disrupted the IPIDEA proxy network , which relied on hidden software kits inside ordinary apps. Later research found that nearly half of the apps on LG and Samsung TVs carried proxy code. The risk also reaches the workplace. One report on a bandwidth-sharing app showed that a single enrolled employee device could give outsiders a way to reach a router’s management page . The White House was not the only surprise. Layer3 Intel logged 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations in Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha. It also saw three observations in Antarctica, all from a Cloudflare WARP address tied to McMurdo Station. Smaller counts came from Pitcairn, Norfolk Island and Svalbard. The Falklands (388 addresses), the Chagos Islands (43), Tokelau (21) and South Georgia (7) also showed activity. Layer3 Intel says it has saved the raw logs and will share them with relevant agencies. Network teams can take simple steps now. They can check DNS logs for known proxy domains and review apps and browser add-ons on work devices for proxy code. They should also keep TV boxes and other low-cost Android devices off sensitive networks, and turn off Android’s debug service where it is not needed. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: How to Export LogPoint Logs
items.summary: Use LogPoint’s Search API, which works in two calls to the same endpoint, /getsearchlogs. The first call sends your query, time range and repos, and returns a search_id. The second call sends that search_id and returns the rows once the search is final. Both calls are form-encoded POSTs authenticated with your username and secret key. LogPoint is a popular SIEM in Europe, and the Search API is the cleanest way to get a defined slice of its data out. Prime Core has 19,598 detection rules for LogPoint, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get logs out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Your secret key. Every API call carries your LogPoint username and secret key. You find the key in your user profile’s access key settings. Treat it like a password. Repo names. Searches run against repos, written as :5504/ , for example 127.0.0.1:5504/_logpoint. The same endpoint family lists them for you (getalloweddata with type logpoint_repos). Time range. time_range takes either a preset like “Last 24 hours” or a pair of epoch seconds. For incident work, use the epoch pair; date -d ‘2026-10-19T00:00:00Z’ +%s computes it. Export with the Search API LP="https://logpoint.example.com" # 1. start the search (2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC) SID=$(curl -sS "$LP/getsearchlogs" \ --data-urlencode "username=$LP_USER" --data-urlencode "secret_key=$LP_KEY" \ --data-urlencode 'requestData={"query": "device_ip=10.0.0.5", "time_range": [1792368000, 1792454400], "limit": 10000, "repos": ["127.0.0.1:5504/_logpoint"]}' \ | jq -r '.search_id') # 2. fetch results until the search is final while :; do R=$(curl -sS "$LP/getsearchlogs" \ --data-urlencode "username=$LP_USER" --data-urlencode "secret_key=$LP_KEY" \ --data-urlencode "requestData={\"search_id\": \"$SID\"}") [ "$(echo "$R" | jq -r '.final')" = "true" ] && break sleep 3 done echo "$R" | jq -c '.rows[]' > logpoint_1019.jsonl echo "$R" | jq -r '.rows[].msg // empty' > logpoint_1019_raw.log Keep the query a filter. A query with | chart or other aggregations returns aggregated rows, not logs. The raw log usually sits in the msg field. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Authentication error Wrong username or secret key Copy the key again from your profile Empty results Wrong repo string, or the time range is in milliseconds List repos via getalloweddata; use epoch seconds Aggregated rows instead of logs Query includes chart or similar Use a plain filter Results cut short limit reached Raise it, or split the window Request rejected Not sent as form data Send application/x-www-form-urlencoded FAQ Can I do this through LogPoint Director? Yes. Director’s API has its own search call for managed LogPoints. Use it if you manage several instances centrally. Does the UI export work? For small, quick exports, yes. For anything you want to repeat or keep tight, the API gives you more control.

items.title: ARTEX Hackers Expose Their Own Servers, Revealing AI Tools Behind South Korean Bank Breaches
items.summary: A hacker’s own mistake has given researchers a rare look at how AI tools were used to break into South Korean financial firms. The operator left several servers open to the public, and the exposed files showed which AI models, scripts and proxies powered the campaign. Between late September and early October 2026, seven South Korean financial institutions had data stolen through internet-facing systems. Roughly 66,000 to 67,000 people and about 2,200 companies were affected. Names, jobs, income details and loan information were exposed. CrowdStrike first tied the activity to ARTEX, an open-source, China-developed AI penetration testing framework. CrowdStrike judged, with moderate confidence, that a single Chinese-speaking, financially motivated lone operator used ARTEX instead of a known hacking group. The public reports named one key server at 38.244.50[.]120 and a reseller domain, xcai[.]pro, used to reach AI models. Genians later confirmed the same findings, and the ARTEX GitHub page and Docker image were taken down on October 11, though copies remain online. Researchers at Hunt.io noted that the public indicators were only part of the picture. While pivoting off the known server, they found a new open directory at 23.248.226[.]250, a Hong Kong jump server that held far more of the operator’s working files. ARTEX Hackers Expose Their Own Servers, Revealing AI Tools The Hong Kong server held a state file showing the operator ran Claude Code, version 2.1.221, and had started it 510 times since August 4, 2026. The software was not talking to Anthropic, though. A router called Claude Code Router, plus small Python helper scripts, sent every request through the xcai[.]pro reseller to DeepSeek. This resembles other cases where Claude Code and DeepSeek were joined in one workflow. One helper script even carried a note in Chinese describing the route in the operator’s own words. Other files showed a Zhipu AI key for GLM models and a tunnel named grok2api, which fits CrowdStrike’s finding that DeepSeek, GLM and Grok were all in use. Schematic overview of the suspected cyberattack infrastructure and intrusion pathway (Source – Hunt.io) The state file also listed 19 custom “skills,” which are reusable instruction sets for the AI agent, used 147 times in total. They covered reconnaissance, code review, web testing, firewall bypass checks, Android app analysis and cloud phone control. One skill tested payment logic, and a nearby file held three test accounts for a cash-in deposit service. That setup suggests the operator was checking for insecure direct object reference flaws. These flaws let a user view or change another person’s data by altering an ID. A credentials file named .secrets was also found, along with a backup copy. A Chinese comment inside it said it was the “sole source of credentials” and warned against pasting passwords into a session. Three scripts used that same root login to keep a reverse SSH tunnel alive and to copy the AI’s memory files to the jump host. Wider Tools, Hunting Pivots and Defense The exposed folders held more than bank-related tools. Hunt.io found a proxy service at 154.201.79[.]246:443 that gave 79 unique exit IP addresses from the first 100 identities tested. It also found a staged JNDI and LDAP setup for remote code execution, with a DNS callback to confirm success. Other files included cryptocurrency exchange scripts, Linux privilege escalation exploits and iOS and Android tooling. Hunt.io says the link between these items and the bank breaches is unconfirmed. Hunt.io then built three ways to find more ARTEX servers. A certificate search returned 19 IP addresses, a malware-tag search returned 1,303, and a search on the console’s page title returned about 1,300. AttackCapture Search Procedure for Identifying ARTEX-Linked Open Directories (Source – Hunt.io) A separate search for open directories returned 280 results. The tags covered 30 countries, led by the United States, then China and Hong Kong. This shows the framework is spreading well beyond one case, which matches reports of ARTEX automating enterprise attacks elsewhere. Defenders should close public access to admin services and place them behind a VPN or allowlist. They should also reset SSH passwords and rotate API keys, proxy logins and tokens that may have sat in exposed files. Teams should watch for odd LDAP or JNDI traffic, strange DNS callbacks, remote script downloads and unexpected outbound connections. They should also lock down access to AI model gateways. Later, South Korean police arrested a suspected hacker over a separate case that also involved ARTEX, though the shared tool does not prove the same people were involved. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator Type Context 38.244.50[.]120 IPv4 address ARTEX console host and SSH tunnel destination in recovered configuration 23.248.226[.]250 IPv4 address Hong Kong jump host with exposed directories and tooling 154.201.79[.]246 IPv4 address Proxy service used by proxy enumeration scripts xcai[.]pro Domain AI service reseller domain tied to the campaign direct[.]xcai[.]pro Domain Endpoint in the model-routing configuration fofoapi[.]com Domain Third-party API used by the recovered FOFA client u6ud2s[.]dnslog[.]cn Domain DNS callback host in the staged exploit 38.244.50.120:8000 IP and port Exposed directory with scripts and files 23.248.226.250:18099 IP and port Exposed directory with 42 files across two subdirectories 23.248.226.250:8001 IP and port Directory hosting the JNDI/LDAP exploitation setup C7A884AFCD7F91408921890D9617BEF6BFAC3DAE992BC25BB9C48C0395A60842 SHA-256 certificate fingerprint TLS certificate on 38.244.50[.]120 with issuer organization ARTEX ARTEX – 自主渗透测试控制台 HTTP title ARTEX console title used for Hunt.io searches Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. A router called Claude Code Router, plus small Python helper scripts, sent every request through the xcai[.]pro reseller to DeepSeek. This resembles other cases where Claude Code and DeepSeek were joined in one workflow.

One helper script even carried a note in Chinese describing the route in the operator’s own words. Other files showed a Zhipu AI key for GLM models and a tunnel named grok2api, which fits CrowdStrike’s finding that DeepSeek, GLM and Grok were all in use.

Schematic overview of the suspected cyberattack infrastructure and intrusion pathway (Source – Hunt.io)

The state file also listed 19 custom “skills,” which are reusable instruction sets for the AI agent, used 147 times in total. They covered reconnaissance, code review, web testing, firewall bypass checks, Android app analysis and cloud phone control.

One skill tested payment logic, and a nearby file held three test accounts for a cash-in deposit service. That setup suggests the operator was checking for insecure direct object reference flaws. These flaws let a user view or change another person’s data by altering an ID.

A credentials file named .secrets was also found, along with a backup copy. A Chinese comment inside it said it was the “sole source of credentials” and warned against pasting passwords into a session.

Three scripts used that same root login to keep a reverse SSH tunnel alive and to copy the AI’s memory files to the jump host.

Wider Tools, Hunting Pivots and Defense

The exposed folders held more than bank-related tools. Hunt.io found a proxy service at 154.201.79[.]246:443 that gave 79 unique exit IP addresses from the first 100 identities tested.

It also found a staged JNDI and LDAP setup for remote code execution, with a DNS callback to confirm success.

Other files included cryptocurrency exchange scripts, Linux privilege escalation exploits and iOS and Android tooling. Hunt.io says the link between these items and the bank breaches is unconfirmed.

Hunt.io then built three ways to find more ARTEX servers. A certificate search returned 19 IP addresses, a malware-tag search returned 1,303, and a search on the console’s page title returned about 1,300.

AttackCapture Search Procedure for Identifying ARTEX-Linked Open Directories (Source – Hunt.io)

A separate search for open directories returned 280 results. The tags covered 30 countries, led by the United States, then China and Hong Kong.

This shows the framework is spreading well beyond one case, which matches reports of ARTEX automating enterprise attacks elsewhere.

Defenders should close public access to admin services and place them behind a VPN or allowlist. They should also reset SSH passwords and rotate API keys, proxy logins and tokens that may have sat in exposed files.

Teams should watch for odd LDAP or JNDI traffic, strange DNS callbacks, remote script downloads and unexpected outbound connections.

They should also lock down access to AI model gateways. Later, South Korean police arrested a suspected hacker over a separate case that also involved ARTEX, though the shared tool does not prove the same people were involved.

items.title: How to Export NetWitness Logs
items.summary: In NetWitness Investigate, run your query in the Events view, select the events (or all of them), and download the logs. Pick Text to get the raw log lines, or JSON for structured events. Large downloads run as jobs; you collect the file from the Jobs tray when it’s ready. By default, one export can include up to 100,000 sessions. NetWitness, formerly RSA NetWitness, stores logs on Log Decoders and makes them searchable through Concentrators and Brokers. Prime Core has 18,461 detection rules for NetWitness, mapped to 631 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get logs out, sanitize them, and investigate them for free in LogTotal. Before you start Access to Investigate. You need a role that can investigate the service (Broker or Concentrator) holding the logs. Set the export format once. In Profile → Preferences → Investigation , the Export Log Format preference decides the default format for downloads: Text, XML, CSV or JSON. Choose Text for raw logs. If it’s left empty, NetWitness asks every time. Retention. How far back you can go depends on Log Decoder storage. Older logs may only exist in an archiver, if you have one. Export from Investigate Open Investigate → Events , pick the service, and set the time range. Query with meta keys (example below). Run the query and check the count. Select the events you want, or none to take all of them, and choose the download option for logs (Text or JSON). Open the Jobs tray (the stopwatch icon) and download the file when the job finishes. A query for one Linux host looks like this. For Windows logs, device.type = ‘winevent_nic’ is the common log parser. device.type = 'rhlinux' && alias.host = 'web-03' For a single event, the Text tab of the event details has its own download options for the raw log. The Max Session Export setting caps how many sessions one export can include (100,000 by default). For bigger windows, split by time. Option 2: REST API on the services Concentrators and Brokers expose a REST interface that can run queries and return log content. That suits scripted exports. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. What this looks like on real data. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix The download contains network sessions or meta, not logs Wrong download option Choose the logs download, not meta or PCAP Export stops at 100,000 sessions Max Session Export limit Split by time, or ask an admin to raise the limit No file appears It’s a background job Collect it from the Jobs tray Query returns nothing Wrong service or meta key values Check device.type values in the meta panel FAQ Text or JSON? Text when you want the original log lines, which suits syslog-style sources. JSON when you want NetWitness’s parsed meta alongside each event. Can I export packets too? Yes, as PCAP, but that’s network traffic, not logs. LogTotal works with the logs.
