How to Export Devo Logs
items.summary: Use the Devo Query API: send a LINQ query, a time range and an output mode to the /search/query endpoint of your region, authenticated with an API token or key and secret. Ask for a JSON mode and you get structured events; select the message field from raw tables to get the original lines back. The official Python SDK (devo-sdk) wraps the same API if you prefer code to curl. Devo stores large volumes of security and operational data in the cloud, often with long retention. Prime Core has 23,653 detection rules for Devo, mapped to 664 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Credentials. Create an API token, or an API key and secret, in your Devo domain’s credentials settings, with access to the tables you need. Your region’s endpoint. The Query API host depends on where your domain lives, for example apiv2-us.devo.com or apiv2-eu.devo.com. Table names. Devo organizes data in tables like box.unix or firewall.fortinet.traffic. Find yours in the Data Search area, and build the query there first. Export with the Query API curl -sS -X POST "https://apiv2-eu.devo.com/search/query" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVO_TOKEN" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{ "query": "from box.unix where hostname = \"web-03\" select eventdate, hostname, message", "from": 1792368000, "to": 1792454400, "mode": {"type": "json/simple"} }' > devo_web03_1019.json The from and to values above are epoch seconds for 2026-10-19 00:00 UTC to 2026-10-20 00:00 UTC. If the response is one JSON object per line, upload it as-is. If it’s an array, flatten it with jq -c ‘.[]’. For raw lines, extract message. Python alternative. pip install devo-sdk, then use the API client from the devo.api package with your token, the same query and dates. It handles the request signing for key-and-secret authentication. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix 401 Wrong token, or a key/secret signature problem Check the credentials; try the SDK, which signs requests for you Connection errors Wrong regional endpoint Use your domain’s region Empty results Wrong table name, or milliseconds instead of seconds Check the table in Data Search; check time units Output is a table you didn’t expect Mode doesn’t match what you need Pick a JSON mode FAQ Raw or parsed? For syslog-style sources, select message and upload the raw lines. For JSON sources, upload the parsed events. Can I schedule exports? Yes, the same API works in scheduled jobs. For continuous forwarding, Devo also has data export features.

Vizio and Samsung TVs both appeared to send this data even when researchers opted out of ACR. Only four out of eight smart TVs appeared to completely honor ACR opt-out. If you thought that opting out of surveillance on your smart TV would give you your privacy back, think again. A study by researchers at Northeastern University found that some smart TVs still seem to send information about what you’re watching to third parties, even after you pressed the opt-out button. The study, ‘ Watching the watchers ‘, tested twelve smart TVs from ten manufacturers to find out how well they respected opt-outs from automatic content recognition (ACR). ACR is a TV feature that captures audio and/or video content from smart TVs and uploads it to a third party (typically the TV manufacturer). The third party converts this content into digital fingerprints to understand what you’re watching, and can then use it to send targeted advertising or allow others to do the same. It’s on most if not all smart TVs, and 82% of US households had a smart TV as of last year. The test took in the eight operating systems behind roughly 95% of US smart TVs, and ran ten viewing scenarios on each of them. These ranged from viewing antenna TV through to viewing via screen mirroring from another device. The researchers tested viewing the first-party streaming services provided free with the manufacturers’ operating systems, along with sessions using third-party streaming apps. And they tested sessions where the TV was connected to another device via its HDMI port. The study ran all of its tests both with ACR left on, and with the opt-out setting selected. The whole test involved over 5,000 automated sessions. Vizio continued to send 100% of what looked like traffic when viewing its first-party streaming services and antenna-based TV services, even after people had opted out, the study said. It also sent the same amount of traffic when idle. However it didn’t send any ACR traffic for third-party streaming data, according to the report. Samsung did appear to leak some traffic from third-party streaming services after the researchers opted out of its ACR function. They tested 30 runs of Samsung’s built-in streaming service after opting out of ACR, and found that it still showed traffic “consistent with ACR”. After opt-out, the Samsung TV’s Tizen OS seemed to send ACR-related traffic about Netflix in 7% of runs, YouTube in 10% of runs, and Tubi TV in 20%. It sent ACR 60% of the time from HDMI sessions. Like the Vizio TV, it also sent ACR traffic for all of its first-party streaming sessions. Late last month, a researcher reverse-engineered a Samsung Smart TV and cast doubt on whether disabling ACR worked on the device. There was good news, though. Four smart TV operating systems went completely silent after the researchers turned off ACR: LG’s WebOS, Sony’s Google TV OS, Amazon’s FireTV OS, and Supersonic’s VIDAA OS. Encryption is a research challenge Vizio agreed to pay $2.2 million in a 2017 FTC settlement over charges that it collected viewing histories on eleven million smart TVs without user consent. At the time, it agreed to allow people to opt out of ACR. The Vizio TV that the researchers tested sent traffic to Kinesis, an Amazon-run data ingestion service that the manufacturer uses to analyze data from its smart TVs. The researchers noticed no dip in traffic to this domain when they opted out of ACR on a Vizio TV. They said: “The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint. However, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.” That’s a challenge to this research because most smart TVs encrypt their ACR traffic, including Samsung. So the researchers had to infer that this was ACR traffic based on signals such as where it was being sent, along with timing, volume, and protocol details. One exception was Supersonic’s VIDAA OS, which sent ACR data to servers unencrypted. The servers responded unencrypted with a genre for what they recognized. Anyone watching the network could see it all, they warned. And because the servers didn’t require a login at the time of the test, over 57 million ACR detection results from other people’s TVs were accessible. Vizio’s first-party streaming service WatchFree+ also dropped unencrypted titles of any show or channel being watched into online communications with the free TV service provider. There’s no way to turn that off, the researchers warned. Walmart acquired Vizio for $2.3 billion in 2024, partly to help “advertisers to meaningfully connect with customers at scale and boost product discovery”. The retailer also runs Walmart Connect, a retail media business that uses its customers’ data to help other businesses target them with ads. Walmart was particularly interested in Vizio’s advertising business it, said at the time: “Pairing it with Walmart Connect will be impactful and allow us to invest in our business even further on behalf of our customers.” What smart TV owners can do What can you do to protect yourself from a smart TV that might be sending your viewing data elsewhere? The researchers have some suggestions: WebOS (LG), Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS on Supersonic all appeared to honor ACR opt-out, so selecting it on these TVs should be safe. Disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device. That way the TV can’t send back data, even if it picks it up from the HDMI connection. Use a blocklist. This takes a little more technical knowledge. If you run an internet router that can accept blocklists, then you can add a list of known ACR endpoints that will stop your TV’s traffic reaching them. The researchers provide one here . Stop threats before they can do any harm. Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks phishing pages and malicious sites automatically. Free, one click to install. The Vizio TV that the researchers tested sent traffic to Kinesis, an Amazon-run data ingestion service that the manufacturer uses to analyze data from its smart TVs. The researchers noticed no dip in traffic to this domain when they opted out of ACR on a Vizio TV. They said:

“The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint. However, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement.”

That’s a challenge to this research because most smart TVs encrypt their ACR traffic, including Samsung. So the researchers had to infer that this was ACR traffic based on signals such as where it was being sent, along with timing, volume, and protocol details.

items.title: CVE-2026-109518: APT Flaw Enables MitM Root Code Execution
items.summary: A high-severity vulnerability in APT, the package management system used by Debian, Ubuntu, and derivative Linux distributions, could allow an on-path attacker to replace a verified software package with a malicious one and execute arbitrary code with root privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-109518, the flaw carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7 and affects APT’s HTTP download and retry handling. The vulnerability is caused by improper handling of hard links when APT follows HTTP redirects and retries failed package downloads. Under the right conditions, two different downloads can be merged after a redirect causes them to resolve to the same URI. An attacker able to manipulate traffic between an APT client and a repository can abuse this behavior to substitute an attacker-controlled .deb package after verification has already taken place. Because Debian packages can execute installation scripts with root privileges, successful exploitation can result in complete system compromise. However, exploitation requires several conditions: the victim must initiate a package installation, APT must communicate over manipulable HTTP, and the Acquire::Retries option must be set to a non-zero value. Ubuntu 22.04 LTS and newer releases are exposed by default because retries are enabled. Debian has similarly enabled retries by default since APT 2.3.2, including Debian 12. The exploit first leaks a kernel pointer to bypass KASLR and then uses the same use-after-free condition to corrupt memory and redirect kernel control flow. Anthropic has not released the exploit code.

Importantly, the underlying vulnerability is not limited to MPTCP. Red Hat confirms that systems with ordinary IPv4 TCP networking remain vulnerable even when MPTCP is disabled, including default Red Hat Enterprise Linux configurations.

Contact Sales

As of November 4, 2026, no Linux vendor, CERT, or other reviewed source has reported confirmed exploitation of the flaw in real-world attacks. CVE-2026-98432 analysis

CVE-2026-98432 affects the IPv4 TCP connection-handling code in Linux kernels containing the vulnerable implementation introduced in Linux 4.4. The Linux kernel CVE team classifies the issue as critical with a CVSS 3.1 score of 9.8 and the vector AV/AC/PR/UI/S/C/I/A.

The vulnerability is a use-after-free condition caused by a race during concurrent TCP connection processing. When an IPv4 TCP connection is established, tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers IP options associated with the pending request to the newly created socket without making a separate copy.

Another CPU can simultaneously process a retransmitted SYN associated with the same request socket. During that process, functions responsible for generating the SYN-ACK continue reading the IP options while protected by an RCU read-side critical section.

However, the child socket can be destroyed while that operation is still underway. The kernel then frees the associated inet_opt structure using kfree(), leaving another CPU potentially accessing memory that has already been released. The resulting stale reference creates a use-after-free condition in ip_options_build().

A similar race exists during request socket migration, including configurations using net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1 or BPF-based SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE. The upstream fix replaces the unsafe memory release with RCU-aware freeing, ensuring readers have finished accessing the object before its memory can be reclaimed.

The first issue specifically affects IPv4. The kernel advisory states that IPv6 is not vulnerable to that particular race because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock() duplicates the relevant options instead of transferring them in the same manner.

Remote exploitation requires specially constructed network traffic and precise manipulation of the race condition. Red Hat notes that the likely outcomes can include a kernel crash, memory corruption, and potentially remote code execution. The lack of authentication and user interaction substantially increases the risk for systems exposing TCP services to untrusted networks.

Anthropic demonstrated that the vulnerability can be transformed into a full remote-root exploit. Its research model targeted a Linux server accepting Multipath TCP connections and used two stages to achieve command execution.

During the first stage, the exploit repeatedly triggers the race and manipulates a length value so the kernel returns additional adjacent memory in a network response. Eventually, one of these responses contains a kernel pointer. That disclosure reveals information about the kernel memory layout and allows the exploit to defeat Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR).

During the second stage, the exploit uses the same vulnerability to cause a buffer overflow and overwrite a callback pointer. The pointer is redirected toward a payload previously placed in kernel memory using legitimate protocol functionality. When the kernel invokes the modified callback, existing kernel functions are chained together until an attacker-selected shell command is executed as root.

A particularly important characteristic of the exploit is that losing the race does not necessarily crash the server. Instead, the connection attempt can simply fail, allowing the attacker to retry repeatedly. In Anthropic’s test environment, obtaining a useful kernel pointer took approximately 48 minutes, followed by another five minutes to achieve root command execution.

This demonstration should not be interpreted to mean that MPTCP is required for exploitation. Anthropic demonstrated one successful exploit path involving an MPTCP listener, but the vulnerable code resides in ordinary IPv4 TCP handling. Red Hat explicitly warns that disabling MPTCP does not fully address the vulnerability and that default RHEL installations remain affected even though MPTCP is disabled by default.

The CVE-2026-98432 PoC situation is also important to distinguish from the existence of a complete weaponized exploit. Anthropic developed a functioning remote-root proof of concept internally but has not published it. Public code reported by security researchers can demonstrate or detect aspects of the underlying race and memory disclosure, but the reviewed sources do not document publicly released code reproducing Anthropic’s complete remote code execution chain.

The vulnerability was reported by Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge. The upstream Linux fix was applied on October 5, 2026, while the Linux kernel CVE record was published on October 15. Anthropic publicly described its full exploitation research on October 27.

The Linux kernel project identifies the following upstream fixed versions:

  • Linux 5.10.272
  • Linux 5.15.223
  • Linux 6.1.190
  • Linux 6.6.159
  • Linux 6.12.113
  • Linux 6.18.56
  • Linux 7.2.10
  • Linux 7.3

The kernel team recommends upgrading to the latest stable kernel rather than cherry-picking individual commits.

Distribution-specific exposure and remediation differ because Linux vendors maintain their own kernels and backport security fixes. Red Hat currently rates the issue Critical at 9.8 and has released fixes for multiple RHEL 8, 9, and 10 streams. OpenShift and layered products that depend on affected RHEL kernels also require attention.

Ubuntu likewise rates the vulnerability Critical at 9.8. Ubuntu 26.10 has received a fixed generic kernel, while fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 26.04 LTS were available in the -proposed testing pocket as of early November, with additional supported releases awaiting fixes. Administrators should use Canonical’s CVE page rather than relying solely on upstream kernel version numbers.

For CVE-2026-98432 detection, security teams should combine network and host telemetry. Potential network-level hunting signals include unusual inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options, especially repeated connection attempts containing Record Route or Timestamp options and abnormal patterns of SYN retransmission. The presence of such traffic alone does not confirm exploitation, but it provides a useful hunting pivot when correlated with vulnerable systems.

Host-level monitoring should include Linux kernel crashes, kernel warnings, memory-corruption indicators, unexpected service restarts, and anomalous activity immediately following suspicious network traffic. Because successful exploitation could theoretically provide root code execution, defenders should also monitor for unexpected privileged processes, newly created files, configuration changes, persistence mechanisms, and unexplained outbound connections.

There are currently no attacker-specific CVE-2026-98432 IOCs such as confirmed malicious IP addresses, domains, or malware hashes because the reviewed sources have not reported real-world exploitation. Defenders should therefore prioritize behavior-based detection and exposure assessment rather than relying on static indicators.

CVE-2026-98432 Mitigation

The definitive remediation is to install a vendor-provided kernel containing the security fix. The Linux kernel CVE team recommends moving to the latest supported stable kernel, while Linux distribution users should install packages supplied specifically by their vendor because fixes are commonly backported without changing to an upstream kernel version.

Administrators should prioritize internet-facing Linux servers and other systems accepting inbound IPv4 TCP connections. The attack surface is broad because the vulnerability exists in the kernel networking stack rather than in an individual application or server product.

Organizations should take the following steps:

  1. Inventory Linux servers and identify the running kernel with tools such as uname -r.
  2. Check the relevant Linux distribution’s security advisory rather than determining exposure solely from the upstream version number.
  3. Install the vendor-provided fixed kernel as soon as it becomes available.
  4. Reboot affected systems after installing the updated kernel to ensure the patched kernel is running.
  5. Prioritize internet-facing servers and infrastructure accepting inbound IPv4 TCP traffic.
  6. Review externally exposed TCP services and limit unnecessary network accessibility.
  7. Continue monitoring vendor advisories because fix availability differs across Linux distributions, kernel variants, cloud kernels, and support channels.

Red Hat and Ubuntu have also documented an interim packet-filtering approach that drops incoming IPv4 TCP packets containing IP options. The recommended nftables condition checks for an IPv4 header length greater than five and drops matching TCP packets before they reach the vulnerable socket-handling path.

This measure can reduce exposure because the known exploitation path requires IPv4 options. However, both vendors warn that packet filtering is not a complete replacement for installing the corrected kernel. It can also interfere with workloads that legitimately depend on IPv4 options and therefore should be tested before production deployment.

Disabling MPTCP alone should not be treated as sufficient protection. Although Anthropic’s working exploit targeted an MPTCP listener, the underlying vulnerability is in normal IPv4 TCP handling. Red Hat specifically notes that RHEL remains vulnerable in its default configuration even though MPTCP is disabled.

For environments using Go applications, disabling automatic MPTCP behavior can reduce exposure to the specific exploit demonstrated by Anthropic, but this remains an incomplete risk-reduction measure. Systems without an MPTCP listener should not automatically be considered safe because other exploitation techniques may target the same underlying race.

Because no real-world compromise campaign has been confirmed, incident-response guidance should currently focus on identifying potentially vulnerable systems and suspicious exploitation behavior rather than searching for a known attacker infrastructure set. Organizations that observe unusual TCP traffic followed by kernel instability or unexpected privileged execution should treat the activity as potentially malicious and preserve network and host telemetry for investigation.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-98432 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-98432 is a critical use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s IPv4 TCP networking subsystem. During concurrent processing of TCP connection requests, IP option memory can be freed while another CPU is still accessing it. Specially timed remote network requests can trigger the race, potentially causing crashes, memory corruption, information disclosure, or remote code execution.

When was CVE-2026-98432 first discovered?

The vulnerability was reported by Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge. The upstream Linux fix landed on October 5, 2026, and the Linux kernel CVE record was published on October 15. Anthropic publicly disclosed its research and working remote-root exploitation technique on October 27, 2026.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-98432 on systems?

A remote unauthenticated attacker can trigger a use-after-free condition in the Linux kernel over IPv4 TCP traffic. Possible consequences include denial of service through a kernel crash, kernel memory disclosure or corruption, and potentially arbitrary command execution with root privileges. Anthropic demonstrated successful remote root execution against a system with an MPTCP listener.

Can CVE-2026-98432 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems running vulnerable Linux kernels remain exposed until the appropriate vendor security update is installed and the patched kernel is running. The underlying bug has existed since Linux 4.4, and affected distributions include major enterprise Linux platforms. However, as of November 4, 2026, the reviewed sources do not report confirmed exploitation of the vulnerability in real-world attacks.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-98432?

Install the latest fixed kernel provided by your Linux distribution and reboot the system to activate it. Prioritize servers accepting inbound IPv4 TCP connections and verify exposure using the vendor’s advisory. Where immediate patching is impossible, filtering inbound IPv4 TCP packets containing IP options can reduce risk, but it is not a complete substitute for updating. Security teams should continue reviewing vendor advisories for updated details for CVE-2026-98432 as additional fixes and research become available.

items.title: kpt v1.0.0 is released
items.summary: After many years and much development, the kpt community has released v1.0.0 of the kpt toolchain. This is a big step in maturing the kpt project after having it in pre-release status for several years. In the last twelve months the community has focused on stabilising the APIs, deprecating unused features and integrating the Porch (Package ORCHestration) service back into the kpt organization. With the complete toolchain under a common governance the community delivers a comprehensive system for GitOps based package management, which is modular enough to integrate and add value to any workflow. Standalone kpt provides lightweight configuration package management for applications running on Kubernetes, based on the config as data principles. These principles allow declarative manipulation and verification of the configuration of cloud native applications, clusters or indeed any resources managed through Kubernetes APIs. In kpt everything is expressed using KRM and kpt provides a framework to describe the manipulation and validation steps for KRM resources in a package, autonomously converting generic KRM into deployable models for a specific site or application. This allows reproducible KRM resource manipulation without the limitations of templating. Porch provides a framework to support the orchestration of kpt packages at scale in a zero-touch GitOps workflow. With the recent release of version 1.0.0, the kpt community is announcing the readiness of kpt for widespread adoption, having demonstrated that all the components of the project are stable and the community is actively working to build a simple, comprehensive, lightweight and modular framework for the lifecycle management of any Kubernetes resources. Join us! The kpt project meets weekly, on Wednesdays at 2pm CET. We use GitHub to collaborate on issues and discussions and we use the kpt channel on the Kubernetes slack for ad hoc communication. If what you see interests you and you would like to know more, please reach out. If you are already using kpt and would like to see a new feature, or want to help improve it, please reach out – we would be delighted to see you!

items.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
items.summary: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available. Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts. Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC. Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

items.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
items.summary: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health , Chemical , Food and Agriculture , and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) , developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure : Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [ CPG 3.S ]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices : Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [ CPG 3.I ]. Enforce credential security : Change default passwords [ CPG 3.A ], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [ CPG 3.B ]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [ CPG 3.F ]. Apply patches : Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [ CPG 2.A , 2.B ]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access : Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [ CPG 3.H ]. Have reliable backups : Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [ CPG 3.O ]. Monitor and report : Enable logging [ CPG 3.Q ] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges : Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office . When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts. Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. The authoring organizations do not endorse any commercial entity, product, company, or service, including any entities, products, or services linked within this document. items.summary_html:
Overview

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization.

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access.

Threat

The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.

Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors:

  • Authentication bypass;
  • Arbitrary code injection; and
  • Weak configurations.

Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects:

  • Change of temperature, which could:
    • Affect the service life of the system;
    • Create a fire hazard;
    • Cause loss of inventory; or
    • Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage.
  • Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition).
Mitigations

The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement:

  • Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices.
  • Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I].
  • Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F].
  • Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance.
  • Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H].
  • Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O].
  • Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity.
    • For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets.
  • Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations.
Resources

The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations:

  • CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology
  • CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security
  • CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance
  • United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT
Contact Information

The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet:

  • Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident:
    • Date, time, and location of the incident;
    • Type of activity;
    • Number of people affected;
    • Type of equipment used for the activity; and
    • Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact.
  • Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts.
Disclaimer

items.title: Keeper Security Launches Self-Managed PAM Solution for Air-Gapped and Critical Infrastructure Environments
items.summary: Keeper Security has announced the launch of Self-Managed Keeper, a new self-hosted deployment option designed to bring privileged access management (PAM) capabilities to highly restricted and disconnected environments. The solution enables government agencies, critical infrastructure operators and highly regulated enterprises to manage credentials, secrets and privileged sessions entirely within their own infrastructure, without depending on external cloud services. The launch aims to address the security and operational challenges faced by organisations in sectors such as defence, energy, utilities, financial services and industrial operations, where network connectivity may be restricted or prohibited due to regulatory, security or operational requirements. Self-Managed Keeper allows organisations to deploy PAM capabilities across on-premises infrastructure, private cloud environments, air-gapped networks and Operational Technology (OT) systems. By removing external cloud dependencies, the solution gives security teams greater control over where sensitive data is stored and how privileged access is managed. “For organisations operating in disconnected or highly restricted environments, dependence on external cloud connectivity can create unacceptable operational risks,” said Craig Lurey, CTO and Co-founder of Keeper Security. “Self-Managed Keeper brings enterprise-grade privileged access management to these environments while enabling organisations to maintain complete control over their security infrastructure.” For critical infrastructure operators, maintaining access to privileged credentials during connectivity disruptions can be essential to restoring systems and sustaining operations. Self-Managed Keeper addresses this requirement by providing credential management, secrets management and privileged session management through the KeeperPAM Gateway. The platform also includes KeeperDB, the Keeper Admin Console and Keeper APIs. Running in Docker containers on customer-controlled Linux infrastructure, the solution enables organisations to maintain privileged access capabilities independently of external internet connectivity. According to Keeper, the platform offers several key capabilities, including support for fully air-gapped networks, customer-controlled data residency and self-hosted deployment management. It also retains Keeper’s zero-knowledge architecture, with credentials and secrets encrypted and decrypted on users’ devices. The new deployment option complements Keeper’s existing cloud-native offerings, extending its PAM capabilities to organisations that must maintain strict control over their infrastructure and sensitive information. “Organisations operating complex OT and defence networks face a unique challenge: maintaining strict security and operational requirements while keeping pace with modern cybersecurity capabilities,” said Shane Barney, CISO of Keeper Security. “Self-Managed Keeper bridges that gap, bringing advanced privileged access management to highly restricted environments where conventional cloud deployments are not an option. Security teams can modernise how they protect critical systems without compromising the infrastructure requirements that keep those environments secure.”

items.title: Hackers Hide Marsalek Malware in Fake Roblox and Fortnite Cheats to Steal Passwords and Crypto Wallet Data
items.summary: Hackers are hiding a free information stealer called Marsalek inside fake cheats and tools for games such as Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2. The files look like helpful game add-ons. In the background they steal saved passwords, browser cookies, Discord tokens, and crypto wallet data from Windows PCs. Marsalek ran from about December 2025 to May 2026 as malware-as-a-service, so anyone could sign up on a public site, build a malicious file, and watch victims on a dashboard. The free tier did not even ask for a Discord or email account. Similar fake game cheat campaigns have pushed other stealers through GitHub and Reddit, which shows how popular this trick has become. Analysts at McAfee Labs identified the malware and counted more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs. They also linked Marsalek to WeedHack, a Minecraft-focused service, because both point customers to the same Telegram support channel, @MetaMaskenMann. Hackers Hide Marsalek Malware in Fake Roblox and Fortnite Cheats Most of the lures copy tools that gamers already search for. McAfee saw fake versions of Roblox script executors such as Swift, Solara, MatrixHub External, and Matcha External. Fake Minecraft clients such as Shadow Client and Boss Client also appeared, and a sample named Fortnite_tweaks.exe is in the indicator list. The files spread through look-alike websites, Discord, and GitHub. Customers can start an infection with a PowerShell script, a ClickFix page, a Python file, or an EXE file. Bitdefender reported a related case with fake Roblox Xeno cheats that also targeted younger players. After the first step, the chain is almost the same every time. The starter script downloads a portable Python package and a second file called python_setup.py. That file tries to gain admin rights with a Windows tool called CMSTP, then hides the permission prompt and presses Enter for the user. It then adds 8 paths and 15 processes to Microsoft Defender’s exclusion list, so later files are not scanned. Hackers are hiding a free information stealer called Marsalek inside fake cheats and tools for games such as Roblox, Fortnite, and Counter-Strike 2.

The files look like helpful game add-ons. In the background they steal saved passwords, browser cookies, Discord tokens, and crypto wallet data from Windows PCs.

Marsalek ran from about December 2025 to May 2026 as malware-as-a-service, so anyone could sign up on a public site, build a malicious file, and watch victims on a dashboard.

The free tier did not even ask for a Discord or email account. Similar fake game cheat campaigns have pushed other stealers through GitHub and Reddit, which shows how popular this trick has become.

Analysts at McAfee Labs identified the malware and counted more than 1,560 registered accounts, over 400 malicious files, and more than 29 distribution URLs.

They also linked Marsalek to WeedHack, a Minecraft-focused service, because both point customers to the same Telegram support channel, @MetaMaskenMann.

Hackers Hide Marsalek Malware in Fake Roblox and Fortnite Cheats

Most of the lures copy tools that gamers already search for. McAfee saw fake versions of Roblox script executors such as Swift, Solara, MatrixHub External, and Matcha External.

Fake Minecraft clients such as Shadow Client and Boss Client also appeared, and a sample named Fortnite_tweaks.exe is in the indicator list.

The files spread through look-alike websites, Discord, and GitHub. Customers can start an infection with a PowerShell script, a ClickFix page, a Python file, or an EXE file. Bitdefender reported a related case with fake Roblox Xeno cheats that also targeted younger players.

After the first step, the chain is almost the same every time. The starter script downloads a portable Python package and a second file called python_setup.py.

That file tries to gain admin rights with a Windows tool called CMSTP, then hides the permission prompt and presses Enter for the user. It then adds 8 paths and 15 processes to Microsoft Defender’s exclusion list, so later files are not scanned.

Attack Vector (Source – McAfee)

The ClickFix page is a fake Cloudflare check, a trick also seen in the Warden Stealer malware campaign that tells victims to paste commands into Windows.

The third file, svc.py, does the main stealing in over 1,400 lines of code. It goes after 32 Chromium-based browsers and Firefox.

It also gets around Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption by injecting a DLL into a suspended Chrome, Edge, or Brave process, so the browser itself unlocks the key.

The malware checks 26 Discord paths, copies Telegram session data, and reads Mullvad VPN account details. It scans for 56 browser extensions and 12 wallet apps, and it looks for files with words like “seed,” “passphrase,” and “wallet.” In Exodus and Atomic Wallet it swaps in two .asar files to leave a backdoor.

Dual-Hook Design Turns Customers Into Victims

The last stage is PureLog, a low-cost stealer sold for as little as $59 a month. It is hidden with .NET Reactor, decrypted with Triple DES, and run only in memory.

It targets 35 browsers, 48 extensions, and 12 desktop apps, takes a screenshot, and sets a scheduled task that runs RunetimeBroker.exe every five minutes. It sends data to a separate server, telemetrydata.to.

Marsalek’s EXE Builder (Source – McAfee)

This setup is called a dual hook. The customers think they own the stolen logs, but Marsalek’s author also gets a copy and may use a high-value victim’s accounts first.

The built-in FAQ even teaches buyers how to use stolen cookies and tokens and how to launder coins through Monero. McAfee saw the most activity in the United States, followed by Germany, the United Kingdom, India, and Brazil.

Gaming profiles are worth money, and it is easy to see attackers steal gaming accounts and then sell the items or reuse the same logins elsewhere.

Marsalek’s Dashboard (Source – McAfee)

The best defense is simple. Download games and tools only from official sources, never turn off antivirus because a site says it is a false alarm, and never paste commands from a web page.

Anyone who ran a suspicious cheat should change passwords from a clean device, sign out of all sessions, move crypto to a new wallet, and reinstall Windows. Readers can find the full technical details in the McAfee Labs Marsalek report.

items.title: Tata Motors iRA App Flaws Could Let Hackers Impersonate Car Owners and Access Vehicle Services
items.summary: Tata Motors’ iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev mobile apps contain four security flaws that could let attackers steal credentials, impersonate car owners, and access vehicle services. India’s Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, rated the issues as High severity in an advisory published on November 4, 2026. The warning covers iRA 2.0 versions 26.7.3 and earlier, alongside iRA.ev versions 26.7.2 and earlier. These apps serve petrol, diesel, and electric vehicle customers, providing remote vehicle commands, status checks, health monitoring, and trip information. CERT-In credits security researcher Pranav Rajendran with reporting the vulnerabilities. Embedded Credentials and Stolen Tokens The first flaw, CVE-2026-121144, involves service account credentials, API keys, and authorization tokens stored inside the app package. An attacker needs no login to download the package and extract these secrets. The issue reflects risks previously covered in Cybersecurity News’ reporting on hardcoded credentials in mobile apps . Those exposed credentials could provide access to backend services, potentially allowing data theft or unauthorized operations. This weakness matters because the sensitive information comes from the distributed application itself. An attacker would not first need to steal a particular owner’s password to extract the embedded credentials. CVE-2026-121145 affects WebView, the component that displays web content inside the apps. Insufficient checks on loaded URLs and their origins could let malicious content interact with app functions and obtain live bearer authentication tokens. An attacker could then misuse those tokens to impersonate the associated owner. According to CERT-In’s advisory , CVE-2026-121146 exposes authentication tokens through application logs used for development and debugging. Exploitation requires local access to those logs. An attacker who retrieves the exposed session tokens could misuse them to access vehicle information and services as the affected user. The fourth flaw, CVE-2026-121147, involves an improper implementation of SSL certificate pinning in the network security configuration. CERT-In says the resulting controls are ineffective. An attacker positioned to intercept network traffic could exploit the weakness to intercept or change communications between the mobile application and its backend services. The findings highlight how connected vehicle security depends on mobile apps and supporting servers, not only vehicle hardware. Earlier automotive API vulnerability research documented separate weaknesses affecting vehicle services across several manufacturers. Those findings provide context, but their specific vehicle-control impacts should not be assumed for Tata Motors. Fixed Versions Available CERT-In advises affected users to upgrade iRA 2.0 to version 26.8.2 and iRA.ev to version 26.9.1. Its advisory links to the official Google Play and Apple App Store listings for both applications. Installing the recommended release is the agency’s stated solution for addressing these vulnerabilities. The advisory does not report active exploitation, identify affected vehicle models, or confirm that attackers demonstrated control over specific driving functions. Its stated risks concern sensitive information, user impersonation, and unauthorized data changes using an owner’s privileges. The distinction keeps the warning focused on documented application weaknesses rather than unverified claims about vehicle takeovers. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Why waiting for quantum computers to arrive could leave your security exposed
items.summary: By Tim Hudson, President, OpenSSL Corporation For organisations preparing for post-quantum cryptography, one of the biggest risks is assuming they can wait until a sufficiently powerful quantum computer arrives before taking action. Whilst it’s understandable to focus on the point when quantum computers might be able to break today’s cryptography, nobody can predict exactly when that will happen. A more useful question is much simpler: if you had to change your cryptography, how long would it take? For many organisations, the answer is uncomfortable. Encryption and other cryptographic technologies are built into almost every part of modern IT. They protect communications, verify identities and safeguard sensitive information. items.summary_html:
By Tim Hudson, President, OpenSSL Corporation

For organisations preparing for post-quantum cryptography, one of the biggest risks is assuming they can wait until a sufficiently powerful quantum computer arrives before taking action.

Whilst it’s understandable to focus on the point when quantum computers might be able to break today’s cryptography, nobody can predict exactly when that will happen. A more useful question is much simpler: if you had to change your cryptography, how long would it take? For many organisations, the answer is uncomfortable. Identifying where cryptography is used, assessing dependencies and introducing alternatives could take years, particularly in complex environments.

Encryption and other cryptographic technologies are built into almost every part of modern IT. They protect communications, verify identities and safeguard sensitive information. They are also deeply embedded in applications, infrastructure, connected devices and software supplied by other organisations. They work so reliably that organisations rarely need to think about them. Until they need to change them.

Mapping your dependencies should be the starting point

The first stage of post-quantum preparation isn’t choosing a new algorithm. It is understanding what you already have.

Where is cryptography being used? Which algorithms are involved? What information are they protecting? How long does that information need to remain confidential? Which systems depend on them? Which elements can you control directly, and which rely on suppliers?

For a small technology environment, answering those questions might be relatively straightforward. Across a large enterprise with years of accumulated infrastructure and software dependencies, it can be considerably harder.

That discovery work has value regardless of when quantum computing reaches the point that concerns cryptographers. An organisation that understands its cryptographic dependencies is better prepared to respond when standards change, algorithms are retired or vulnerabilities emerge. Post-quantum cryptography is exposing a broader resilience issue: organisations need to become better at changing cryptography.

New standards still face real-world deployment challenges

We have already passed an important milestone. Post-quantum algorithms have moved beyond academic research into published standards and real implementations. OpenSSL Library 3.5, for example, introduced support for the NIST-standardised ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA algorithms. That is significant, but publishing and implementing standards does not mean the transition is finished.

The mathematics behind post-quantum cryptography is different from the mathematics underpinning established approaches such as RSA and elliptic curve cryptography. Those differences create practical engineering considerations.

Signature sizes are one example. An algorithm might offer the security properties cryptographers are looking for, but if using it dramatically increases the amount of data that needs to move through an existing protocol, that matters.

Performance matters too. So does interoperability with systems that will not all migrate at exactly the same time. Security cannot exist only on paper. Cryptography has to work inside the infrastructure people actually use.

Why cryptographic scrutiny matters

There is still disagreement within the cryptographic community about aspects of the post-quantum transition. I don’t think organisations should be surprised by that.

Cryptographers challenge assumptions. They examine standards closely and look for weaknesses. When technology may eventually protect enormous amounts of sensitive information, scrutiny is healthy.

One of the practical questions is whether organisations should move entirely to new post-quantum algorithms or combine them with established classical cryptography.

Hybrid approaches allow both to be used together. For organisations that want the protection offered by a new post-quantum approach without relying on it alone, that can be an attractive option during the transition. Different organisations will make different decisions.

OpenSSL’s approach is not to pick favourites between published national or international standards. We implement standards and give users choices. That allows organisations to evaluate their own circumstances rather than being forced into a single answer.

Today’s encrypted data could become tomorrow’s exposure

There is another reason some organisations may need to think about migration sooner than others. Sensitive information does not stop being valuable simply because it is encrypted today.

An attacker can collect encrypted information now and retain it. If technology capable of defeating the cryptography protecting that information becomes available later, data that still has value could become exposed.

The significance of that risk depends heavily on the information involved. Data that becomes irrelevant after a few hours is very different from government, healthcare or commercial information that may need to remain confidential for decades.

This is why a universal migration date isn’t particularly useful. Organisations need to understand their own information, infrastructure and risk.

Building systems that can adapt

If post-quantum migration teaches us anything, I hope it is that changing cryptography should not be an extraordinary event. Algorithms will change again, and the technologies we trust today will eventually be replaced.

Organisations therefore need the ability to identify where cryptography is used and change it without rebuilding enormous parts of their infrastructure every time. That is cryptographic agility, and it may ultimately be one of the most valuable outcomes of the post-quantum transition.

The organisations best prepared for the quantum era won’t necessarily be those that rushed to deploy a particular algorithm first. They will be the ones that understood their dependencies, tested new approaches carefully and built systems capable of adapting as the technology develops.

The next challenge is putting post-quantum security into practice

With standards and implementations now available, the difficult questions are increasingly about deployment. How will new algorithms perform within existing infrastructure? Which systems should organisations prioritise? And how can they make changes without creating more technical debt?

Those questions require input from more than cryptographers. Developers need to understand the challenges facing security teams, while researchers need to hear from those implementing new approaches. Organisations also need to understand what these standards mean for the technology they already depend on.

Events such as this year’s OpenSSL Conference in Prague provided an opportunity to bring these different perspectives together. But the conversation is far from over. As the focus moves from developing standards to applying them to real-world environments, new questions and challenges will emerge. These discussions will remain important well beyond the conference itself.

We still cannot say when a quantum computer capable of breaking today’s cryptography will arrive. But organisations do not need that answer to start preparing. They can begin by understanding their systems and building the ability to change them when necessary.

Quantum computing still has an uncertain timetable. The preparation work is concrete, and it can start now.

items.title: How Online Maps Lay Bare the US Military Bases Targeted by Iran
items.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . Become a member and support our work here . In September, CBS News obtained new images of the aftermath of attacks on US bases in the Middle East from active service members. One told the news channel : “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face,” they added. While reports have detailed how Iran used Russian intelligence , including satellite imagery , to identify US troops, ships and aircraft, Bellingcat found that publicly available mapping platforms also reveal detailed and potentially sensitive information about US military bases in the Middle East. Google Maps and other online mapping services contain dozens of labels identifying facilities including headquarters, accommodation, gyms and fuel points. Publicly available photographs and videos, including material published by the US military, provide further details about how these facilities are used. Experts told Bellingcat that such information could have helped inform Iranian targeting decisions by revealing where personnel gather and how bases operate. However, they cautioned that Iran would also have had access to other sources of intelligence. Reporting from Reuters earlier this year also highlighted how US officials believed commercially available location data was being used to target US troops in war zones. The bases examined by Bellingcat are not secret and have operated for years in a region where US forces maintained a strong sense of security. Joseph Jarnecki, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute , said the US had been able to maintain aerial superiority and was understood to have significant air defence capabilities, but that Iran’s missile and drone campaign has undermined both assumptions. Iranian strikes have damaged at least 20 US military sites across Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Jordan, Kuwait, Iraq and Saudi Arabia since the conflict began in February this year. Governments can request that Google blur or remove sensitive information from its services and Google publishes data on government requests for content removal. Bellingcat contacted the US Department of Defense who asked us to reach out to CENTCOM about the details in this story. We also contacted Google. However, we did not receive responses to questions from these respondents before publication. We examined four of the largest and most heavily affected US military installations by Iran’s missile and drone campaign: Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait, Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar. At each one, we found publicly available Google Maps information providing details about facilities inside the bases and how they are used. A map detailing four US bases that were attacked by Iran during 2026 conflict. Camp Buehring At Camp Buehring in Kuwait, Google Maps identifies what is labelled as the main headquarters building, as well as a gym and a self-help facility, all of which were among locations destroyed by recent Iranian strikes. In addition to Google Maps place markers there are dozens of reviews and user-uploaded photographs. Left: Screengrab showing “Camp Beuhring Main HQ, Bldg. 100” Google Maps label. Right: Same building seen destroyed on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency. Bellingcat verified that this was a headquarters building by matching the flagpoles and layout in a photo published by the US military’s Defense Visual Information Distribution Service (DVIDS) showing soldiers posing in front of the building to the Google Maps satellite image. Geolocation diagram using dvids photo to verify Google Maps Buehring main headquarters location, confirming the accuracy of the Google Maps place marker. We also identified details about one of the camp’s gyms, including the building’s layout and roof structure, as well as Google reviews that indicate when it is busiest. Left: Google Maps label showing “Camp Beuhring Gym” Right: Destroyed gym building on satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on 6 April 2026. Among the images published by CBS News in September was that of a heavily damaged tent-like structure with smoke rising from it. Bellingcat matched the location of this image to the above satellite imagery, verifying that it shows the gym building pinned on Google Maps. Exclusive images released showing damage to E-3 Sentry AWACS aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, plus damage to US military camps Arifjan and Buehring in Kuwait from Iranian strikes. Images sent to CBS by active US military personnel. (IRIB News) https://t.co/1urA44f4xz — Middle East Observer (@ME_Observer_) September 15, 2026 Left: Google Maps shows images of the gym’s interior and exterior. Right: Google Maps reviews indicate when the gym is busy (names blurred by Bellingcat). A building labeled on Google as “DPW Self-Help Center” was also destroyed at Camp Buehring. Its Google Maps listing includes opening hours, and a photo posted by a Master Sergeant in 2017 labeled “ My office in Kuwait ” shows the interior of an office. Some of the notices on the walls inside the office are legible, including what appears to be a floor plan. Left: Google maps “DPW Self-Help Center” listing. Right: Same building seen destroyed on a satellite image published by Iran’s Tasnim news agency on April 6, 2026. A Google Maps placemark labelled “ Transient Tent ” identifies a large accommodation area, while another review includes a ground-level photograph of one of the tents. The dining facility can also be seen from the inside, including information regarding meal times . Left: Google image that appears to show an accommodation area. Right: Photos of the dining facility, including information on meal times (names blurred by Bellingcat). William Goodhind of Contested Ground , a visual forensics consultancy that uses OSINT and satellite imagery to analyse military sites, said the information available on Google Maps could reveal “the camp’s layout, the division between secure and non-secure areas, confirms likely accommodation areas, and shows day/time periods of low and high activity.” Camp Arifjan A satellite image of Kuwait’s Camp Arifjan, captured by Planet on March 4, 2026 and published by the The Washington Post , shows damage to numerous structures at the base. Bellingcat compared the image with publicly available mapping data to identify two damaged facilities. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Media Trending (@tmctrending) A Google Maps listing for a lodging facility labelled “ TPE FOR ARIFJAN ” includes a soldier’s review discussing room reservations, accommodation shortages and cleaning schedules, indicating that the building was used for military housing. Although Google’s satellite imagery of the base is blurred, the facility is visible in unblurred Bing Maps imagery using coordinates obtained from its Google Maps listing. The satellite image published by The Washington Post shows heavy damage to the facility. Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review (name blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Unblurred Bing maps satellite image showing the same location. A “ 24hr Fuel Point ” tagged on Google Maps is also blurred, but when the coordinates are copied and pasted into Bing Maps a clear satellite image of the fuel station appears. This facility is also seen destroyed on the satellite imagery published by The Washington Post . Left and centre: Blurred Google Maps satellite image with Google review. Right: Unblurred Bing Maps satellite image. Bellingcat contacted Microsoft to ask why the facility was not blurred out in the Bing Maps service. A spokesperson said: “When an entity requests removal from visibility on Bing Maps, we work through our process and act accordingly.” Muwaffaq Salti Air Base Three US service members were killed in Iranian ballistic missile strikes on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan on July 17, 2026. The strikes appear to have caused extensive damage to a barracks in the north of the base, with satellite imagery released by Iran showing at least 20 structures destroyed. Less than 40 metres from the nearest destroyed structure, and within the same living quarters area, Google Maps reveals the location of an “ Airman’s Attic ”. These are volunteer-run thrift shops for US Air Force personnel. A five-star review posted last year by a soldier includes a ground-level image of the facility, showing uniform drop-off points and fortifications along the perimeter. The listing provides information about the area’s use, while photographs of the shop’s exterior make it possible to match the satellite imagery to the location on the ground. A Sky News investigation also found that 80 percent of the runs shared publicly on the sporting app Strava at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base during the April ceasefire started or finished in this northern barracks. Satellite image showing damage, highlighted in red, published by Iran’s Fars News Agency. Less than 100 meters from the destroyed area, “ LSA DFAC ” is pinned on Google maps. “DFAC” is the standard US military acronym for “dining facility”, according to Stars and Stripes . Several Google reviews also discuss the steak being served in this location. Left: Google reviews for the dining facility (names blurred by Bellingcat). Right: Google Earth satellite image with the Airman’s Attic and dining facility visible in the area targeted by Iran. Al Udeid Air Base Similar mapping information is available for Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the largest US military installation in the Middle East. The base appears unblurred on Google Maps and entries on the platform identify the functions of numerous buildings. These include lodging facilities , which videos and reviews indicate are used by US Air Force crews and show the interior layout of the facility. Google reviews for “Al Udeid Lodging” indicate the presence of US Air Force crews (names blurred by Bellingcat). Meanwhile, Russia’s Yandex Maps details the site of two cinemas, a bar and a school on the base. This appears to match information provided on Google Maps. While Al Udeid Air Base was damaged during Iranian attacks earlier this year, the areas that were struck do not appear to be among those listed on Google. Business Insider reported that a geodesic dome that housed secure communications equipment was hit in the strikes. ABC News detailed how another building had been damaged near the centre of the base. Google Maps shows a large warehouse-like structure at the location where ABC News reported this strike. A New Reality in the Middle East Former US Air Force targeting specialist Wes J. Bryant said the problem facing US bases in the Middle East reflected a broader assumption within the military that bases in allied countries were safe from serious attack. He said the belief that these were rear-area bases where “nothing’s going to happen out here” was a fundamental miscalculation, and that the Google Maps issue was an example of the military failing to account for that vulnerability. Matthew Savill, Director of Military Sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, said Western militaries do not have consistent policies governing what information can be publicly posted about sensitive sites. He said the issue needs to be considered before a conflict begins, rather than when attacks are already underway. “The start point should be, can we enforce operational security discipline?” Savill pointed to restrictions already in place at some UK military facilities, including Faslane, a naval base that houses the UK’s nuclear submarines, where he said personnel are not permitted to use mobile phones on site. Savill told Bellingcat that the different pieces of data available on Google Maps, even if outdated, provided a “pattern of life” about US bases in the Middle East. But he added that the use of Google to help with the military targeting of Western bases is not new, saying he encountered the issue while deployed to Iraq more than 20 years ago. “When I was in Iraq, we knew for a fact that insurgents and militants had been using commercial imagery, including Google Earth, to try and map our bases,” he said. “We have known for more than 20 years that there is a vulnerability that if you don’t stop the collection and layering of data early on, that your bases can be heavily mapped.” The use of open-source information to support military targeting has been documented in Ukraine. In 2022, Foreign Policy detailed how Ukrainian private intelligence company Molfar used photographs of Russian soldiers published by Russian media alongside Google Earth satellite imagery to identify their location. Molfar passed its findings to Ukrainian intelligence, and the site was subsequently struck by the Ukrainian military. The security risks of publicly mapping military installations were recognised by the US military in 2008, when the Pentagon banned Google’s Street View from documenting the interiors of its bases. Since the Iran war started, US military commanders have also warned service members about posting photographs and videos from bases after Iranian attacks, cautioning that such footage could help Iran assess the effects of its strikes. Iranian attacks have forced US personnel to evacuate many additional locations that were deemed too vulnerable to further strikes. In total, 23 US service members have been killed and 865 wounded in the US-Iran war, according to the Pentagon . Bellingcat’s Jake Godin, Charlotte Maher and Merel Zoet contributed to this report. items.title: GhostMap: The Android flaw that crashes your phone before you open the app
items.summary: Bitdefender Labs researchers found that installing a specially crafted app can leave an Android phone stuck in a crash loop, even if you never open it or grant it a single permission. The app contains no code and never needs to run.
